children.name: Stylommatophora
Polygyridae
Neohelix
children.description: Whitelips are medium-sized land snails known for their distinctive white or pale lip around the opening of their shells. These terrestrial mollusks are commonly found in wooded areas throughout New England, where they feed on decaying plant matter and fungi on the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic white or whitish lip (peristome) around the shell opening sets whitelips apart from other land snails in the region. Their shells are typically brown with a somewhat flattened, globe-like shape.
children.funFact: Whitelip snails are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, but they still need to mate with another snail to reproduce.

children.name: Triodopsis
children.description: Threeteeth are small to medium-sized land snails that get their name from the three distinctive tooth-like projections found inside their shell opening. These terrestrial mollusks are commonly found in woodland habitats throughout eastern North America, where they feed on decaying plant matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The three prominent teeth (called lamellae) located in the aperture of their shells are the key identifying feature that separates them from other land snails. Their shells are typically brown and have a somewhat flattened, disc-like shape.
children.funFact: These snails are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, but they still need to mate with another snail to reproduce.

children.name: Euchemotrema
children.description: Pillsnails are small terrestrial snails that get their name from their ability to withdraw completely into their shells and seal the opening, resembling tiny pills. These land snails have compact, rounded shells and are found in forest habitats throughout eastern North America. They are part of the larger family of land snails that breathe air rather than living in water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pillsnails are distinguished from other land snails by their very rounded, globe-like shells and their unique ability to completely seal themselves inside using a temporary door called an epiphragm.
children.funFact: When threatened or during dry conditions, pillsnails can create a temporary limestone door to seal their shell opening, allowing them to survive for weeks without food or water in a state similar to hibernation.

children.name: Stenotrema
children.description: Slitmouths are small to medium-sized land snails that get their name from the distinctive narrow, slit-like opening in their shells. These terrestrial mollusks are native to eastern North America and live in forest leaf litter and under logs where they feed on decaying plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining characteristic of slitmouths is their shell's aperture (opening), which is constricted into a narrow slit by internal ridges or teeth, quite different from the round or oval openings of most other land snails.
children.funFact: The Hairy Slitmouth gets its name from the tiny hairs that cover its shell surface, making it feel fuzzy to the touch - an unusual texture for a snail shell.

children.description: Polygyridae is a family of terrestrial snails that are commonly found throughout New England's forests and woodlands. These land snails are characterized by their relatively small to medium-sized shells and their preference for moist, leaf-littered environments where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically have shells with distinctive tooth-like structures or ridges inside the shell opening, which is reflected in names like 'Threeteeth' and 'Slitmouths.' Their shells are often brown or amber-colored with intricate sculptural patterns.
children.funFact: Many Polygyridae snails can live for several years and hibernate underground during winter, emerging in spring to continue their slow-paced lives as nature's recyclers in the forest ecosystem.

children.name: Arionidae
Arion
children.description: Arion slugs are a group of terrestrial gastropods that lack external shells and are common throughout New England's gardens, forests, and other moist habitats. These soft-bodied mollusks are characterized by their slimy mucus trails and their ability to contract into a rounded shape when threatened. They play important ecological roles as decomposers, feeding on decaying plant matter, fungi, and organic debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arion slugs can be distinguished from other slug groups by their breathing pore (pneumostome) located in the rear half of their mantle shield, and their ability to contract into a distinctive hemispherical ball when disturbed.
children.funFact: Many Arion slugs can live for 2-3 years and are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, though they still need to mate with another slug to reproduce.

children.description: Roundback slugs are terrestrial mollusks that have lost their external shells through evolution, leaving them with soft, elongated bodies. They are characterized by their distinctive rounded or arched back profile, which gives the family its common name. These slugs are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other slug families, roundback slugs have their breathing pore (pneumostome) located in the rear half of the mantle shield rather than the front. They also typically have a more pronounced, dome-like mantle that covers much of their back.
children.funFact: Many roundback slugs can actually retract their tentacles completely into their head when threatened, unlike some other slug families whose tentacles can only be partially withdrawn.

children.name: Gastrodontidae
Zonitoides
children.description: Gloss snails are tiny terrestrial snails that get their name from their distinctively shiny, polished-looking shells. These minute creatures are typically less than 6mm across and live in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist forest floor habitats throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other small land snails, gloss snails have exceptionally smooth, glossy shells that appear almost glass-like. Their shells are also notably flattened and disc-shaped rather than tall and conical.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, gloss snails are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping to break down dead plant material and recycle nutrients back into the soil.

children.name: Glyphyalinia
children.description: Glyphyalinia are tiny, delicate land snails with beautifully sculpted, translucent shells that look almost glass-like. These miniature mollusks are often called 'glyph snails' because their shells feature intricate carved patterns and ridges. They're found in moist woodland habitats where they feed on decaying organic matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These snails are distinguished by their remarkably thin, almost transparent shells with distinctive sculptured surfaces that create intricate patterns. Unlike many other small land snails, Glyphyalinia have notably flattened, disc-like shells with sharp, delicate edges.
children.funFact: Despite being so small you could fit several on your fingernail, these snails are accomplished climbers and can often be found scaling tree trunks and rocks in search of microscopic fungi to eat.

children.name: Perpolita
children.description: Perpolita is a genus of tiny land snails known for their remarkably transparent, glass-like shells that allow you to see right through them. These delicate snails are so small they can easily fit on your fingernail, and they live quietly among leaf litter and moss in forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Perpolita apart from other small snails is their exceptionally clear, amber-tinted shells that are almost perfectly transparent, earning them the common name 'glass snails.'
children.funFact: These snails are so translucent that you can actually watch their internal organs working through their shell walls!

children.name: Ventridens
children.description: Dome Snails are a genus of tiny land snails that get their name from their distinctive dome-shaped shells. These small terrestrial mollusks are part of the larger family of glass snails and are known for their delicate, translucent shells that often have a glossy appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dome Snails can be identified by their characteristic dome-like shell shape that is higher and more rounded than many other small land snails. Their shells are typically thin, somewhat transparent, and have a distinctive sculptured surface with fine ridges.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size (usually less than 5mm across), Dome Snails play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose leaf litter and organic matter on the forest floor.

children.description: Gastrodontidae is a family of small, delicate land snails that are commonly found in moist woodland habitats throughout New England. These snails are characterized by their thin, translucent shells that often have a glossy or glassy appearance, earning some members the common name "gloss snails." They typically feed on decaying organic matter, fungi, and microscopic organisms in leaf litter and soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be distinguished from other land snails by their extremely thin, fragile shells that are often semi-transparent and highly polished. Many species also have distinctive dome-shaped or flattened shells with fine spiral ridges.
children.funFact: Some Gastrodontidae snails are so small and have such transparent shells that you can actually see their internal organs through the shell wall when they're alive!

children.name: Helicidae
Cepaea
children.description: Cepaea is a genus of colorful land snails that are among the most recognizable terrestrial mollusks in New England. These medium-sized snails are known for their beautifully banded shells that come in various colors including yellow, pink, and brown. Both species in this genus are actually European natives that have become well-established in North American gardens and natural areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cepaea snails are distinguished from other land snails by their glossy, globular shells with distinctive dark bands and their prominent lip coloration - either brown or white - which gives each species its common name.
children.funFact: The shell color and banding patterns in Cepaea snails are determined by genetics and have been extensively studied by scientists as a classic example of natural selection, with different patterns providing camouflage in different habitats.

children.name: Cornu
children.description: Cornu is a genus of large land snails that are native to the Mediterranean region but have spread worldwide through human activity. These terrestrial gastropods are characterized by their robust, spiral shells and are well-adapted to living in gardens, agricultural areas, and urban environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cornu are distinguished from other land snails by their relatively large size, thick-walled shells with distinctive banding patterns, and their preference for calcium-rich environments that help maintain their substantial shells.
children.funFact: The Garden Snail can live up to 10 years and has both male and female reproductive organs, allowing any two snails to mate and both produce offspring.

children.name: Otala
children.description: Otala is a genus of medium to large terrestrial snails that are native to the Mediterranean region. These land snails are characterized by their robust, globular shells and are well-adapted to dry, rocky environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Otala snails have distinctively thick, rounded shells with a wide opening and are typically larger than most other common land snails in the region.
children.funFact: The Milk Snail gets its name from its creamy white shell color and was historically eaten as a delicacy in Mediterranean countries, leading to its accidental introduction to New England.

children.name: Helix
children.description: Helix is a genus of large, air-breathing land snails that are among the most well-known terrestrial gastropods in the world. These snails are characterized by their substantial size, robust spiral shells, and ability to survive in various terrestrial habitats from gardens to woodlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Helix snails are distinguished by their relatively large size compared to other land snails, with shells that can reach several inches in diameter, and their thick, sturdy shells with distinctive spiral patterns.
children.funFact: The most famous member of this genus is the Roman snail (Helix pomatia), which has been considered a delicacy in European cuisine for over 2,000 years and was actually farmed by the ancient Romans.

children.description: Helix snails are medium to large-sized land snails that carry distinctive spiral shells on their backs. These terrestrial gastropods are commonly found in gardens, woodlands, and other moist habitats where they feed on plants, fungi, and decaying organic matter. They're known for their ability to seal themselves into their shells during dry or cold periods to survive harsh conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Helix snails are distinguished by their relatively large, robust shells with well-developed spiral coiling and typically have a rounded aperture. Unlike many other land snail families, they often display colorful banding patterns on their shells and can retract completely into their shells, sealing the opening with a mucus barrier.
children.funFact: Many helix snails are actually non-native species that were introduced to New England, either accidentally through trade or intentionally by European settlers who brought familiar garden snails with them to the New World.

children.name: Philomycidae
Philomycus
children.description: Philomycus is a genus of terrestrial slugs known as mantleslugs, named for their distinctive large mantle that covers much of their back. These are relatively large, native North American slugs that lack the external shell found in snails, instead having only a small internal shell plate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mantleslugs are distinguished from other slug groups by their prominent mantle that extends well beyond the head region, giving them a distinctive cape-like appearance. They also have a characteristic breathing pore (pneumostome) located on the right side of their mantle.
children.funFact: Despite being slugs, mantleslugs are surprisingly fast movers and can actually contract their bodies to 'jump' short distances when threatened, which is unusual behavior among terrestrial gastropods.

children.name: Pallifera
children.description: Pallifera is a genus of small, terrestrial slugs known as mantleslugs that live in forest leaf litter and under logs throughout New England. These soft-bodied mollusks lack external shells and have a distinctive mantle (the fleshy covering over their back) that helps protect their internal organs. They play an important role in forest ecosystems by breaking down decaying plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mantleslugs can be identified by their prominent mantle that covers much of their back, giving them their common name. Unlike many other slug groups, Pallifera species tend to be smaller and have a more elongated body shape with a relatively large mantle-to-body ratio.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'mantleslugs,' these creatures are actually more closely related to snails than to the common garden slugs most people know - they're essentially snails that have lost their external shells over evolutionary time.

children.name: Megapallifera
children.description: Megapallifera is a genus of terrestrial slugs known for their distinctive large mantle that covers much of their body. These slugs are part of the family Philomycidae and are characterized by their ability to change color and appearance based on their environment and activity level.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their exceptionally large mantle (the fleshy covering) that extends well beyond the typical slug proportions, giving them their 'mega mantle' name.
children.funFact: The Changeable Mantleslug can dramatically alter its coloration from pale gray to dark brown or even reddish hues, making it a master of disguise in the forest floor.

children.description: Mantleslugs are terrestrial slugs that get their name from their distinctive mantle - a fleshy, cape-like covering that extends over much of their body. Unlike many other slugs, they lack an external shell and have their breathing pore located toward the back of the mantle rather than on the side.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mantleslugs can be identified by their mantle covering most of their back and their posterior breathing pore position. They also tend to be more elongated and less slimy than many other slug families.
children.funFact: When threatened, mantleslugs can contract their entire body under their protective mantle, making them look like a small, featureless blob on the forest floor.

children.name: Limacidae
Limax
children.description: Limax is a genus of large, air-breathing land slugs that are native to Europe but have been introduced to many parts of North America. These slugs are shell-less gastropods that breathe through a lung-like cavity and move by gliding on a trail of mucus they secrete.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Limax slugs are typically larger than most other slug genera and have a distinctive breathing pore (pneumostome) located on the right side of their body. They also have a unique internal shell remnant called a limacella.
children.funFact: The Leopard Slug in this genus can stretch to nearly 8 inches long and performs an elaborate aerial mating dance, suspended from a strand of mucus!

children.name: Lehmannia
children.description: Banded Garden Slugs are medium-sized terrestrial slugs that are commonly found in gardens, parks, and other human-modified environments. They are characterized by their distinctive banded or striped patterns along their bodies, which help distinguish them from other slug species. These slugs are primarily active at night and feed on decaying plant matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key identifying feature of Lehmannia slugs is their prominent pale stripe or band running down the center of their back, often accompanied by darker stripes on either side. Unlike many other garden slugs, they tend to be more elongated and can often be found climbing on trees and vertical surfaces.
children.funFact: The Tree Slug (Lehmannia marginata) is an excellent climber and is often found high up on tree trunks and walls, earning it the nickname 'tree slug' despite being a terrestrial mollusk.

children.name: Ambigolimax
children.description: Threeband slugs are small, soft-bodied mollusks that get their name from the distinctive three dark stripes or bands that run along their backs. These terrestrial gastropods lack external shells and move by gliding on a trail of mucus they secrete from their undersides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The three parallel dark bands running lengthwise along their pale bodies make these slugs easily recognizable among New England's slug species. They are typically smaller and more slender than many other common garden slugs.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'greenhouse slugs,' these adaptable creatures can survive outdoors year-round in New England by hibernating under logs, rocks, or leaf litter during winter months.

children.name: Limacus
children.description: Cellar slugs are medium to large terrestrial gastropods that have adapted to living in human-made environments like basements, cellars, and other damp indoor spaces. These slugs are typically nocturnal and feed on organic matter, fungi, and sometimes other slugs. They are characterized by their ability to thrive in the cool, moist conditions found in underground or semi-underground human habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cellar slugs can be distinguished from other slug genera by their relatively large size, distinctive coloration patterns, and their strong preference for anthropogenic (human-influenced) habitats over natural forest environments.
children.funFact: The Yellow Cellar Slug can live up to 3 years and has the remarkable ability to remember and return to the same hiding spots night after night, creating well-worn slime trails that act like highways in your basement!

children.description: Keelback slugs are a family of terrestrial gastropods that get their name from the prominent ridge or 'keel' that runs along the back of their body. These slugs are typically medium to large in size and are commonly found in gardens, forests, and other moist environments throughout New England. They are herbivorous creatures that feed on decomposing plant matter, fungi, and sometimes fresh vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining characteristic of keelback slugs is the sharp ridge or keel that extends along their back, which is much more pronounced than in other slug families. They also tend to be larger and more elongated than many other common slug species.
children.funFact: Some keelback slugs can stretch to over 6 inches long when fully extended, making them among the largest slugs you might encounter in a New England garden!

children.name: Discidae
Discus
children.description: Disc snails are tiny terrestrial snails that get their name from their distinctive flattened, disc-like shells that look almost like miniature coins. These small mollusks live in leaf litter and under logs in forest environments, where they feed on decaying organic matter and microscopic fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their shells are notably flat and circular when viewed from above, much more compressed than typical snail shells. The shell opening is distinctively shaped and often has internal ridges or teeth that help identify different species.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 3-6 millimeters across, disc snails can live for several years and are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, helping to break down fallen leaves into soil nutrients.

children.name: Gonyodiscus
children.description: Gonyodiscus is a genus of tiny terrestrial snails that live in leaf litter and soil in forested areas. These minuscule gastropods are part of the diverse world of land snails that help decompose organic matter on the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their very small, rounded shells with a distinctive coiled structure that gives them their name (which means 'angled disc').
children.funFact: These snails are so small that you could easily fit several on the tip of your pinky finger, yet they play an important role in recycling nutrients in forest ecosystems.

children.name: Anguispira
children.description: Tigersnails are medium-sized land snails known for their distinctive striped shell patterns that resemble tiger markings. These terrestrial mollusks are typically found in wooded areas where they feed on decaying plant matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tigersnails can be identified by their flattened, disc-shaped shells with characteristic alternating light and dark bands or stripes that spiral around the shell.
children.funFact: The Flamed Tigersnail gets its name from the flame-like pattern created by its alternating brown and yellow stripes, which helps it blend in perfectly with fallen leaves on the forest floor.

children.description: Discidae is a family of small to medium-sized land snails that includes some of New England's most distinctive terrestrial mollusks. These snails are characterized by their flattened, disc-like shells that often have intricate sculptural patterns on their surfaces. They are typically found in moist woodland environments, hiding under logs, leaves, and rocks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be distinguished by their relatively flat, coiled shells that resemble tiny discs when viewed from above. Unlike many other land snails, Discidae species often have prominent ridges, ribs, or hair-like projections on their shell surfaces.
children.funFact: The tigersnails in this family get their name from the bold, zigzag stripes that pattern their shells, making them some of the most beautifully marked snails in New England's forests.

children.name: Vertiginidae
Vertigo
children.description: Vertigo snails are tiny land snails that are so small they're often overlooked, with most species measuring less than 3 millimeters across. These miniature mollusks live in moist soil, leaf litter, and mossy areas where they feed on decaying organic matter and microscopic fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Vertigo snails have distinctive spiral shells that are typically barrel-shaped or cylindrical, and many species have small tooth-like projections inside their shell opening that help identify different species.
children.funFact: These snails are so tiny that you could fit several of them on the head of a pin, yet they play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose organic matter.

children.description: Whorl snails are tiny land snails that get their name from their distinctively coiled, spiral shells that resemble miniature whorls or spinning tops. These minute mollusks are among the smallest snails you'll find in New England, with most species measuring less than 3 millimeters across. They live in moist environments like leaf litter, moss, and rotting logs where they feed on decaying organic matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Whorl snails can be identified by their extremely small size and tightly coiled, often barrel-shaped or cylindrical shells with multiple whorls. Unlike many other small land snails, their shells typically have a narrow opening and distinctive tooth-like projections inside the aperture.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, whorl snails are incredibly hardy and some species can survive being frozen solid during winter, essentially entering a state of suspended animation until spring arrives.

children.name: Agriolimacidae
Deroceras
children.description: Smooth Land Slugs are small, soft-bodied mollusks that glide along the ground on a trail of mucus. These shell-less gastropods are commonly found in gardens, fields, and moist areas throughout New England, where they feed on decaying plant matter and sometimes living vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike snails, these slugs have no external shell, and their smooth, streamlined bodies lack the prominent ridges or bumps found on many other slug groups. They can be identified by their relatively small size and the distinctive patterns on their mantles.
children.funFact: The Milky Slug gets its name from the milky-white mucus it produces when disturbed, which serves as a defense mechanism against predators.

children.description: Agriolimacidae is a family of small to medium-sized land slugs that have evolved to live entirely on land, unlike their aquatic ancestors. These slugs are characterized by their smooth, slimy bodies that help them glide across surfaces and retain moisture in terrestrial environments. They are herbivorous creatures that play important roles in decomposing organic matter and cycling nutrients through forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their smooth, relatively streamlined body shape and their ability to produce copious amounts of mucus for locomotion. Unlike some other slug families, they lack prominent ridges or tubercles on their skin surface.
children.funFact: These slugs can actually stretch their bodies to nearly three times their resting length when moving, allowing them to reach food sources and navigate obstacles that would otherwise be inaccessible.

children.name: Valloniidae
Vallonia
children.description: Grass-snails are tiny terrestrial snails that live in grassy areas, leaf litter, and mossy habitats throughout New England. These miniature mollusks have distinctively coiled, spiral shells that are typically whitish or pale brown in color. Despite their small size (usually less than 3mm across), they play important roles in decomposing organic matter in soil ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Vallonia snails are distinguished by their very small, tightly coiled shells with a characteristic depressed or flattened spiral shape. Their shells often have distinctive ridges or ribs running across the surface, which helps separate the different species within this genus.
children.funFact: These tiny snails are so small that you could fit several of them on your fingernail, yet they're found on multiple continents and are among the most widely distributed land snails in the world.

children.name: Zoogenetes
children.description: Zoogenetes is a genus of tiny land snails that are among the smallest gastropods found in terrestrial environments. These microscopic mollusks are part of the larger group of minute snails that live in leaf litter, moss, and soil where they feed on organic matter and microorganisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Zoogenetes are distinguished by their extremely small size and their tightly coiled, dome-shaped shells that often have distinctive ribbing or sculpturing patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Zoogenetes snails play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose organic matter in the soil.

children.description: Grass snails are tiny land snails that live in moist habitats like grasslands, leaf litter, and moss. These miniature mollusks have delicate, translucent shells that are usually less than 3mm across - so small you might mistake them for grains of sand! They feed on decaying plant matter and microscopic fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Grass snails can be identified by their extremely small size and thin, nearly transparent shells that are often pale white or yellowish. Their shells typically have a distinctive rounded, low-spired shape that sets them apart from other tiny land snails.
children.funFact: These snails are so small that dozens could fit on a penny, yet they play an important role in recycling nutrients in forest and grassland ecosystems.

children.name: Achatinidae
Subulina
children.description: Subulina is a genus of tiny land snails known as awlsnails, named for their distinctive elongated, needle-like shells that taper to a sharp point. These miniature gastropods are among the smallest snails you might encounter, with shells typically measuring less than 10 millimeters in length. They are primarily tropical and subtropical species that feed on decaying organic matter in soil and leaf litter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Subulina snails are distinguished by their extremely slender, cone-shaped shells that are much more elongated and pointed than typical land snails. Their shells are also notably smooth and glossy, lacking the pronounced ridges or decorative patterns found in many other small land snail genera.
children.funFact: The Miniature Awlsnail found in New England is actually a tropical species that has been accidentally introduced through the plant trade and can sometimes survive indoors in greenhouses or as a temporary outdoor resident in warm weather.

children.name: Rumina
children.description: Rumina is a genus of predatory land snails that are known for their unusual carnivorous diet. Unlike most snails that feed on plants, these snails actively hunt and consume other snails and their eggs. They are medium-sized terrestrial gastropods with elongated, cone-shaped shells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rumina snails are distinguished by their predatory behavior and their characteristic habit of 'decollating' or breaking off the tip of their shell as they grow. Their shells are typically smooth, glossy, and taper to a pointed spire.
children.funFact: The Decollate Snail gets its name from its unique growth pattern - it literally decapitates its own shell by breaking off the pointed tip as it matures, sealing the break with new shell material.

children.name: Lissachatina
children.description: Giant Agate Snails are large terrestrial snails originally from Africa that have distinctive cone-shaped shells with beautiful agate-like patterns. These snails are among the largest land snails in the world and are unfortunately considered invasive species when found outside their native range.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be distinguished from other land snails by their impressive size - often reaching 6-8 inches in length - and their distinctive pointed, cone-shaped shells with swirled brown and cream colored bands.
children.funFact: A single Giant Agate Snail can lay up to 1,200 eggs per year, which is why they're considered one of the world's most problematic invasive species when introduced to new environments.

children.description: Giant Land Snails are a family of terrestrial gastropods known for their impressive size, with some species growing shells over 8 inches long. These snails are typically found in tropical and subtropical regions, though a few smaller species have established populations in temperate areas like New England. They are herbivorous creatures that play important roles in their ecosystems as decomposers and soil aerators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other land snail families, Achatinidae members have distinctively large, elongated cone-shaped shells and can grow to remarkable sizes. They also have a unique reproductive system where they are hermaphroditic but typically require a partner to reproduce.
children.funFact: The Giant African Land Snail can live up to 10 years and has over 25,000 microscopic teeth on its feeding structure called a radula!

children.name: Succineidae
Novisuccinea
children.description: Novisuccinea is a genus of small, amber-colored land snails commonly known as ambersnails. These terrestrial gastropods have thin, translucent shells that give them their characteristic amber appearance. They are typically found in moist environments like wetlands, stream edges, and other areas with high humidity.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Novisuccinea snails are distinguished from other amber snail genera by their oval-shaped shells and specific anatomical features of their reproductive systems. Their shells are relatively thin and fragile compared to many other land snail groups.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'land snails,' ambersnails require very moist conditions to survive and are often found so close to water that they're sometimes mistaken for aquatic species.

children.name: Oxyloma
children.description: Oxyloma is a genus of small, air-breathing land snails known as ambersnails. These delicate gastropods have thin, translucent shells with an amber or yellowish color that gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oxyloma snails are distinguished by their oval-shaped shells that are wider at the bottom than the top, and their shells are notably thin and fragile compared to other land snails.
children.funFact: Despite being land snails, Oxyloma species prefer very moist environments and are often found near wetlands, making them important indicators of healthy aquatic ecosystems.

children.description: Amber snails are small terrestrial gastropods with thin, translucent shells that have a characteristic amber or yellowish color, giving them their common name. These tiny mollusks are commonly found in moist environments like wetlands, stream banks, and areas with high humidity where they feed on decaying plant matter and algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amber snails can be distinguished from other land snails by their notably thin, fragile shells that are often translucent with an amber tint, and their preference for very wet habitats rather than typical terrestrial environments.
children.funFact: Despite being land snails, amber snails are so dependent on moisture that they're often found partially submerged in water or on wet mud, making them some of the most aquatic-adapted terrestrial gastropods.

children.name: Oxychilidae
Oxychilus
children.description: Typical Glass Snails are small land snails with thin, translucent shells that you can almost see through, giving them their 'glass' name. They are tiny creatures, usually less than half an inch across, that live in moist places like under logs, leaf litter, and garden debris. These snails are active at night and feed on decaying plant matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their shells are distinctively clear and glossy, appearing almost crystal-like compared to the opaque shells of most other land snails. The shells also have a characteristic flattened, disc-like shape rather than being tall and cone-shaped.
children.funFact: The Garlic Snail gets its name because it releases a strong garlic-like smell when handled or disturbed, which may help protect it from predators.

children.description: Glass snails are small land snails known for their remarkably thin, translucent shells that you can often see through like glass. These tiny gastropods are typically less than half an inch across and prefer moist environments like leaf litter, under logs, or in garden soil. They are carnivorous or scavenging snails that feed on other small invertebrates, dead organic matter, and sometimes other snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their most distinctive feature is their extremely thin, glossy, and semi-transparent shell that gives them their 'glass' name. Unlike many other land snails, glass snails are primarily predatory rather than herbivorous.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, glass snails are actually fierce micro-predators that will hunt and consume other snails, including members of their own species!

children.name: Cochlicopidae
Cochlicopa
children.description: Pillars are a genus of very small land snails with elongated, cylindrical shells that resemble tiny pillars or towers. These minute gastropods are terrestrial mollusks that live in leaf litter and soil, feeding on decaying organic matter and microscopic fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pillar snails are distinguished by their distinctively tall, narrow shells that are much longer than they are wide, giving them a column-like appearance that sets them apart from rounder snail shells.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 5-6 millimeters long, Glossy Pillar snails are found across multiple continents and are considered one of the most widely distributed land snail species in the world.

children.description: Pillar snails are tiny terrestrial gastropods that get their name from their distinctive elongated, pillar-like shells. These small land snails are typically found in leaf litter, under logs, and in other moist terrestrial habitats where they feed on decaying organic matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their shells are characteristically tall and narrow with a pointed spire, giving them a distinctive pillar or column-like appearance that sets them apart from other small land snails. The shell opening is typically oval and relatively small compared to the overall shell height.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size (often less than 3mm tall), pillar snails can be surprisingly long-lived for such small creatures, with some species living for several years while slowly growing their tower-like shells.

children.name: Hygromiidae
Trochulus
children.description: Trochulus is a genus of small terrestrial snails that live in moist woodland habitats and leaf litter. These snails are characterized by their distinctive hairy or bristly shells, which help them blend into their forest floor environment. They are part of the larger family of air-breathing land snails that play important roles in decomposition and nutrient cycling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most notable feature of Trochulus snails is their shells covered in fine hairs or bristles, which distinguishes them from most other land snail genera that have smooth or ridged shells.
children.funFact: The hairs on their shells aren't just for show - they help trap moisture from the air, allowing these snails to stay hydrated in dry conditions and survive in habitats where smooth-shelled snails might struggle.

children.description: Leaf snails are small to medium-sized land snails that typically live in moist environments like leaf litter, under logs, and in forest debris. They are terrestrial gastropods with spiral shells and belong to a diverse family found across many parts of the world. These snails are important decomposers in forest ecosystems, feeding on decaying plant material and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Leaf snails can be distinguished from other land snail families by their relatively flattened, disc-like shells and their preference for living directly in leaf litter rather than on vegetation or in trees.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'leaf snails,' they don't actually eat living leaves - instead they feed on the bacteria and fungi that grow on decomposing plant matter, making them nature's tiny recyclers.

children.name: Strobilopsidae
Strobilops
children.description: Pinecone snails are tiny land snails that get their name from their distinctive shell shape, which resembles a miniature pinecone with raised ridges and spiral patterns. These microscopic mollusks are among the smallest snails you'll find in New England forests, typically measuring less than 3 millimeters across. They live in leaf litter and decaying wood, feeding on fungi and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other land snails, pinecone snails have shells with prominent raised ribs or ridges that create a textured, pinecone-like appearance. Their shells also have a unique labyrinthine pattern of internal walls and chambers that sets them apart from smooth-shelled relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that you could fit several on your fingernail, the Maze Pinecone snail has one of the most complex shell interiors of any North American land snail, with intricate internal walls that create a maze-like structure.

children.description: Strobilopsidae is a small family of tiny land snails known as pinecone snails due to their distinctive cone-shaped shells that resemble miniature pinecones. These microscopic mollusks are among the smallest terrestrial snails, typically measuring less than 3mm across. They live in leaf litter and forest floor debris where they feed on decaying organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pinecone snails are easily recognized by their unique sculptured shells with raised spiral ridges and distinctive cone-like shape. Unlike most other small land snails, their shells have a characteristic ribbed pattern that gives them their pinecone appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're often overlooked, pinecone snails are considered living fossils, with their basic shell design remaining virtually unchanged for millions of years.

children.name: Vitrinidae
Vitrina
children.description: Vitrina is a genus of tiny land snails known as glass snails because of their remarkably transparent, delicate shells. These diminutive mollusks are terrestrial gastropods that live in moist forest environments, feeding on decaying plant matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Glass snails are distinguished by their extremely thin, translucent shells that are so clear you can see the snail's body through them. Their shells are also notably fragile and have a distinctive glossy, almost glass-like appearance.
children.funFact: The shell of a Pellucid Glass-snail is so transparent that you can actually watch the snail's internal organs working through its see-through shell wall!

children.description: Glass snails are tiny terrestrial snails named for their remarkably thin, translucent shells that are so delicate they appear almost glass-like. These miniature mollusks are among the smallest land snails you'll encounter, typically measuring less than 5mm across. They live in moist forest environments where they feed on decaying organic matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Glass snails are easily recognized by their extremely thin, nearly transparent shells that often have a greenish or amber tint. Unlike most other land snails, their shells are so fragile and translucent that you can often see the snail's body through the shell wall.
children.funFact: The shells of glass snails are so incredibly thin that they can actually flex slightly without breaking, making them more resilient than you might expect despite their delicate appearance.

children.name: Euconulidae
Euconulus
children.description: Euconulus is a genus of tiny land snails known for their translucent, glass-like shells that are so clear you can see right through them. These minute gastropods are among the smallest snails you might encounter, with shells typically measuring less than 3 millimeters across. They live in moist soil and leaf litter where they feed on microscopic fungi and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size and remarkably transparent shells that have a distinctive glassy appearance. Their shells are typically low-spired and have a smooth, shiny surface that lacks the opacity found in most other land snails.
children.funFact: The Tawny Glass-snail's shell is so transparent that you can actually see the snail's internal organs through it, making it like a living window into gastropod anatomy.

children.description: Hive snails are tiny terrestrial snails that get their name from their distinctive shell shape, which resembles a small beehive or cone. These miniature mollusks are among the smallest land snails you'll encounter, typically measuring less than 3mm across. They live in leaf litter and soil, feeding on decaying organic matter and microscopic fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hive snails can be identified by their characteristic conical, beehive-shaped shells that are much taller than they are wide. Unlike many other small land snails, their shells have a distinctly pointed spire and relatively few whorls.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're often overlooked, hive snails play an important role as decomposers, helping to break down fallen leaves and recycle nutrients back into forest ecosystems.

children.name: Punctidae
Punctum
children.description: Punctum is a genus of tiny land snails that are among the smallest terrestrial mollusks in North America. These miniature gastropods have delicate, translucent shells that are so small they're often overlooked despite being relatively common in forest leaf litter and soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Punctum snails are characterized by their extremely small size (shells typically less than 2mm across) and their smooth, glossy, amber-colored shells with a distinctive low spire.
children.funFact: The Small Spot is so tiny that dozens of individuals could fit on a single penny, yet despite their minute size, they play an important role in forest ecosystems by helping to decompose organic matter.

children.description: Dot snails are tiny terrestrial snails that get their name from their minute size - they're so small they often look like little dots on the ground. These microscopic mollusks live in leaf litter, soil, and mossy areas where they feed on decomposing organic matter and fungi.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dot snails are distinguished by their extremely small size (usually less than 2mm across) and their translucent, yellowish-brown shells with very fine spiral ridges. Their shells are so small and delicate that they're easily overlooked without magnification.
children.funFact: Despite being smaller than a pinhead, dot snails play an important ecological role as decomposers, helping to break down dead plant material in forest ecosystems throughout New England.

children.name: Zachrysiidae
Zachrysia
children.description: Zachrysia is a genus of medium to large terrestrial snails native to the Caribbean region. These land snails are characterized by their robust, globular shells and are part of the family Zachrysiidae, which includes several tropical and subtropical species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Zachrysia can be distinguished by their thick, rounded shells with a relatively low spire and wide aperture. Their shells typically have a brown or amber coloration with darker banding patterns.
children.funFact: The Cuban Brown Snail was accidentally introduced to New England and can survive surprisingly cold winters by burrowing deep into soil and leaf litter to hibernate.

children.description: Zachrysiidae is a small family of land snails that includes medium to large-sized species with distinctively shaped shells. These terrestrial gastropods are primarily found in warmer regions, with only one species making its way to New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their relatively large, often colorful shells with distinctive spiral patterns and robust construction compared to many other land snail families.
children.funFact: The single New England representative of this tropical family likely arrived through human activity, as these snails are more commonly found in warmer climates like the Caribbean and southern United States.

children.description: Common Land Snails and Slugs are terrestrial mollusks that have adapted to life on land, breathing air through a lung-like structure instead of gills. They include both shelled snails and shell-less slugs that glide along on a muscular foot, leaving behind a trail of slime. These creatures are found in gardens, forests, and fields throughout New England, playing important roles as decomposers and food for other animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their aquatic relatives, these mollusks have two pairs of retractable tentacles with eyes at the tips of the longer pair, allowing them to see and smell their surroundings. They also possess a specialized breathing pore called a pneumostome that opens and closes to regulate air flow to their lung.
children.funFact: Many species in this group are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, though they still typically need to mate with another individual to reproduce.

children.name: Nudibranchia
Trinchesiidae
Tenellia
children.description: Tenellia is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs known as aeolids that live in New England's coastal waters. These soft-bodied marine creatures have finger-like projections called cerata covering their backs, which they use for both digestion and breathing. They are active predators that crawl along the seafloor and underwater surfaces hunting for their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tenellia species can be distinguished from other aeolid sea slugs by their relatively simple body structure and the arrangement of their cerata in distinct clusters or rows. Many species in this genus also display vibrant colors and patterns that help with identification.
children.funFact: Some Tenellia species can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and store them in the tips of their cerata to use as their own defense mechanism against predators.

children.description: Trinchesiidae is a family of small, colorful sea slugs known as aeolid nudibranchs. These marine gastropods are characterized by finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for both digestion and defense.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be distinguished from other aeolid nudibranchs by their specific cerata arrangement and the structure of their reproductive organs. They typically have relatively few, well-spaced cerata compared to some other aeolid families.
children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the cnidarians they eat and store them in the tips of their cerata, essentially borrowing their prey's weapons for their own protection.

children.name: Eubranchidae
Eubranchus
children.description: Eubranchus is a genus of tiny, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine waters. These soft-bodied creatures are characterized by their distinctive finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for breathing and digestion. They are small predators that feed primarily on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Eubranchus are distinguished by their club-shaped cerata (gill projections) that give them their common name of 'club-gilled nudibranchs.' Unlike some other nudibranch groups, their cerata are relatively simple in structure and arranged in distinct clusters along their backs.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny creatures often less than an inch long, Eubranchus nudibranchs can steal and use the stinging cells from their hydroid prey, incorporating them into their own cerata for defense against predators.

children.name: Eubranchulus
children.description: Eubranchulus is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs known as aeolid nudibranchs. These soft-bodied marine animals are characterized by numerous finger-like projections called cerata that cover their backs, which they use for both digestion and defense. They are specialized predators that feed primarily on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Eubranchulus are distinguished from other aeolid nudibranchs by their specific body proportions and the arrangement of their cerata. They typically have a more compact body form with densely packed cerata that give them a distinctly bushy appearance.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and store them in the tips of their cerata, effectively turning their predator's weapons into their own defense system.

children.description: Eubranchidae is a family of tiny, delicate sea slugs known as aeolid nudibranchs. These small marine creatures have soft, translucent bodies adorned with finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs. They are carnivorous mollusks that crawl along the seafloor and underwater surfaces in search of their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their relatively simple body structure and smooth, unbranched cerata arranged in distinct rows. Unlike some other aeolid families, their cerata lack complex branching patterns and tend to be more uniformly shaped.
children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs can actually steal and store stinging cells from the hydroids they eat, incorporating them into their own cerata as a defense mechanism against predators.

children.name: Onchidorididae
Onchidoris
children.description: Onchidoris is a genus of small, soft-bodied sea slugs called dorids that crawl along rocky surfaces in shallow coastal waters. These marine mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their ability to blend in with their surroundings and their specialized feeding habits for survival.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively smooth, oval-shaped bodies with a ring of feathery gills around their rear opening, and many species have small bumps or tubercles covering their back.
children.funFact: As their common name suggests, the barnacle-eating dorid has such a specialized diet that it feeds almost exclusively on barnacles, using its radula (a ribbon-like feeding organ) to scrape them off rocks.

children.name: Adalaria
children.description: Adalaria is a genus of small sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in cold marine waters. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on other defense mechanisms to survive in their ocean habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Adalaria are characterized by their tuberculate (bumpy) body surface and belong to the dorid group of nudibranchs, which have gills arranged in a circle around their rear end.
children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs can actually incorporate stinging cells from the hydroids they eat into their own skin for protection, essentially stealing weapons from their prey!

children.description: Onchidorididae are small sea slugs that belong to the nudibranch group, marine gastropods that have lost their shells through evolution. These colorful creatures crawl along rocky surfaces in shallow coastal waters, using their specialized feeding structures to scrape sponges and other organisms from rocks and seaweed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their flattened, oval-shaped bodies and distinctive gill plumes that can be retracted into pockets on their backs when threatened.
children.funFact: These sea slugs are often called 'dorid nudibranchs' and can regenerate their external gills if they're damaged by predators or rough waves.

children.name: Polyceridae
Palio
children.description: Palio is a genus of small, soft-bodied sea slugs called nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These delicate creatures are shell-less mollusks that crawl along the seafloor and underwater surfaces using their muscular foot.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Palio nudibranchs are characterized by having a distinctive rim or ridge around the back edge of their body, which gives them their common name of rim-backed nudibranchs.
children.funFact: Like many nudibranchs, Palio species can incorporate stinging cells from the jellyfish and hydroids they eat into their own tissues for protection against predators.

children.name: Polycerella
children.description: Polycerella is a genus of tiny sea slugs that are specialized predators of hydroids, small colonial animals that look like miniature sea anemones growing on rocks and seaweed. These delicate nudibranchs are extremely small, typically measuring only a few millimeters in length, and have translucent bodies that make them nearly invisible underwater. They belong to the diverse group of sea slugs known as nudibranchs, which are famous for their beauty and variety.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Polycerella sea slugs are distinguished by their extremely small size and their specialized diet of hydroids, along with their simple body plan that lacks the elaborate projections found on many other nudibranchs. They have a relatively smooth, elongated body with simple tentacle-like projections called cerata.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're easily overlooked, Polycerella sea slugs are such specialized hunters that they can completely strip a hydroid colony of its polyps, essentially 'mowing' their prey like an underwater lawn.

children.name: Thecacera
children.description: Thecacera is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their bright colors and specialized body structures for protection and survival.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Thecacera are characterized by their distinctive wing-like projections (called cerata) along their backs and their often vibrant coloration patterns that help them blend with their surroundings.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'winged' sea slugs, Thecacera species can't actually fly - their wing-like structures are used for respiration and digestion instead!

children.description: Polyceridae are a family of small, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their bright colors and specialized body structures for protection. They are carnivorous creatures that feed on various small marine organisms like hydroids, sponges, and other invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by having finger-like projections called cerata on their backs, along with distinctive head tentacles called rhinophores that help them detect chemicals in the water. Unlike some other nudibranch families, polycerid sea slugs often have relatively few but prominent cerata arranged in specific patterns.
children.funFact: Some polycerid sea slugs can steal stinging cells from their prey and incorporate them into their own body tissues for defense, essentially borrowing weapons from their food!

children.name: Dotidae
Doto
children.description: Doto is a genus of tiny, delicate sea slugs that are specialized predators of hydroids - small, plant-like marine animals that grow in colonies. These colorful nudibranchs are typically less than an inch long and crawl along the seafloor or on kelp and rocks where their hydroid prey grows. They're true marine snails that have lost their shells and developed external gills called cerata.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Doto sea slugs are distinguished by their club-shaped cerata (finger-like projections) that are arranged in rows along their back, often with distinctive knobby or tubercled surfaces. Unlike many other nudibranchs, their cerata don't contain branches of the digestive system.
children.funFact: Many Doto species are masters of camouflage, perfectly matching the color and texture of the specific hydroid species they feed on, making them nearly invisible to both predators and human observers.

children.description: Dotidae are tiny sea slugs that are specialized predators of hydroids, which are small colonial animals that look like underwater plants. These delicate nudibranchs have translucent bodies and distinctive finger-like projections called cerata on their backs that help them digest food and breathe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs, dotids have cerata that contain branches of their digestive system, and they lack the feathery gills that many nudibranchs possess. Their cerata are also notably club-shaped and often translucent, making their internal structures visible.
children.funFact: Some dotid sea slugs can actually steal and use the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat, incorporating them into their own cerata for protection against predators.

children.name: Dendronotidae
Dendronotus
children.description: Dendronotus is a genus of nudibranchs, which are soft-bodied sea slugs that have lost their shells through evolution. These marine creatures are characterized by their tree-like or branching projections called cerata that extend from their backs, giving them a bushy, plant-like appearance. They are carnivorous mollusks that crawl along the seafloor and rocky surfaces in cold ocean waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other nudibranchs, Dendronotus species have highly branched, tree-like cerata (finger-like projections) that are arranged in rows along their backs, resembling tiny underwater forests. Their cerata are more elaborate and bushy compared to the simpler projections found on most other nudibranch genera.
children.funFact: Despite looking like tiny underwater plants, Dendronotus nudibranchs are actually skilled predators that primarily hunt hydroids and other small marine organisms, using their radula (a ribbon-like feeding organ) to scrape food into their mouths.

children.description: Dendronotidae is a family of colorful sea slugs known as dendronotid nudibranchs. These soft-bodied marine creatures are characterized by their tree-like or branched projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for breathing and digestion. They are active predators that crawl along the seafloor and rocky surfaces in search of their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nudibranch families, dendronotids have highly branched, tree-like cerata that are often translucent and can be quite elaborate in their branching patterns. Their cerata contain extensions of the digestive system, allowing them to process food throughout their body.
children.funFact: Many dendronotid sea slugs are master mimics that can perfectly match the color and texture of the hydroids they feed on, making them nearly invisible to both predators and prey.

children.name: Coryphellidae
Coryphella
children.description: Coryphella is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs called nudibranchs that crawl along the ocean floor and rocky surfaces. These marine gastropods are characterized by their finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for both digestion and defense. They are carnivorous creatures that primarily feed on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Coryphella can be distinguished from other nudibranch genera by their distinctive arrangement of cerata in clusters or rows, and their relatively elongated body shape. Their cerata often have specialized tips that can store stinging cells stolen from their prey.
children.funFact: Coryphella nudibranchs are essentially solar-powered thieves - they steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata for protection against predators.

children.description: Coryphellidae is a family of small, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied creatures lack shells and instead have finger-like projections called cerata covering their backs, which they use for breathing and digestion. They are carnivorous predators that primarily feed on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their numerous slender, elongated cerata arranged in distinct rows or clusters on their backs. Unlike some other nudibranch families, Coryphellidae have cerata that contain extensions of their digestive system and often display vibrant colors and patterns.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata for defense, essentially borrowing weapons from their prey.

children.name: Goniodorididae
Ancula
children.description: Ancula is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs that belong to the nudibranch family. These marine gastropods are specialized predators that feed primarily on hydroids, using their radula (feeding organ) to scrape prey from surfaces. They are soft-bodied mollusks that have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on other defense mechanisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ancula sea slugs are characterized by their distinctive body shape with prominent humps or ridges along their back, and they typically have multiple pairs of projections called cerata. Unlike many other nudibranchs, they have a relatively smooth body surface and lack the elaborate branching structures found in some related groups.
children.funFact: Despite being shell-less, Ancula sea slugs can incorporate stinging cells from the hydroids they eat into their own tissues, essentially stealing their prey's defense system to protect themselves from predators.

children.name: Okenia
children.description: Okenia is a genus of tiny, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their small size and cryptic lifestyle for protection. They are specialized predators that typically feed on specific prey like bryozoans or other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Okenia species are characterized by their small size, distinctive body projections called cerata, and often vibrant coloration. They can be distinguished from other nudibranch genera by their specific body shape and the arrangement of their finger-like projections.
children.funFact: The New England species Okenia ascidicola gets its name from its close association with sea squirts (ascidians), often living and feeding on or near these filter-feeding animals.

children.description: Goniodorididae is a family of small, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their bright colors and specialized body structures for protection. They are carnivorous creatures that crawl along the seafloor and rocky surfaces using their muscular foot.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by having club-shaped or finger-like projections called cerata on their backs, and they typically have a distinctive pattern of gills arranged around their anus. Unlike some other nudibranch families, goniodoridids tend to have relatively simple, unbranched cerata.
children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs are specialist predators that often feed exclusively on specific types of bryozoans (moss animals), using their radula - a ribbon-like feeding organ covered in tiny teeth - to scrape their prey from hard surfaces.

children.name: Facelinidae
Facelina
children.description: Facelina is a genus of colorful sea slugs called nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied creatures lack shells and breathe through finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs. They are carnivorous predators that feed primarily on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Facelina nudibranchs are distinguished by their numerous club-shaped cerata arranged in distinct rows along their back, and their four oral tentacles near the mouth. Unlike some other nudibranch groups, they lack true gills and instead use their cerata for both breathing and digestion.
children.funFact: Facelina sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata for defense, essentially becoming armed with their prey's weapons.

children.name: Cratena
children.description: Cratena is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs called nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied creatures are shell-less mollusks that crawl along the seafloor and underwater surfaces using their muscular foot.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cratena nudibranchs are characterized by their distinctive finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for both digestion and respiration.
children.funFact: These remarkable sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata for defense against predators.

children.description: Facelinidae are a family of colorful sea slugs called nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on finger-like projections called cerata on their backs for protection and digestion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their elongated cerata arranged in clusters along their backs, and they typically have two pairs of tentacles on their heads for sensing their environment.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata, essentially weaponizing their digestive system for defense!

children.name: Aeolidiidae
Aeolidia
children.description: Aeolidia is a genus of nudibranchs, which are soft-bodied sea slugs that have lost their shells through evolution. These marine gastropods are characterized by their numerous finger-like projections called cerata that cover their backs, giving them a distinctive shaggy appearance. They are specialized predators that feed primarily on sea anemones.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aeolidia can be distinguished from other nudibranch genera by their extremely numerous, densely packed cerata that create a distinctive shag-carpet-like texture. Unlike many other nudibranchs, they lack obvious rhinophores (sensory tentacles) and have a relatively large, robust body.
children.funFact: Aeolidia nudibranchs can steal and use the stinging cells (nematocysts) from the sea anemones they eat, storing them in the tips of their cerata for their own defense.

children.description: Aeolidiidae is a family of sea slugs known as aeolid nudibranchs, which are soft-bodied marine gastropods that have lost their shells through evolution. These colorful creatures are characterized by numerous finger-like projections called cerata that cover their backs, which they use for both digestion and defense. They are active predators that crawl along the ocean floor and on rocky surfaces hunting for their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aeolidiids are distinguished from other nudibranch families by their numerous cerata arranged in rows or clusters, and their ability to store stinging cells from their cnidarian prey in specialized sacs at the tips of these projections.
children.funFact: These sea slugs are essentially solar-powered pirates - they steal stinging cells from the sea anemones and hydroids they eat, then store these weapons in their colorful back projections to use for their own defense.

children.name: Dorididae
Archidoris
children.description: Archidoris is a genus of sea slugs known as dorid nudibranchs, which are shell-less marine snails that crawl along the ocean floor. These soft-bodied creatures have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on chemical defenses and camouflage for protection. They are specialized predators that feed primarily on sponges using their rasping tongue called a radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Archidoris species are characterized by their tough, leathery skin covered in small bumps called tubercles, and their ability to retract their gills and sensory tentacles completely into their body when threatened. They typically have a flattened, oval shape and muted colors that help them blend in with the sponges they feed on.
children.funFact: When disturbed, sea lemons in the genus Archidoris can release a strong citrus-like smell, which is how they got their common name and serves as a chemical defense against predators.

children.description: Dorididae is a family of sea slugs known as dorid nudibranchs, which are shell-less marine snails that crawl along the ocean floor. These soft-bodied creatures have a distinctive ring of feathery gills around their rear end and feed primarily on sponges. They're part of the larger group of nudibranchs, which are among the most colorful and diverse sea slugs in the ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dorididae members have their gills arranged in a circular pattern around the anus at the rear of their body, and their body surface is typically smooth or covered in small bumps. Unlike some other nudibranchs, they don't have finger-like projections (cerata) on their backs.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can actually incorporate toxic compounds from the sponges they eat into their own tissues, making themselves poisonous to potential predators.

children.name: Acanthodorididae
Acanthodoris
children.description: Acanthodoris is a genus of sea slugs known as dorids, which are shell-less marine mollusks that crawl along the ocean floor. These soft-bodied creatures are characterized by their flattened, oval shape and the ring of feathery gills that surrounds their rear opening. They are specialized predators that feed primarily on sponges using their rasping tongue-like radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Acanthodoris are distinguished from other dorids by their densely packed, hair-like projections called caryophyllidia that cover their back, giving them a fuzzy or hairy appearance. This texture helps them blend in with the spongy surfaces where they live and feed.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'hairy,' the fuzzy projections on their backs are actually tiny finger-like extensions of their skin that help with respiration and camouflage among the sponges they eat.

children.description: Acanthodorididae is a family of sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on other defense mechanisms. They are characterized by their distinctive body structure with cerata (finger-like projections) or other specialized appendages on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their relatively simple body plan and the presence of rhinophores (sensory tentacles) that help them detect chemicals in the water. They typically have a more subdued coloration compared to many other nudibranch families.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can incorporate stinging cells from their prey into their own bodies for protection, essentially stealing weapons from other marine animals to defend themselves.

children.name: Tergipedidae
Tergipes
children.description: Tergipes is a genus of tiny sea slugs called nudibranchs that live in marine waters. These delicate creatures are carnivorous mollusks that have lost their shells through evolution and instead display colorful, finger-like projections called cerata on their backs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tergipes species are distinguished by their small size, translucent bodies, and distinctive club-shaped cerata that contain branches of their digestive system. They have two pairs of tentacles on their heads and typically feed on hydroids.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Johnston's balloon eolis can inflate parts of its body with water when threatened, making it appear larger to potential predators.

children.description: Tergipedidae is a family of small, delicate sea slugs known as aeolid nudibranchs. These marine gastropods are characterized by their numerous finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for both digestion and defense. They are active predators that feed primarily on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tergipedid sea slugs can be distinguished from other aeolid families by their relatively simple body structure and the arrangement of their cerata in distinct clusters or rows. Unlike some related groups, they typically have fewer, more organized cerata rather than dense, chaotic arrangements.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata, essentially borrowing their prey's weapons for their own defense against predators.

children.name: Cuthonellidae
Cuthonella
children.description: Cuthonella is a genus of small sea slugs called aeolids that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks are characterized by their finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for both digestion and defense.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cuthonella can be distinguished from other aeolid genera by their specific arrangement of cerata and the structure of their reproductive organs. They typically have a more compact body form compared to many of their relatives.
