children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the cnidarians they eat and store them in the tips of their cerata, essentially turning their prey's weapons into their own defense system.

children.description: Cuthonellidae is a small family of sea slugs known as nudibranchs, which are shell-less marine gastropods that crawl along the ocean floor. These colorful creatures have soft, elongated bodies and are distinguished by finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs. They are carnivorous animals that feed primarily on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have relatively few, thick cerata arranged in distinct rows along their backs, unlike other nudibranch families that may have numerous thin projections or different body arrangements.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can actually steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata for protection against predators.

children.name: Scyllaeidae
Scyllaea
children.description: Scyllaea is a genus of highly specialized sea slugs that have evolved to live exclusively among floating sargassum seaweed in the open ocean. These remarkable nudibranchs have flattened, leaf-like bodies with elaborate camouflage that perfectly mimics the brown algae they call home. They are true pelagic creatures, spending their entire lives drifting with sargassum mats far from shore.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most nudibranchs that crawl along the seafloor, Scyllaea species have compressed, laterally flattened bodies with wing-like extensions that allow them to cling to and move through floating seaweed. Their intricate camouflage patterns and coloration are specifically adapted to match sargassum algae rather than typical bottom-dwelling environments.
children.funFact: The Sargassum Nudibranch is so perfectly camouflaged that it's nearly impossible to spot among the seaweed - it even sways with the algae's movement to complete its disguise as a piece of sargassum!

children.description: Scyllaeidae is a small family of sea slugs that are perfectly adapted for life among floating seaweed in the open ocean. These remarkable nudibranchs have evolved to look almost exactly like the sargassum seaweed they live on, making them nearly invisible to both predators and prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have flattened, leaf-like body extensions called cerata that perfectly mimic seaweed fronds, and their coloration matches the golden-brown tones of floating sargassum.
children.funFact: These sea slugs are so well-camouflaged that they were among the last nudibranchs to be discovered by scientists, since they blend seamlessly with the seaweed mats they call home.

children.name: Flabellinidae
Carronella
children.description: Carronella is a small genus of sea slugs known as nudibranchs, which are shell-less marine mollusks that crawl along the ocean floor. These delicate creatures are specialized predators that feed on hydroids and other small marine organisms using their radula, a rasping feeding structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Carronella are characterized by their translucent bodies and distinctive red or orange-colored gills that give them their common name of red-gilled nudibranchs.
children.funFact: Despite being mollusks like clams and snails, nudibranchs in the genus Carronella have completely lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their translucent bodies for camouflage among the marine plants they inhabit.

children.description: Flabellinidae are a family of colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied creatures have finger-like projections called cerata covering their backs, which contain extensions of their digestive system and help with both digestion and respiration. They are carnivorous predators that primarily feed on hydroids and other small marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their numerous club-shaped cerata arranged in rows along their backs, and their ability to store stinging cells from their prey in special sacs at the tips of these projections.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can actually steal and reuse the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat, effectively turning their prey's weapons into their own defense system!

children.name: Corambidae
Corambe
children.description: Corambe is a genus of tiny sea slugs that live in marine environments, particularly in shallow coastal waters. These small mollusks are specialized predators that feed on other marine organisms like hydroids and bryozoans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Corambe are distinguished by their extremely small size (often less than 5mm) and their smooth, elongated body shape with reduced or absent cerata (finger-like projections) compared to other sea slug groups.
children.funFact: Despite being so tiny that they're easily overlooked, Corambe sea slugs are voracious hunters that can consume prey nearly as large as themselves.

children.description: Corambidae is a small family of tiny sea slugs that are highly specialized parasites living on other marine organisms. These minute nudibranchs are among the smallest sea slugs in the ocean, typically measuring just a few millimeters in length. They spend their entire lives attached to their hosts, feeding and reproducing in this intimate relationship.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most sea slugs that crawl freely on the seafloor, corambids are permanently attached to their hosts through specialized structures. They have extremely reduced body forms compared to other nudibranchs, lacking many typical sea slug features due to their parasitic lifestyle.
children.funFact: These sea slugs are so small and well-camouflaged on their hosts that they were among the last major groups of nudibranchs to be discovered by scientists, with many species still being found today.

children.name: Dendrodorididae
Doriopsilla
children.description: Doriopsilla is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs called nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their bright colors and defensive chemicals for protection. They are specialized predators that feed primarily on sponges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Doriopsilla nudibranchs are distinguished by their cerata (finger-like projections) that cover their backs and contain extensions of their digestive system. Unlike many other nudibranchs, they have a relatively smooth body surface and their cerata are arranged in clusters rather than rows.
children.funFact: The lemon drop nudibranch gets its common name from its bright yellow coloration, which serves as a warning to predators that it contains toxic chemicals absorbed from the sponges it eats.

children.description: Dendrodorididae are a family of sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live on the ocean floor. These soft-bodied marine animals have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on other defense mechanisms. They are part of a group called dorids, which are characterized by their flattened, oval-shaped bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have branched, tree-like gills (called cerata) arranged around their rear end, which gives them their name 'dendro' meaning tree-like. Unlike some other nudibranchs, they have a relatively smooth body surface without many bumps or projections.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can actually incorporate stinging cells from the sponges and other creatures they eat, recycling them as their own defensive weapons against predators.

children.name: Cadlinidae
Cadlina
children.description: Cadlina is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs called nudibranchs that live on the ocean floor. These soft-bodied marine animals are shell-less mollusks that crawl along rocks and other surfaces using their muscular foot, feeding primarily on sponges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cadlina species are characterized by their smooth, often translucent white or pale bodies with distinctive gill plumes arranged in a circle around their back end. They lack the cerata (finger-like projections) found on many other nudibranch groups.
children.funFact: Despite being called sea slugs, Cadlina nudibranchs are actually more closely related to snails than to the slugs you might find in your garden!

children.description: Cadlinidae is a family of sea slugs known as dorid nudibranchs that live on the ocean floor. These soft-bodied marine animals are specialized predators that feed primarily on sponges, using their radula (a rasping feeding organ) to scrape off pieces of their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their smooth, often translucent bodies and the arrangement of their gills in a circular pattern around their anus on the back end of their body.
children.funFact: These sea slugs can actually incorporate defensive chemicals from the sponges they eat into their own bodies, making themselves toxic to potential predators.

children.name: Cuthonidae
Cuthona
children.description: Cuthona is a genus of small, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead rely on their bright colors and specialized body structures for protection. They are carnivorous creatures that feed primarily on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cuthona nudibranchs are characterized by their numerous finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which contain extensions of their digestive system. Unlike some other nudibranch groups, they typically have a more elongated body shape and their cerata are arranged in distinct clusters or rows.
children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs can actually steal and use the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat, storing them in the tips of their cerata to defend themselves from predators!

children.description: Cuthonidae is a family of small, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks are characterized by their numerous finger-like projections called cerata that extend from their backs, which they use for both digestion and breathing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nudibranch families, cuthonids have cerata arranged in clusters or rows along their backs, and they typically feed on hydroids and other small marine organisms using a specialized feeding structure called a radula.
children.funFact: Many cuthonid sea slugs can steal stinging cells from the hydroids they eat and incorporate them into their own cerata for defense, essentially turning their prey's weapons into their own protection system.

children.name: Paracoryphellidae
Ziminella
children.description: Ziminella is a genus of marine bryozoans, which are tiny colonial animals that form encrusting or branching structures on underwater surfaces. These filter-feeding creatures build calcium carbonate skeletons and live in colonies where hundreds of individual animals work together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ziminella bryozoans are distinguished by their distinctive box-like individual chambers (zooids) arranged in regular patterns, with specialized feeding structures that can be retracted when threatened.
children.funFact: Despite being animals, bryozoan colonies like Ziminella are often mistaken for seaweeds or corals due to their plant-like or coral-like appearance when growing on rocks and shells.

children.description: Paracoryphellidae is a family of small, colorful sea slugs known as nudibranchs that live in marine environments. These soft-bodied mollusks have lost their shells through evolution and instead display beautiful external gills and finger-like projections called cerata on their backs. They are carnivorous creatures that feed on hydroids and other small marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive cerata (finger-like projections) that contain extensions of the digestive system, and their specific arrangement of gills and sensory tentacles called rhinophores.
children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs can actually steal and use the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat, incorporating them into their own cerata for defense against predators.

children.description: Nudibranchs are soft-bodied sea slugs that have lost their shells through evolution, creating some of the ocean's most colorful and bizarre creatures. These marine gastropods breathe through exposed gills or finger-like projections called cerata on their backs, which is where their name 'nudibranch' (meaning 'naked gill') comes from. They range from tiny translucent creatures to vibrant, alien-looking animals that crawl along the seafloor and underwater surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs, nudibranchs have their breathing structures completely exposed on the outside of their bodies rather than hidden in a cavity. They also lack the protective shell that most other gastropods possess, making them appear more like colorful underwater aliens than typical snails.
children.funFact: Many nudibranchs can steal and use the stinging cells from their prey - when they eat jellyfish or sea anemones, they transfer the victim's stinging cells to their own body parts for protection!

children.name: Littorinimorpha
Naticidae
Euspira
children.description: Euspira moonsnails are large, predatory sea snails with smooth, rounded shells that can grow several inches across. These marine gastropods are active hunters that burrow through sandy ocean floors in search of clams and other shellfish to eat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euspira moonsnails have distinctively large, bulbous bodies that can extend far beyond their shells when active, and they create characteristic collar-shaped egg masses made of sand and mucus.
children.funFact: These moonsnails drill perfectly round holes in clam shells using their rasping tongue (radula) and acidic secretions, leaving behind telltale evidence of their predatory activities that beachcombers often find on empty shells.

children.name: Neverita
children.description: Neverita is a genus of predatory sea snails known for their smooth, rounded shells and distinctive hunting behavior. These marine gastropods are commonly called moon snails due to their circular, moon-like appearance when viewed from above.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Neverita species have notably glossy, globular shells with a large body whorl and can extend their soft body to completely envelop their shell when active.
children.funFact: These snails are skilled hunters that drill perfectly round holes through the shells of clams and other mollusks to access the soft tissue inside, leaving behind telltale evidence of their predatory activity on beach-washed shells.

children.name: Polinices
children.description: Polinices is a genus of predatory sea snails commonly known as moonsnails. These marine gastropods are characterized by their smooth, round shells and their ability to burrow through sand and mud on the ocean floor in search of prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctively smooth, globular shells with a large body whorl and can extend their soft body parts to completely envelop their shell when active.
children.funFact: Moonsnails are voracious predators that drill perfectly round holes through the shells of clams and other mollusks to feed on the soft tissue inside.

children.name: Amauropsis
children.description: Amauropsis is a genus of marine snails known as necklace shells, which are predatory mollusks that live in cold ocean waters. These sea snails have smooth, rounded shells and are known for their distinctive hunting behavior of drilling holes into other mollusks to feed on them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amauropsis shells are notably smooth and glossy compared to many other marine snails, with a characteristic rounded, somewhat flattened shape. They can be distinguished from other necklace shells by their specific shell proportions and the details of their aperture opening.
children.funFact: The Iceland Necklace-shell creates distinctive spiral egg masses that look like delicate ribbons or necklaces wrapped around rocks and shells on the seafloor, which is how necklace shells got their common name.

children.description: Moon snails are marine gastropods known for their smooth, rounded shells that often have a glossy, moon-like appearance. These predatory snails are commonly found burrowing in sandy or muddy bottoms of coastal waters, where they hunt for clams and other mollusks. They have a distinctive large, muscular foot that they can inflate with water to help them glide through sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moon snails are easily recognized by their globular, often glossy shells and their enormous foot that can extend far beyond the shell opening when active. Unlike many other snails, they lack prominent sculpture or spines on their shells, giving them their characteristic smooth appearance.
children.funFact: Moon snails drill perfectly round holes in clam shells using a specialized rasping tongue called a radula combined with acid secretions, leaving behind distinctive evidence of their predation that can be found on empty shells along the beach.

children.name: Littorinidae
Littorina
children.description: Littorina is a genus of small sea snails commonly known as periwinkles that live along rocky shores and in tidal zones. These hardy marine gastropods have thick, spiral shells that protect them from crashing waves and help them retain moisture when the tide goes out. All members of this genus are well-adapted to life in the challenging intertidal environment where they graze on algae and other small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Littorina snails are distinguished from other marine snails by their robust, cone-shaped shells and their remarkable ability to survive long periods out of water during low tide. Their shells typically have a rounded opening and lack the prominent spines or ridges found in many other sea snail genera.
children.funFact: Common periwinkles can seal themselves inside their shells with a trapdoor-like structure called an operculum and survive out of water for weeks, essentially holding their breath until the next high tide arrives.

children.name: Lacuna
children.description: Lacuna snails are small marine gastropods that live in cold northern waters along rocky coastlines. These tiny snails have distinctive spiral shells and are commonly found grazing on seaweeds and algae in the intertidal zone.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lacuna snails are characterized by their small size (usually less than half an inch), relatively smooth spiral shells, and a distinctive groove or channel (called an umbilicus) near the shell opening.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Lacuna snails are important herbivores that help control algae growth on rocky shores, and they can survive being submerged and exposed to air twice daily with the changing tides.

children.description: Periwinkle snails are small marine gastropods that live in the intertidal zone, where they graze on algae and tiny organisms growing on rocks, seaweed, and other surfaces. These hardy little snails are perfectly adapted to life between the tides, able to survive both underwater and exposed to air as the ocean levels change throughout the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many marine snails, periwinkles have thick, sturdy shells that can seal tightly shut to prevent water loss during low tide. Their shells are typically cone-shaped or rounded, and they lack the breathing siphon found in many other marine gastropods.
children.funFact: Some periwinkle species can survive out of water for weeks at a time by sealing themselves inside their shells with a trapdoor-like structure called an operculum.

children.name: Calyptraeidae
Crepidula
children.description: Typical Slippersnails are small marine gastropods with distinctive slipper-shaped shells that have a flat internal shelf or platform inside. These sea snails are commonly found attached to rocks, shells, and other hard surfaces in shallow coastal waters throughout New England. They are filter feeders that strain tiny particles and plankton from the water using specialized feeding structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other marine snails, slippersnails have a characteristic internal shelf (called a septum) that partially divides the shell cavity, giving them their slipper-like appearance. Their shells are typically flattened and cap-shaped rather than spiraled like most gastropods.
children.funFact: Slippersnails are sequential hermaphrodites that start life as males and change to females as they grow larger, often forming chains or stacks where smaller males sit on top of larger females during mating season.

children.name: Crucibulum
children.description: Cup-and-Saucer Limpets are small marine snails that have evolved a unique shell shape resembling a tiny cup sitting on a saucer. Unlike typical cone-shaped limpets, these gastropods have a distinctive internal shelf or cup-like structure inside their rounded, cap-shaped shells. They are filter feeders that attach themselves to hard surfaces on the ocean floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The internal cup or shelf structure inside their shell is what sets them apart from other limpets and marine snails. This shelf-like feature gives them their distinctive "cup-and-saucer" appearance when viewed from below.
children.funFact: Cup-and-saucer limpets start life as males but can change into females as they grow larger and older, a strategy that helps ensure successful reproduction in their population.

children.description: Slippersnails are marine gastropods with cone-shaped or cap-like shells that often stack on top of each other in chains or clusters. They are filter feeders that attach themselves to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or other slippersnails, where they remain for most of their adult lives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical snails, slippersnails have shells with a distinctive internal shelf or cup-like structure that supports their body. Their shells are typically flattened and cone-shaped rather than spiraled like most gastropods.
children.funFact: Many slippersnail species are sequential hermaphrodites that start life as males and change to females as they grow larger, with the largest individuals in a stack typically being female.

children.name: Rissoidae
Onoba
children.description: Onoba is a genus of tiny marine snails that live in shallow coastal waters. These microscopic mollusks have small, cone-shaped shells and are part of the diverse world of sea snails that crawl along the ocean floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their very small size and pointed, spiral shells that are typically less than 5mm tall.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these little snails are important members of marine ecosystems, helping to break down organic matter on the seafloor.

children.name: Frigidoalvania
children.description: Frigidoalvania is a genus of tiny marine snails that live in cold ocean waters. These microscopic gastropods are part of the rissooid family and are found in deep, chilly marine environments where they feed on organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is distinguished by its extremely small size and adaptation to frigid marine conditions, as reflected in its name which means 'cold' in Latin.
children.funFact: The genus name Frigidoalvania literally means 'cold Alvania,' reflecting these snails' preference for some of the coldest marine waters where few other small gastropods can survive.

children.description: Spire-shells are tiny marine snails that live in cold northern waters, including the rocky shores and shallow depths of New England's coast. These small gastropods have tall, pointed spiral shells that give them their common name, and they're often found crawling on seaweed, rocks, or sandy bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spire-shells are characterized by their distinctively tall, narrow shells with many whorls that create an elongated spire shape. Unlike many other small marine snails, they typically have a smooth or only finely sculptured shell surface.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, spire-shells are important grazers in marine ecosystems, helping control algae growth on surfaces where they feed.

children.name: Hydrobiidae
Ecrobia
children.description: Ecrobia is a genus of tiny freshwater and brackish water snails that are so small they're often overlooked by casual observers. These minute gastropods have simple, cone-shaped shells and are typically found in shallow water environments like ponds, streams, and coastal marshes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ecrobia snails are distinguished by their extremely small size (usually less than 5mm) and their truncated or cut-off shell apex, which gives them a distinctive stubby appearance compared to other small aquatic snails.
children.funFact: Despite being less than a quarter-inch long, Ecrobia snails can be important indicators of water quality and salinity levels in coastal ecosystems.

children.name: Floridobia
children.description: Floridobia is a genus of tiny freshwater snails that live in sandy and silty sediments at the bottom of streams, ponds, and wetlands. These microscopic gastropods are part of the larger group of hydrobiid snails, which are known for their small size and aquatic lifestyle. They play an important role in aquatic ecosystems by feeding on organic matter and algae in sediments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Floridobia snails are distinguished from other hydrobiid snails by their extremely small size (usually less than 2mm) and their preference for fine sediments rather than rocky surfaces. Their shells are typically smooth and translucent with a distinctive spiral pattern.
children.funFact: Despite being named Floridobia (meaning 'Florida-living'), this genus has representatives far beyond Florida, including the New England Siltsnail found in our region's quiet waters.

children.description: Hydrobiid mud snails are tiny freshwater and brackish water snails that typically measure less than 5mm in length. These small gastropods have cone-shaped or elongated shells and are commonly found in muddy sediments, hence their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be distinguished from other small aquatic snails by their very small size, simple shell shape without elaborate sculpturing, and their preference for muddy substrates in estuarine and freshwater environments.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, some hydrobiid mud snails are incredibly successful invaders - they can reproduce both sexually and asexually, allowing a single individual to establish an entire population in a new location.

children.name: Amnicolidae
Amnicola
children.description: Amnicola is a genus of tiny freshwater snails that live in springs, streams, and other clean water sources throughout North America. These small gastropods have cone-shaped shells and are part of the larger group of aquatic snails that breathe through gills rather than lungs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amnicola snails are distinguished by their small size (usually less than 5mm), smooth cone-shaped shells, and their preference for cold, clean spring water and headwater streams.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, Amnicola snails are important indicators of water quality - they're so sensitive to pollution that their presence often signals a healthy aquatic ecosystem.

children.name: Lyogyrus
children.description: Lyogyrus is a genus of tiny freshwater snails that live in streams, springs, and other clean water habitats. These minute gastropods are part of the hydrobiid family and are known for their small, spiraled shells that are typically less than 5 millimeters in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lyogyrus snails can be distinguished from other small freshwater snails by their squat, dome-shaped shells with relatively few whorls and their preference for flowing water habitats rather than still ponds or lakes.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're often overlooked, Lyogyrus snails are important indicators of water quality - their presence typically signals clean, well-oxygenated water systems.

children.description: Duskysnails are tiny freshwater snails that live in springs, streams, and other clean water sources throughout New England. These miniature gastropods have small, cone-shaped shells that are typically brown or gray in color, which gives them their common name. They are part of the larger group of freshwater snails but represent some of the smallest species you'll encounter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Duskysnails are distinguished from other freshwater snails by their extremely small size (usually less than 4mm) and their preference for very clean, well-oxygenated water like springs and fast-flowing streams. Their shells are typically more elongated and cone-shaped compared to the rounder shells of pond snails.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, duskysnails are excellent indicators of water quality - they can only survive in very clean, unpolluted water, making them like little environmental watchdogs for our waterways.

children.name: Bithyniidae
Bithynia
children.description: Bithynia is a genus of small freshwater snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These aquatic gastropods have cone-shaped shells and breathe through gills, spending their entire lives underwater grazing on algae and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bithynia snails can be distinguished from other freshwater snails by their distinctive operculum (a plate-like door that seals the shell opening) and their relatively smooth, glossy shells with prominent growth lines.
children.funFact: The Mud Bithynia found in New England is actually a European native that was accidentally introduced to North American waters in the 1800s, likely through ballast water from ships.

children.description: Bithyniidae is a small family of freshwater snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These aquatic gastropods have gills for breathing underwater and feed primarily on algae and organic debris they scrape from surfaces using their radula (a specialized feeding organ).
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bithyniidae snails are distinguished from other freshwater snails by their operculum (a door-like structure that can seal their shell opening) and their elongated, cone-shaped shells with distinct growth lines.
children.funFact: Some Bithyniidae species can serve as intermediate hosts for parasitic flatworms, playing an important role in aquatic ecosystem food webs and parasite life cycles.

children.name: Skeneopsidae
Skeneopsis
children.description: Skeneopsis is a genus of tiny marine snails that live in shallow coastal waters. These miniature gastropods have small, flattened spiral shells that coil in a flat plane rather than forming a tall spire like most snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their shells are notably flat and disc-like, coiling almost entirely in one plane, which gives them a planispiral appearance similar to a miniature nautilus or flat coil of rope.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, these tiny snails are important members of marine ecosystems, grazing on microscopic algae and bacteria on rocks and seaweed.

children.description: Skeneopsidae is a small family of tiny marine snails that live in shallow coastal waters. These microscopic gastropods have delicate, translucent shells that are typically less than 5mm in size and often go unnoticed by casual beachcombers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their extremely small size and thin, nearly transparent shells with a distinctive smooth, glossy surface that lacks the ridges or sculpture found in many other marine snails.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, skeneopsid snails are active grazers that feed on microscopic algae and bacteria growing on rocks and seaweed in the intertidal zone.

children.name: Aporrhaidae
Arrhoges
children.description: Arrhoges is a genus of marine gastropod mollusks commonly known as pelicanfoot shells due to their distinctive shell shape. These sea snails are characterized by their unique shell structure that develops finger-like projections as they mature, creating a shape reminiscent of a pelican's webbed foot.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature of Arrhoges is the dramatic transformation of their shell as they age, developing long, flared projections that extend outward from the shell opening, unlike the smooth, spiral shells of most other sea snails.
children.funFact: Young pelicanfoot shells look completely different from adults - they start with normal spiral shells and only develop their characteristic 'foot' projections when they reach maturity.

children.description: Pelican's Foot Snails are a family of marine gastropods known for their distinctive shell shape that resembles a bird's webbed foot. These sea snails have shells with flared outer lips that extend into finger-like projections, creating their characteristic appearance. They are typically found in deeper waters along continental shelves and slopes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other sea snails, Pelican's Foot Snails have shells with dramatically flared outer lips that form wing-like or finger-like extensions, giving them their unique pelican foot appearance.
children.funFact: The elaborate shell extensions of Pelican's Foot Snails don't fully develop until the snail reaches maturity - juvenile shells look quite ordinary and only transform into their distinctive pelican-foot shape as adults.

children.name: Tateidae
Potamopyrgus
children.description: Potamopyrgus is a genus of tiny freshwater snails that originally come from New Zealand and Australia. These small gastropods have cone-shaped shells and are found in streams, rivers, and lakes where they feed on algae and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small size (usually under 6mm), pointed spire shells, and ability to reproduce both sexually and asexually through parthenogenesis.
children.funFact: The New Zealand Mudsnail can reproduce without mating, allowing a single individual to establish an entire population in a new location, which has made it one of the world's most successful aquatic invaders.

children.description: Tateidae is a family of very small freshwater snails that typically live in springs, streams, and other clean water environments. These tiny gastropods have cone-shaped or elongated shells and are often less than 6mm in length. They are found worldwide and play important roles in freshwater ecosystems as both grazers of algae and food sources for other animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tateidae snails are distinguished from other freshwater snails by their small size, typically smooth shells, and their preference for clean, well-oxygenated water habitats. They have a unique gill structure and reproductive system that sets them apart from similar-looking freshwater gastropods.
children.funFact: The New Zealand mud snail (Potamopyrgus antipodarum), New England's only Tateidae species, reproduces through cloning - most populations consist entirely of females that produce genetic copies of themselves without needing to mate!

children.name: Velutinidae
Limneria
children.description: Limneria is a genus of small, flattened marine snails that have evolved to live as parasites or commensals on other sea creatures. These unusual gastropods have transparent, ear-shaped shells that are often quite thin and delicate. They are part of the velutinid family and are found in marine environments where they associate closely with their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical snails, Limneria species have extremely flattened, translucent shells that allow them to press closely against their hosts. Their shell shape is distinctively ear-like or oval, making them easily distinguishable from other marine gastropods.
children.funFact: These snails are so well-adapted to their parasitic lifestyle that they can actually absorb nutrients directly through their thin shell and body wall from their host organisms.

children.description: Velutinidae are a family of small to medium-sized sea snails known for their distinctive soft, velvety appearance. These marine gastropods are characterized by their thin, often translucent shells that may be partially or completely covered by the animal's mantle tissue.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other sea snails, velutinids have shells that are often overgrown or completely enveloped by their soft body tissues, giving them a unique velvety or smooth appearance rather than the typical hard, exposed shell.
children.funFact: Some velutinid snails are specialized predators that feed exclusively on sponges, using their radula (feeding organ) to rasp away at these sessile marine animals.

children.name: Assimineidae
Angustassiminea
children.description: Angustassiminea is a genus of tiny freshwater and brackish water snails that are found in coastal areas and salt marshes. These microscopic gastropods are so small they're often overlooked, typically measuring just a few millimeters in length. They live in the muddy sediments and vegetation of tidal areas where fresh and salt water mix.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These snails are distinguished by their extremely small size and their ability to tolerate varying salinity levels in coastal environments. Their shells are typically smooth and conical, adapted for life in the shifting conditions of salt marshes and estuaries.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny enough to fit on the tip of your finger, these snails play an important role in salt marsh ecosystems by helping to break down organic matter in the mud.

children.description: Assimineidae is a family of very small freshwater and brackish water snails that live in coastal areas and wetlands. These tiny gastropods typically have smooth, cone-shaped or oval shells and are often found in muddy areas near salt marshes, estuaries, and the edges of ponds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These snails are distinguished by their extremely small size (usually less than 5mm) and their preference for transitional habitats between freshwater and saltwater environments, unlike most other freshwater snails that stick to purely freshwater habitats.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, some assimineids can actually breathe air and survive out of water for extended periods, making them well-adapted to the changing water levels of tidal areas.

children.description: Littorinimorpha is a diverse order of marine and freshwater snails that includes many species commonly found along New England's shores and waterways. These gastropods range from tiny mud snails in salt marshes to the familiar periwinkles clinging to rocky coastlines and the predatory moon snails that burrow through sandy beaches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group typically have relatively simple, spiral shells and most possess an operculum (a trap door-like structure) that can seal the shell opening for protection. They show remarkable diversity in feeding strategies, from grazing algae to filter-feeding to being active predators.
children.funFact: Moon snails in this group are expert drillers that use their rasping tongue (radula) and acid secretions to bore perfectly round holes through the shells of clams and other mollusks to access the soft tissue inside.

children.name: Neogastropoda
Muricidae
Nucella
children.description: Nucella is a genus of predatory sea snails commonly known as dogwhelks or rock snails. These marine gastropods are characterized by their thick, sturdy shells and their carnivorous lifestyle, feeding primarily on barnacles and mussels by drilling through their shells with a specialized feeding structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nucella species can be distinguished from other whelks by their relatively small size, robust ribbed shells, and their ability to bore perfectly round holes in the shells of their prey using both chemical secretions and a rasping radula.
children.funFact: Dogwhelks can change their shell color and thickness based on their diet and environment - those feeding on mussels often develop darker shells, while those in wave-exposed areas grow thicker shells for protection.

children.name: Urosalpinx
children.description: Urosalpinx is a genus of small marine snails commonly known as oyster drills. These predatory gastropods are equipped with specialized feeding structures that allow them to bore through the shells of bivalves like oysters, clams, and mussels. They are important members of marine ecosystems along rocky shores and oyster beds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oyster drills have a distinctive elongated, spiral shell with prominent ridges and a pointed spire. They possess a radula (rasping tongue) that works like a drill bit to create perfectly round holes in their prey's shells.
children.funFact: An oyster drill can take up to 24 hours to bore a single hole through an oyster shell, but once successful, it can consume the entire oyster through that tiny opening.

children.name: Eupleura
children.description: Eupleura is a genus of predatory sea snails known as drill snails or oyster drills. These marine gastropods are equipped with a specialized feeding apparatus that allows them to drill through the shells of other mollusks, particularly oysters and other bivalves, to feed on the soft tissue inside.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Eupleura are characterized by their robust, thick-lipped shells with prominent ridges and spines, and most notably their ability to bore perfectly round holes through prey shells using both mechanical rasping and chemical secretions.
children.funFact: The Thick-lipped Drill can take several hours to drill a single hole through an oyster shell, but once successful, it inserts its proboscis to consume the oyster's body, making it both a fascinating predator and a significant pest in commercial oyster beds.

children.description: Murex snails are marine gastropods known for their thick, robust shells often decorated with spines, ridges, or knobs. These predatory sea snails are skilled hunters that use their specialized feeding apparatus to drill holes through the shells of other mollusks like clams, mussels, and oysters. They are commonly found in rocky intertidal zones and shallow coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Murex snails can be distinguished from other sea snails by their heavy, sculptured shells with pronounced ridges, spines, or tubercles, and their ability to produce a specialized enzyme that helps them bore through prey shells.
children.funFact: Some murex snails were historically prized for producing Tyrian purple dye, a color so valuable in ancient times that it was worth more than gold and reserved for royalty.

children.name: Nassariidae
Ilyanassa
children.description: Ilyanassa is a genus of small marine snails commonly known as mudsnails that live in salt marshes, mudflats, and shallow coastal waters. These hardy gastropods have cone-shaped shells and are excellent scavengers, feeding on dead organic matter, algae, and detritus in the muddy sediments where they thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ilyanassa mudsnails are distinguished from other marine snails by their robust, thick shells with pronounced spiral ridges and their ability to tolerate dramatic changes in salinity and temperature in tidal environments.
children.funFact: Eastern mudsnails can survive being buried in mud for weeks during low tide by sealing their shell opening with a trap door-like structure called an operculum.

children.name: Phrontis
children.description: Phrontis is a genus of small marine snails commonly known as nassa mud snails or basket shells. These sea snails are scavengers that live in shallow coastal waters, feeding on dead organic matter and small organisms they find in the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phrontis snails have thick, sturdy shells with a distinctive tall spire and rounded body whorl, along with a well-developed siphonal canal that helps them breathe while buried in mud or sand.
children.funFact: These industrious little snails are nature's cleanup crew, playing an important role in marine ecosystems by recycling nutrients from dead plants and animals on the seafloor.

children.description: Nassa mudsnails are small marine snails that live in muddy or sandy coastal areas like salt marshes, tidal flats, and shallow bays. These hardy little gastropods are scavengers that feed on dead organic matter, playing an important role as nature's cleanup crew in marine ecosystems. They have thick, sturdy shells that help protect them in their sometimes harsh intertidal environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nassariidae can be identified by their relatively small size, thick shells with pronounced spiral ridges, and their preference for soft sediment habitats. Unlike many other marine snails, they are primarily scavengers rather than grazers or predators.
children.funFact: Some nassa mudsnails can detect the smell of dead fish from remarkable distances underwater and will quickly swarm to a food source, sometimes covering a dead crab or fish so completely that the shell looks like it's moving!

children.name: Columbellidae
Costoanachis
children.description: Costoanachis is a genus of small marine snails commonly known as dove snails, found along the Atlantic coast. These tiny gastropods have elongated, cone-shaped shells with distinctive ribbed patterns that help distinguish the different species. They are carnivorous mollusks that feed on other small marine organisms in shallow coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their ribbed shell sculpture and relatively narrow, elongated shape compared to other dove snails. The prominent ribs or ridges that run along the length of their shells are a key identifying feature.
children.funFact: Despite their peaceful "dove" name, these small snails are actually predators that use their rasping tongue (radula) to drill holes in the shells of even smaller prey.

children.name: Astyris
children.description: Astyris is a genus of small marine snails known as dove shells, characterized by their smooth, glossy shells that are typically elongated and cone-shaped. These tiny gastropods are found in shallow coastal waters where they feed on organic matter and small organisms in the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Astyris dove shells are distinguished from other small marine snails by their particularly smooth, polished shell surface and their characteristic elongated oval shape with a pointed spire.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'dove shells,' these tiny snails are actually carnivorous and use their rasping tongue to feed on microscopic animals and organic debris on the ocean floor.

children.description: Dove snails are small marine gastropods that live in shallow coastal waters, typically found crawling on rocks, seaweed, or sandy bottoms. These tiny snails have elongated, smooth shells that are usually less than an inch long and come in various shades of brown, white, or yellow. They are active predators and scavengers, feeding on small worms, other mollusks, and organic debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dove snails can be identified by their distinctively narrow, elongated shells with a tall spire and relatively small opening. Unlike many other small marine snails, they have a characteristic notch at the outer edge of their shell opening and often display fine spiral ridges or smooth, glossy surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, dove snails are fierce hunters that can drill holes through the shells of other small mollusks using their specialized feeding structure called a radula, which works like a tiny drill bit.

children.name: Mangeliidae
Kurtziella
children.description: Kurtziella is a genus of small, predatory sea snails that live in marine environments. These tiny gastropods are part of the turrid family and are characterized by their elongated, cone-shaped shells with distinctive spiral ridges. They are carnivorous hunters that use a specialized feeding structure to capture prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kurtziella snails can be identified by their slender, tower-like shells with prominent spiral sculpting and a distinctive notch or slit in the outer lip. Their shells typically have a smooth, polished appearance with fine growth lines.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Kurtziella snails are skilled predators that inject venom into their prey using a modified radula tooth, similar to their larger cone shell relatives.

children.name: Pyrgocythara
children.description: Pyrgocythara is a genus of small marine snails known as mangelia snails that live in ocean waters. These tiny predatory gastropods have elongated, spiral shells and are part of the larger group of sea snails called turrids.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small size, typically pointed spire shells, and distinctive sculptural patterns on their shell surface that often include fine ridges or ribs.
children.funFact: These tiny snails are actually skilled hunters that use a specialized feeding structure called a radula with harpoon-like teeth to capture and subdue their prey.

children.name: Propebela
children.description: Propebela is a genus of small marine snails that live in cold ocean waters. These sea snails are carnivorous predators that hunt other small marine animals using a specialized feeding structure called a radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their elongated, spindle-shaped shells with distinctive spiral ridges and a pointed spire that helps distinguish them from other marine snail groups.
children.funFact: These tiny ocean hunters can drill holes through the shells of their prey using their rasping radula, much like a biological drill bit.

children.description: Mangeliidae is a family of small, predatory sea snails that live on the ocean floor. These tiny gastropods have elongated, spindle-shaped shells with distinctive sculptured surfaces and are equipped with a proboscis for hunting small prey like worms and other marine invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their fusiform (spindle-shaped) shells with well-developed spiral sculpture and a distinctive anal sinus - a small notch near the top of the shell opening that helps distinguish them from other similar sea snail families.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size (often less than half an inch long), these sea snails are skilled hunters that use a extensible proboscis to probe into sediment and crevices to capture their prey.

children.name: Busyconidae
Busycotypus
children.description: Busycotypus is a genus of large marine snails known as whelks that live in coastal waters along the Atlantic coast. These predatory gastropods have distinctive spiral shells and are active hunters that feed on other mollusks like clams and oysters. They play an important role in marine ecosystems as both predators and prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Busycotypus whelks are characterized by their large, heavy shells with prominent spiral channels or grooves running along the whorls, which gives the Channeled Whelk its common name.
children.funFact: Channeled Whelks are left-handed snails - their shells spiral counterclockwise, which is the opposite direction from most gastropod shells.

children.name: Busycon
children.description: Busycon is a genus of large marine snails commonly known as whelks, which are predatory mollusks that live in shallow coastal waters. These snails have thick, spiral shells and are active hunters that feed on clams, oysters, and other shellfish by using their muscular foot to pry open prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Busycon whelks are distinguished from other marine snails by their large size, thick heavy shells with pronounced spiral ridges, and their specialized feeding behavior of preying on bivalves.
children.funFact: Whelks lay their eggs in distinctive papery capsule chains that often wash up on beaches, commonly called 'mermaid's necklaces' by beachcombers.

children.description: The Busyconidae family includes large marine snails commonly known as whelks, which are among the biggest sea snails found along the Atlantic coast. These impressive mollusks are carnivorous predators that use their muscular foot to pry open clams and other shellfish, then insert their long proboscis to feed on the soft tissue inside.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Busyconid whelks are distinguished by their large, heavy shells with a distinctive left-handed or right-handed spiral pattern, and they possess a specialized egg-laying structure that creates long strings of papery egg capsules.
children.funFact: Whelk egg case strings, often called 'mermaid's necklaces,' can stretch over 2 feet long and contain dozens of individual capsules, each holding multiple baby whelks that cannibalize their siblings before hatching.

children.name: Buccinidae
Buccinum
children.description: Buccinum is a genus of large marine snails known as whelks, which are predatory sea snails that hunt other mollusks and scavenge on the ocean floor. These robust gastropods have thick, spiral shells and are found in cold northern waters. They play an important role as both predators and scavengers in marine ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Buccinum whelks are distinguished by their large, heavy shells with a distinctive pointed spire and wide opening, along with their carnivorous feeding habits using a long proboscis to drill into prey shells.
children.funFact: Common whelks can live for over 20 years and are considered a delicacy in many European countries, often served as 'whelks and chips' in British seaside towns.

children.name: Neptunea
children.description: Neptune Whelks are large, predatory sea snails that live in cold ocean waters. They have thick, heavy shells with prominent ridges or spirals, and are skilled hunters that feed on other marine animals like clams, worms, and even other snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These whelks are distinguished from other sea snails by their robust, heavily-ridged shells and their impressive size, often reaching several inches in length. Their shells typically have a more angular, sculptured appearance compared to smoother whelk species.
children.funFact: Neptune Whelks can live for over 40 years and are so efficient at drilling through the shells of their prey that they've been called the 'can openers of the sea floor.'

children.description: True whelks are marine snails with thick, spiral shells that live on the ocean floor in cold northern waters. They are carnivorous predators and scavengers that use their muscular foot to move along the seafloor while hunting for clams, worms, and dead animals. These robust mollusks are well-adapted to life in New England's chilly coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True whelks have distinctively thick, heavy shells with a pointed spire and a large opening that can be sealed with a horny plate called an operculum. Unlike some other marine snails, they lack the drilling ability of moon snails and instead use their strong foot and specialized feeding structure to pry open prey.
children.funFact: Whelks are sometimes called the 'wolves of the sea floor' because they hunt in groups and can detect the scent of dead animals from remarkable distances, making them nature's underwater cleanup crew.

children.name: Colidae
Colus
children.description: Colus whelks are medium-sized marine snails that live in cold northern waters, including the deep waters off New England's coast. These predatory gastropods have elongated, spindle-shaped shells with a distinctive long spire and canal at the opening. They are carnivorous hunters that feed on other mollusks, worms, and small crustaceans using their extendable proboscis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Colus whelks can be distinguished from other whelk genera by their particularly elongated shells with a pronounced spire that makes up more than half the shell's length. Their shells also have a distinctive long, narrow siphonal canal at the base.
children.funFact: Despite their relatively small size, Colus whelks are voracious predators that can drill through the shells of their prey using a specialized rasping tongue called a radula, which works like a biological drill bit.

children.description: Colidae is a family of marine snails commonly known as spindle shells or whelks. These sea snails are predatory gastropods that live in ocean waters, using their elongated shells and specialized feeding apparatus to hunt other marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive spindle-shaped or fusiform shells that taper to points at both ends. They possess a long siphonal canal and often have spiral ridges or sculptural patterns on their shells.
children.funFact: These predatory snails can drill holes through the shells of their prey using a specialized rasping tongue called a radula, allowing them to access the soft tissues inside.

children.name: Olividae
Oliva
children.description: Oliva is a genus of predatory sea snails known for their beautifully polished, cylindrical shells that are prized by collectors worldwide. These marine gastropods are active hunters that burrow through sandy ocean floors in search of small clams, worms, and other prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oliva snails are instantly recognizable by their glossy, porcelain-like shells that appear naturally polished without any growth lines or ridges visible on the surface.
children.funFact: The Lettered Olive gets its name from the intricate brown markings on its shell that often resemble hieroglyphic writing or ancient script.

children.description: Olive snails are a family of predatory sea snails known for their smooth, glossy, olive-shaped shells that look like they've been polished. These marine gastropods are active hunters that burrow in sandy ocean bottoms, feeding on other mollusks and marine worms. They're found in warm coastal waters around the world, with most species living in tropical and subtropical regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Olive snails can be identified by their distinctively smooth, shiny shells that lack the ridges or bumps found on most other sea snails. Their shells have a characteristic cylindrical shape that's wider at one end, resembling an olive, and they possess a large foot that helps them glide through sand.
children.funFact: Olive snails are such efficient burrowers that they can completely disappear into sand in just seconds, using their muscular foot like a shovel to dig down and ambush prey from below.

children.description: Neogastropods are a diverse group of marine snails that are among the most advanced gastropods in the ocean. These sea snails are characterized by their well-developed siphon, which they use like a snorkel to draw water over their gills while burrowing in sand or mud. Most are active predators or scavengers, using their specialized feeding structures to hunt other mollusks, worms, and small marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike simpler snails, neogastropods have a distinctive siphonal canal - a groove or tube-like extension of their shell opening that houses their breathing siphon. They also possess a more complex nervous system and often have elaborate shell sculptures with spines, ridges, or intricate patterns.
children.funFact: Many neogastropods are skilled drillers that use their radula (feeding organ) like a tiny drill bit to bore perfectly round holes through the shells of clams and other prey, then insert their proboscis to consume the soft tissues inside.

children.name: Planorbidae
Planorbella
children.description: Planorbella is a genus of freshwater snails known as ramshorn snails, named for their distinctive flat, coiled shells that resemble a ram's horn when viewed from the side. These aquatic gastropods live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they graze on algae and decaying plant matter. They breathe air through a lung-like structure and must periodically surface to replenish their oxygen supply.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Planorbella are distinguished from other ramshorn snails by their larger size and more robust shells, with the mouth opening (aperture) being particularly wide and flared in some species.
children.funFact: Planorbella snails have red blood due to hemoglobin, unlike most other snails that have blue blood, which helps them survive in low-oxygen environments like stagnant ponds.

children.name: Gyraulus
children.description: Gyro snails are tiny freshwater snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These small mollusks have distinctively flat, disc-shaped shells that spiral in a tight coil, making them look like miniature spinning tops when viewed from above.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other freshwater snails that have tall, cone-shaped shells, gyro snails have notably flattened shells that spiral almost entirely in one plane. Their shells typically measure less than 8mm across and have a distinctive disc-like appearance.
children.funFact: Gyro snails get their name from their shell's resemblance to a gyroscope - the flat, tightly coiled spiral looks like it could spin like a top!

children.name: Ferrissia
children.description: Ferrissia is a genus of tiny freshwater limpets that live in lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These small snails have cone-shaped shells that they use to clamp tightly onto rocks, logs, and aquatic plants. Unlike typical snails that can withdraw into spiral shells, these limpets have simple cap-like shells that cover their entire body.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ferrissia limpets can be distinguished from other freshwater limpets by their relatively smooth, oval shells that are typically less than half an inch long. Their shells are also more transparent and delicate compared to the thicker, more robust shells of other limpet genera.
children.funFact: Despite being called limpets like their marine cousins, Ferrissia species are actually more closely related to pond snails and evolved their limpet-like shape independently as an adaptation to life in flowing water.

children.name: Helisoma
children.description: Helisoma is a genus of freshwater snails commonly known as ramshorn snails, characterized by their distinctive flat, coiled shells that spiral in a plane like a ram's horn. These aquatic gastropods live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout North America. They are air-breathing snails that come to the surface to breathe, despite living underwater.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Helisoma snails can be distinguished from other ramshorn snails by their larger size and the presence of distinct ridges or keels on their shells. The shells are typically more robust and have a more pronounced spiral pattern compared to smaller ramshorn species.
children.funFact: Helisoma snails can actually breathe both air and water - they have a lung-like cavity for air breathing but can also extract oxygen from water through their skin when submerged for extended periods.

children.name: Planorbula
children.description: Planorbula is a genus of small freshwater snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These tiny gastropods have distinctively flattened, spiral shells that coil in a flat plane like a miniature parking garage, rather than forming a tall cone like many other snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Planorbula snails are distinguished from other ramshorn snails by their much smaller size and the presence of a distinctive thickened lip around the shell opening when mature.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters across, these tiny snails are important decomposers in aquatic ecosystems, helping to break down dead plant material and algae.

children.name: Promenetus
children.description: Promenetus is a genus of tiny freshwater snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These delicate spiral-shelled creatures are part of the planorbid family, known for their flat, coiled shells that resemble tiny rams' horns. They graze on algae and organic matter along the bottom and on aquatic plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Promenetus snails are distinguished from other planorbid snails by their extremely small size and tightly coiled, lens-shaped shells that are nearly flat on both sides. Their shells typically measure less than 4mm across, making them among the smallest freshwater snails in New England.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Promenetus snails can survive in temporary pools that freeze solid in winter by burrowing into mud and entering a state of dormancy until spring thaw.

children.description: Ramshorn snails are freshwater gastropods with distinctive flat, coiled shells that spiral in a single plane, resembling a ram's horn or a tiny cinnamon roll. These small aquatic snails are commonly found in ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and wetlands throughout New England. They breathe air through a lung-like structure but can also absorb oxygen from water through their skin.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their flat, disc-shaped shells that coil in a horizontal plane make them easily distinguishable from other freshwater snails, which typically have tall, spiral shells. Most ramshorn snails are left-handed (sinistral), meaning their shells coil counterclockwise when viewed from above.
children.funFact: Many ramshorn snails have red blood due to hemoglobin, the same oxygen-carrying protein found in human blood, which is unusual among mollusks that typically have blue, copper-based blood.

children.name: Lymnaeidae
Ladislavella
children.description: Ladislavella is a genus of small freshwater snails that live in ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These aquatic gastropods have thin, translucent shells and breathe air through a simple lung, requiring them to periodically surface for oxygen. They play important roles as both grazers of algae and food sources for fish, birds, and other aquatic animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ladislavella snails can be distinguished from other pond snails by their relatively small size and the specific shape and coiling pattern of their shells. Their shells are typically more delicate and have distinctive aperture shapes that help identify the different species.
children.funFact: Despite being aquatic, these snails are actually air-breathers that must regularly swim to the water surface to refill their primitive lung with fresh air.

children.name: Galba
children.description: Fossarias are small freshwater snails that live in ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These tiny gastropods have elongated, spiral shells and are important members of aquatic ecosystems, feeding on algae and decaying plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fossarias have distinctively tall, narrow shells with a pointed spire, unlike the rounder shells of many other freshwater snails. Their shells are typically thin and translucent with a brownish or amber coloration.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, fossarias play a crucial role as intermediate hosts for various parasites, making them important links in freshwater food webs and disease cycles.

children.name: Pseudosuccinea
children.description: Pseudosuccinea is a genus of small freshwater snails that live in ponds, streams, and other aquatic environments. These snails have thin, translucent shells and are part of the larger group of air-breathing freshwater snails that can be found throughout New England's wetlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pseudosuccinea snails can be distinguished from true Lymnaea snails by their more delicate shell structure and slightly different shell shape, though they are so similar that they were once considered the same group.
children.funFact: The genus name Pseudosuccinea literally means "false amber snail" because these snails were originally thought to be a type of amber snail but were later discovered to be a distinct group.

children.name: Lymnaea
children.description: Great Pond Snails are freshwater gastropods with thin, spiral shells that are typically brown or yellowish in color. They are air-breathing snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These snails are herbivorous, feeding on algae and aquatic plants by scraping surfaces with their rasping tongue called a radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Great Pond Snails can be distinguished from other freshwater snails by their relatively large size (up to 2 inches long) and their distinctive pointed, elongated spiral shell shape. Unlike some aquatic snails that have gills, these snails breathe air and must periodically surface to take in oxygen through a lung-like cavity.
children.funFact: Great Pond Snails are hermaphrodites, meaning each individual has both male and female reproductive organs, but they still need to mate with another snail to reproduce successfully.

children.description: Pond and Melantho Snails are freshwater gastropods that live in ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and other aquatic habitats throughout New England. These air-breathing snails have thin, spiral shells and can often be seen gliding along underwater surfaces or coming to the surface to breathe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other freshwater snails, these species have lungs rather than gills and must surface regularly to breathe air. Their shells are typically left-handed (sinistral) when viewed from above, coiling counterclockwise.
children.funFact: Some species in this family serve as intermediate hosts for parasitic flatworms, playing important ecological roles in freshwater food webs while also affecting the health of birds and mammals that drink from the same waters.

children.name: Pyramidellidae
Boonea
children.description: Boonea is a genus of tiny marine snails known as odostomes that live as parasites on other marine animals like clams, oysters, and worms. These minuscule gastropods have elongated, cone-shaped shells that are usually less than 5mm long. They use a specialized feeding tube called a proboscis to pierce their hosts and feed on their body fluids.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boonea odostomes are distinguished by their small, smooth, tower-like shells with a distinctive fold or tooth-like projection inside the shell opening. This internal tooth structure is a key characteristic that separates them from other small marine snails.
children.funFact: Despite being parasites, Boonea snails don't usually kill their hosts - instead, they maintain a long-term relationship where they feed gradually without causing fatal damage, essentially 'farming' their host for sustenance.

children.name: Turbonilla
children.description: Turbonilla is a genus of tiny marine snails that live as parasites on other marine animals, particularly worms and other mollusks. These microscopic gastropods have elongated, tower-like shells that are often translucent or white in color. They use a specialized feeding structure called a proboscis to pierce their hosts and feed on their body fluids.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Turbonilla snails can be identified by their distinctively tall, narrow shells with many whorls that create a slender, needle-like appearance. Unlike free-living snails, they have specialized mouthparts adapted for parasitic feeding rather than grazing or hunting.
children.funFact: Despite being parasites, Turbonilla snails are so small that they rarely harm their hosts significantly, and some species are so tiny that dozens could fit on the tip of your finger.

children.name: Sayella
children.description: Sayella is a genus of tiny marine snails that live in shallow coastal waters. These microscopic mollusks are part of the diverse family of marine gastropods and can be found crawling on surfaces in the intertidal zone.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sayella snails are distinguished by their extremely small size and smooth, elongated shells that are typically less than 3mm long. Their shells have a distinctive glossy appearance and lack prominent ridges or sculpturing.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, Sayella snails play an important role in marine ecosystems by feeding on microscopic algae and organic matter on underwater surfaces.

children.description: Pyramid snails are tiny marine gastropods with distinctive tall, pointed shells that resemble miniature towers or pyramids. These small mollusks are parasitic, using a specialized feeding tube to pierce and feed on other marine animals like worms, clams, and other snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their elongated, cone-shaped shells with numerous whorls and their parasitic lifestyle set them apart from other small marine snails. Most species have a unique fold on their columella (central shell column) that helps distinguish them from similar-looking gastropods.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny (often less than 5mm long), pyramid snails are sophisticated parasites that can inject enzymes into their hosts to pre-digest their meal before sucking it up through their needle-like proboscis.

children.name: Architaenioglossa
children.commonName: apple snails, river snails, and allies

children.name: Viviparidae
Margarya
children.description: Margarya is a genus of freshwater snails native to Asia, particularly found in lakes and slow-moving waters. These are relatively large aquatic snails that belong to the apple snail family, known for their rounded shells and ability to breathe both underwater and at the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Margarya snails are distinguished from other apple snails by their flatter, more disc-like shell shape and their origin in Asian freshwater systems rather than tropical regions.
children.funFact: The Asian Apple Snail can grow quite large for a freshwater snail, with some specimens reaching over 2 inches across, and they're capable of surviving out of water for extended periods.

children.name: Callinina
children.description: Callinina is a genus of freshwater snails that includes large, spiral-shelled mollusks found in rivers, lakes, and ponds. These snails are characterized by their distinctive banded shell patterns and their ability to breathe both underwater through gills and at the surface using a simple lung. They are important filter feeders that help keep aquatic ecosystems clean by consuming algae and organic debris.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Callinina snails are distinguished from other freshwater snails by their large size, prominent spiral banding patterns on their shells, and their operculum - a hard, plate-like structure that can seal the shell opening when the snail retreats inside.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'mystery snails,' Callinina snails are actually quite predictable - they often float upside-down at the water's surface to breathe air, looking like they're taking a leisurely swim!

children.name: Campeloma
children.description: Campeloma is a genus of freshwater snails that live in streams, rivers, and lakes throughout eastern North America. These aquatic gastropods have spiral shells and breathe through gills, spending their entire lives underwater crawling along the bottom sediments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Campeloma snails are distinguished by their pointed, elongated spiral shells and their ability to give birth to live young rather than laying eggs like most other freshwater snails.
children.funFact: Unlike most snails that lay eggs, Campeloma are ovoviviparous, meaning the eggs develop inside the mother and she gives birth to fully-formed baby snails!

children.name: Heterogen
children.description: Heterogen is a genus of large freshwater snails that are native to East Asia but have been introduced to waterways around the world. These snails are characterized by their substantial size and distinctive spiral shells that can grow quite large compared to native freshwater snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are notably larger than most native New England freshwater snails and have thick, robust shells with pronounced spiral ridges. They also possess an operculum (a door-like structure) that can completely seal their shell opening.
children.funFact: Japanese Mystery Snails can live for several years and are sometimes called 'mystery snails' because they can seemingly appear overnight in new water bodies, though they're actually spread by human activities like aquarium releases.

children.description: River snails are freshwater gastropods that live in rivers, streams, and lakes throughout New England. Unlike many snails that lay eggs, these remarkable creatures give birth to live young, carrying their babies inside their shells until they're ready to emerge as tiny, fully-formed snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: River snails are distinguished from other freshwater snails by their live-bearing reproduction and their typically cone-shaped or globular shells with a distinctive operculum (trap door) that seals the opening when they retract inside.
children.funFact: River snails can live for several years and some species can survive being frozen in ice during winter, becoming active again when the water thaws in spring.

children.description: Architaenioglossa is an order of freshwater snails that includes some of the largest and most ancient snail lineages. These snails are characterized by their unique gill structure and reproductive methods, with many species giving birth to live young rather than laying eggs. They're found in rivers, lakes, and streams throughout the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other freshwater snails, members of this group have a distinctive gill arrangement with specialized breathing structures. Many species are also viviparous, meaning they give birth to fully-formed baby snails instead of laying eggs.
children.funFact: Some apple snails in this group can grow as large as a baseball and are capable of both underwater gill breathing and air breathing through a specialized lung-like organ.

children.name: Ellobiida
Ellobiidae
Carychium
