children.description: Carychium is a genus of tiny land snails that are among the smallest terrestrial gastropods you'll find in New England. These microscopic mollusks typically measure less than 2mm in length and live in moist environments like leaf litter, moss, and the edges of wetlands. Despite their minute size, they play important roles in forest ecosystems by helping decompose organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These snails are distinguished by their extremely small size and distinctive shell shape with a narrow opening. Unlike many other land snails, Carychium species have shells that are translucent to whitish and often appear almost crystalline.
children.funFact: These snails are so small that you could fit dozens of them on a single penny, yet they have fully functional respiratory and digestive systems just like their much larger snail relatives.

children.name: Melampus
children.description: Melampus is a genus of small air-breathing snails that live in salt marshes and coastal areas. These unique mollusks have adapted to life between land and sea, spending time both in and out of water as tides rise and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical marine snails, Melampus species breathe air through a lung rather than gills, and they have distinctive tooth-like projections in their shell opening that help identify different species.
children.funFact: These tiny snails can actually climb up marsh grass stems to avoid drowning during high tides, then crawl back down to feed on decaying plant matter when the water recedes.

children.name: Myosotella
children.description: Myosotella is a genus of tiny air-breathing snails that live in saltwater marshes and tidal areas. These small gastropods are specially adapted to life in the challenging environment where land meets sea, able to survive both in water and air as tides change.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These snails are distinguished by their minute size and their ability to live in salt marsh habitats where most land snails cannot survive. They have a unique respiratory system that allows them to breathe air while tolerating the salty, periodically flooded conditions of their coastal homes.
children.funFact: The name 'Myosotella' means 'little mouse ear,' referring to the small, rounded shape of these tiny snails that can be smaller than a grain of rice.

children.description: Hollow-shelled snails are small terrestrial and semi-aquatic snails with distinctive thin, lightweight shells that often appear somewhat translucent. These tiny gastropods are typically found in moist environments like leaf litter, marshes, and areas near water where they feed on decaying organic matter and microscopic organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other land snails, hollow-shelled snails have remarkably thin, delicate shells that give them their common name. Many species in this family are also amphibious, able to survive in both terrestrial and aquatic environments.
children.funFact: Some hollow-shelled snails can actually breathe air through a simple lung-like structure, while others have gills, making this family a fascinating example of evolutionary adaptation to different environments.

children.description: The Ellobiida are small snails that have adapted to life at the boundary between land and water. These snails have distinctive shell shapes - some are hollow and lightweight, others are ear-shaped or button-like, giving the group its descriptive name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical marine snails, these species have developed air-breathing capabilities and often live in salt marshes, mudflats, and other intertidal habitats where they must survive both underwater and exposed conditions.
children.funFact: Many of these snails can actually drown if kept underwater too long, despite living in coastal areas, because they have evolved to breathe air rather than extract oxygen from water like their marine relatives.

children.name: Cephalaspidea
Haminoeidae
Haminella
children.description: Haminella is a genus of small sea snails known as bubble shells that live in marine environments. These gastropods have thin, delicate shells that are often translucent or glass-like in appearance, giving them their common name of glassy-bubble snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Haminella species are distinguished by their extremely fragile, bubble-like shells that are nearly transparent and their ability to completely retract their soft body parts into the shell when threatened.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, these tiny snails are actually predators that feed on marine worms and other small invertebrates using a specialized feeding structure called a radula.

children.description: Haminoeidae are small, marine sea slugs that belong to a group called bubble snails. These soft-bodied mollusks have thin, fragile shells that are often partially or completely covered by their body when they move around. They live in shallow coastal waters where they glide along sandy or muddy bottoms feeding on algae and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many sea slugs that have lost their shells entirely, Haminoeidae retain delicate, bubble-like shells that are typically translucent or white. Their shells are often too small to fully contain their bodies, giving them a distinctive appearance where soft tissue extends beyond the shell opening.
children.funFact: These bubble snails can actually swim by flapping the wing-like extensions of their body, allowing them to move through the water column rather than just crawling along the bottom.

children.name: Diaphanidae
Diaphana
children.description: Diaphana is a genus of small, delicate sea snails known as bubble shells or paper bubble shells. These tiny marine gastropods have extremely thin, translucent shells that are so delicate they appear almost paper-like. They are specialized predators that feed on other small marine organisms in cold ocean waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Diaphana are distinguished by their remarkably thin, transparent shells that are often described as fragile as tissue paper. Unlike many other sea snails, their shells are so delicate that they can barely contain the animal's soft body.
children.funFact: The Arctic Paperbubble's shell is so thin and translucent that you can actually see the animal's internal organs through it when the snail is alive.

children.description: Diaphanidae is a family of small, delicate sea snails known as bubble shells. These marine gastropods have thin, translucent shells that are often partially or completely covered by the animal's soft body when they're active.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other sea snails, diaphanids have very fragile, glass-like shells that are often colorless or white, and their soft body tissues can extend over much of the shell's surface.
children.funFact: These tiny sea snails are carnivorous hunters that use a specialized feeding structure called a radula to drill holes in their prey, often targeting other small mollusks and marine worms.

children.name: Tornatinidae
Acteocina
children.description: Acteocina is a genus of small sea snails known as barrel-bubble snails, which are marine gastropod mollusks. These tiny creatures have thin, delicate shells that are typically barrel-shaped or cylindrical, and they live in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms where they burrow and feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Acteocina shells are characterized by their smooth, glossy surface and distinctive barrel-like shape with a narrow opening. Unlike many other sea snails, they have very thin, almost transparent shells that can appear quite fragile.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, these tiny snails are actually predators that use a specialized feeding structure called a radula to scrape up small organisms and organic matter from the seafloor.

children.description: Tornatinidae are small marine snails known as barrel bubble shells or miniature bubble snails. These tiny gastropods have delicate, translucent shells that are often cylindrical or barrel-shaped, and they live in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms where they hunt for prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical snails, tornatinids have very thin, fragile shells that are often partially covered by the animal's soft body. Their shells lack the thick, spiraled construction of most marine snails and instead have a smooth, bubble-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their small size and delicate appearance, these bubble snails are actually predators that use a specialized feeding structure to capture and consume tiny marine worms and other small organisms in the sediment.

children.name: Cylichnidae
Cylichna
children.description: Cylichna is a genus of small sea snails known as barrel bubble shells or bubble snails. These marine mollusks have distinctive cylindrical or barrel-shaped shells that are typically smooth and glossy, and they live in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms where they burrow and feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cylichna shells are characterized by their elongated, cylindrical shape that resembles a tiny barrel, with a narrow opening and no visible spire. Unlike many other sea snails, their shells are completely smooth without ridges or spiral patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being snails, Cylichna species are actually predators that use a specialized feeding structure to capture and consume small worms and other tiny marine animals in the sediment.

children.description: Cylichnidae is a family of small sea snails known as bubble shells that have evolved to live a burrowing lifestyle in marine sediments. These gastropods have thin, cylindrical or barrel-shaped shells that are often translucent, and they spend most of their time buried in sand or mud on the ocean floor. They are carnivorous mollusks that hunt for small prey like other marine worms and tiny crustaceans in the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical sea snails, cylichnids have shells that are completely external but often partially or fully covered by the animal's soft body parts called the mantle. Their shells are characteristically smooth, cylindrical, and lack the spiral coiling pattern seen in most other gastropods.
children.funFact: Despite being snails, many cylichnids can actually swim by flapping enlarged portions of their foot like wings, earning some species the nickname 'sea butterflies' when they take to the water column.

children.description: Bubble snails and their allies are small marine gastropods that have evolved a distinctive way of life. These sea snails have reduced or completely internal shells that are often thin and fragile, giving them their 'bubble' appearance when visible.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical snails with prominent external shells, bubble snails have shells that are either very thin and translucent or completely hidden within their soft body tissues. Their shells cannot fully contain their bodies, so the soft parts often extend beyond the shell opening.
children.funFact: Many bubble snails are carnivorous hunters that specialize in eating other small mollusks, using their radula (rasping tongue) to drill through their prey's shells.

children.name: Epitoniidae
Epitonium
children.description: Epitonium is a genus of small to medium-sized sea snails commonly known as wentletraps. These marine gastropods are characterized by their distinctive spiral shells with prominent ridges or ribs that run across the whorls, creating a ladder-like appearance. They are predatory snails that feed primarily on sea anemones and corals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wentletraps are easily recognized by their tall, conical shells with pronounced transverse ribs or ridges that give them a sculptured, step-like appearance. Unlike many other sea snails, their shells are typically white or pale-colored and have a glossy, porcelain-like finish.
children.funFact: When threatened, wentletraps can release a purple dye as a defense mechanism, similar to how squid release ink to confuse predators.

children.name: Gyroscala
children.description: Gyroscala is a genus of small marine snails known as wentletraps, characterized by their distinctive spiral shells with prominent ridges or ribs running across the whorls. These elegant gastropods are predators that feed on sea anemones and other cnidarians, using specialized feeding techniques to consume their prey. They are typically found in shallow coastal waters where their prey is abundant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gyroscala wentletraps are distinguished from other wentletrap genera by their relatively smooth shell surface between the ribs and their specific spiral shell proportions. The genus has a more compact shell shape compared to many other wentletrap species.
children.funFact: When threatened, Gyroscala wentletraps can release a purple dye as a defense mechanism, similar to how some other marine gastropods use ink to confuse predators.

children.name: Boreoscala
children.description: Boreoscala is a genus of small sea snails known as wentletraps, which are marine gastropod mollusks that live in cold northern waters. These delicate snails have distinctive spiral shells with prominent ridges or ribs running across each whorl, giving them a sculptured appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boreoscala species are distinguished from other wentletraps by their robust shell construction and adaptation to Arctic and subarctic marine environments, particularly their ability to thrive in the cold waters of the North Atlantic.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Boreoscala greenlandica, can be found in waters as far north as Greenland and represents one of the most cold-adapted members of the wentletrap family.

children.description: Wentletraps and violet snails are small to medium-sized marine gastropods known for their distinctive spiral shells with prominent ridges or ribs running across the whorls. These predatory snails feed primarily on sea anemones and corals, using specialized feeding strategies to overcome their stinging prey. Most species live in shallow coastal waters, though some can be found in deeper offshore environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their shells are characterized by strong axial ribs or varices that create a ladder-like appearance, giving wentletraps their name (from the Dutch word for 'spiral staircase'). Unlike many other marine snails, they have a specialized proboscis for feeding on cnidarians and can produce a purple dye when threatened.
children.funFact: Some wentletrap species were once so highly prized by collectors that perfect specimens sold for more than their weight in gold, leading to an 18th-century trade in clever ceramic forgeries.

children.name: Limapontiidae
Placida
children.description: Placida is a genus of tiny, delicate sea slugs that are specialized plant-eaters of the marine world. These small mollusks have evolved to feed exclusively on green algae, using their radula (a feeding organ like a rasping tongue) to scrape algae from surfaces in shallow coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Placida are distinguished by their extremely small size, translucent bodies, and highly specialized diet of green algae. Unlike many other sea slugs that eat a variety of prey, Placida species are strict herbivores with bodies adapted specifically for grazing on algae.
children.funFact: Despite being mollusks like clams and oysters, Placida sea slugs have no shell and can incorporate chloroplasts from the algae they eat into their own tissues, temporarily giving them the ability to photosynthesize like plants!

children.name: Alderia
children.description: Alderia is a genus of tiny sea slugs that have evolved an extraordinary ability to steal and use chloroplasts from the algae they eat. These small marine mollusks live in salt marshes and tidal areas where they graze on filamentous green algae. They can photosynthesize like plants by keeping the stolen chloroplasts alive in their tissues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most sea slugs, Alderia species have a smooth, streamlined body without the elaborate projections or gills found in many other nudibranchs. They are distinguished by their ability to retain functional chloroplasts and their preference for salt marsh habitats.
children.funFact: Alderia can survive for months without eating by using the stolen chloroplasts to produce their own food through photosynthesis, essentially turning themselves into solar-powered animals.

children.name: Ercolania
children.description: Ercolania is a genus of tiny sea slugs that live in marine environments, feeding on algae and other small organisms. These soft-bodied mollusks are part of the sacoglossan group, which are known for their plant-like feeding habits. They are among the smaller sea slugs you might encounter in New England waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ercolania sea slugs are distinguished by their small size and relatively simple body structure compared to other sea slug groups. They lack the elaborate projections or bright colors found in many other sea slug species.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny, Ercolania sea slugs are accomplished algae farmers - they can actually steal chloroplasts from the algae they eat and use them to photosynthesize like plants!

children.description: Limapontiidae is a family of tiny sea slugs that have developed an amazing ability to steal chloroplasts from the algae they eat and use them for photosynthesis. These small, soft-bodied marine creatures are essentially solar-powered animals that can make their own food using sunlight. They're typically found in shallow coastal waters where they graze on algae and seaweeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs, members of this family can incorporate functional chloroplasts from their algae prey into their own tissues, allowing them to photosynthesize. They tend to be very small and have simple, elongated body shapes without the elaborate projections seen in many other sea slug families.
children.funFact: These remarkable sea slugs are sometimes called 'solar-powered slugs' because they can survive for weeks or even months without eating, living entirely off the energy produced by their stolen chloroplasts through photosynthesis.

children.name: Physidae
Physella
children.description: Physella is a genus of small freshwater snails commonly known as bladder snails or physa snails. These air-breathing aquatic snails have thin, translucent shells that spiral to the left (sinistral) and are found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most snails, Physella species have shells that coil to the left rather than the right, and their shells are notably thin and fragile. They also have a distinctive pointed spire and can be seen gliding upside-down along the water surface.
children.funFact: These snails can survive out of water for extended periods by sealing themselves inside their shells with a mucus plug, allowing them to wait out dry conditions until their habitat refills with water.

children.name: Sibirenauta
children.description: Sibirenauta is a genus of small freshwater snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These aquatic gastropods are part of the physid family and have thin, elongated spiral shells that help them glide through aquatic vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sibirenauta snails are distinguished by their notably elongated, lance-shaped shells that are more slender than most other freshwater snails in their family.
children.funFact: The Lance Aplexa gets its name from its distinctively narrow, spear-like shell shape that helps it navigate efficiently through dense underwater plant growth.

children.description: Bladder snails are small freshwater snails that get their name from their thin, translucent shells that look like tiny bubbles or bladders. These aquatic gastropods are commonly found in ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and even temporary water bodies throughout New England. They are left-handed snails, meaning their shells spiral in a counterclockwise direction when viewed from above.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other freshwater snails, bladder snails have shells that spiral to the left (sinistral) rather than to the right. Their shells are also notably thin and fragile, often appearing almost glass-like in their transparency.
children.funFact: Bladder snails can survive in temporary pools that dry up completely by burying themselves in mud and entering a dormant state until water returns.

children.name: Pteropoda
Limacinidae
Limacina
children.description: Limacina is a genus of tiny sea snails that have evolved wing-like extensions of their foot, allowing them to 'fly' through the water column. These delicate creatures are part of the plankton community, drifting and swimming in open ocean waters rather than crawling along the seafloor like most snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical sea snails, Limacina species have developed parapodia - wing-like flaps that beat rapidly to propel them through the water. They retain a delicate, often transparent shell that coils in a left-handed (sinistral) spiral.
children.funFact: These 'sea butterflies' can beat their wing-like parapodia up to 600 times per minute, creating tiny whirlpools that help them capture even smaller plankton for food.

children.description: Limacinidae are a family of small, swimming sea snails that live in the open ocean rather than on the seafloor. These tiny marine gastropods have delicate, translucent shells and use modified foot structures like wings to glide through the water column. They are part of the plankton community, drifting with ocean currents while feeding on even smaller organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most snails that crawl along surfaces, Limacinidae have evolved specialized wing-like extensions of their foot that allow them to swim freely through the water. Their shells are typically very thin and often spiral-shaped, adapted for their planktonic lifestyle.
children.funFact: These "sea butterflies" are so numerous in some parts of the ocean that they form massive swarms visible from space, and they play a crucial role in marine food webs as a primary food source for fish, seabirds, and whales.

children.name: Cymbuliidae
Corolla
children.description: Corolla is a genus of small, transparent marine animals that belong to the pteropod group - specialized snails that have adapted to life swimming in the open ocean. These delicate creatures have modified their foot into wing-like structures that they use to gracefully flutter through the water column, earning them the nickname 'sea butterflies.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Corolla species are distinguished by their large, barrel-shaped transparent shell that lacks the typical spiral form of most snails, and their prominent wing-like swimming appendages that extend from the front of their body.
children.funFact: Despite being snails, Corolla species spend their entire lives swimming in the open ocean and never crawl along surfaces like their terrestrial cousins.

children.description: Cymbuliidae is a family of small, transparent sea slugs that live in the open ocean and swim freely through the water column. These delicate marine snails have evolved a unique gelatinous, slipper-shaped shell that helps them maintain buoyancy as they drift with ocean currents. They are part of the larger group of sea butterflies, which are specialized swimming snails found in seas worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea butterflies, cymbuliids have a distinctive gelatinous pseudoconch (false shell) that is transparent and flexible rather than hard and calcified. Their shell opening is positioned on the side rather than at the front, giving them their characteristic slipper-like appearance.
children.funFact: These tiny ocean drifters are important food sources for whales, fish, and seabirds, despite being nearly invisible due to their crystal-clear, jelly-like bodies and shells.

children.name: Cliopsidae
Cliopsis
children.description: Cliopsis is a genus of tiny, transparent sea snails that swim freely in the open ocean rather than crawling along the seafloor like most snails. These delicate marine gastropods are part of the plankton community, drifting with ocean currents while actively hunting for even smaller prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical snails, Cliopsis species have evolved wing-like extensions of their foot called parapodia that they use for swimming, and their shells are extremely thin and cone-shaped to reduce weight in the water column.
children.funFact: Despite being snails, Cliopsis are voracious predators that use a specialized feeding structure to capture and devour other planktonic organisms, including copepods and fish larvae.

children.description: Cliopsidae is a small family of sea slugs known as sea angels or cliones. These transparent, gelatinous marine mollusks swim through ocean waters using wing-like appendages called parapodia that give them an angelic appearance as they gracefully glide through the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs that crawl along the bottom, sea angels are specialized for life in the open ocean and lack shells as adults. Their distinctive wing-like swimming appendages and transparent bodies make them easily recognizable among marine gastropods.
children.funFact: Sea angels are voracious predators that feed almost exclusively on sea butterflies (another type of swimming sea slug), using specialized hooks to extract their prey from their shells.

children.description: Sea butterflies are tiny, free-swimming marine snails that have evolved wing-like extensions of their foot to help them glide through the water column. These delicate creatures spend their entire lives floating in the open ocean, feeding on microscopic plankton and other small organisms. Despite being mollusks like clams and typical snails, they've adapted to a life of perpetual swimming in the sea.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other marine snails that crawl along the seafloor, sea butterflies have developed wing-like parapodia that allow them to 'fly' through the water. Many species have also evolved transparent, gelatinous shells or have lost their shells entirely, making them almost ghost-like in appearance.
children.funFact: Sea butterflies are so abundant in some parts of the ocean that they form the primary food source for bowhead whales, with a single whale consuming millions of these tiny creatures in one feeding session.

children.name: Turritellidae
Vermicularia
children.description: Vermicularia is a genus of marine gastropods known as wormsnails that have abandoned the typical snail lifestyle. Instead of crawling around with their shells, these mollusks permanently attach themselves to hard surfaces like rocks and coral reefs. They live inside irregularly coiled, tube-like shells that grow in twisted, worm-like patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical snails that can move freely, Vermicularia species cement themselves in place and feed by extending sticky mucus nets to capture plankton and organic particles from the water. Their shells grow in irregular, loosely coiled spirals rather than the neat, symmetrical coils of most gastropods.
children.funFact: These "wormsnails" are actually more closely related to typical garden snails than to marine worms, despite their deceiving name and appearance!

children.name: Tachyrhynchus
children.description: Tachyrhynchus is a genus of small weevils, which are beetles known for their distinctive elongated snouts or rostrums. These tiny insects are part of the diverse weevil family and are typically found in association with plants, where they feed and develop.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be identified by their characteristic long, narrow snout and small size, along with specific features of their body structure and wing covers that separate them from other weevil genera.
children.funFact: The name Tachyrhynchus literally means 'swift snout' in Greek, referring to these beetles' prominent elongated mouthparts that they use like tiny drills to bore into plant material.

children.name: Turritellinella
children.description: Turritellinella is a genus of marine snails known for their distinctive tall, spiral shells that resemble tiny towers. These gastropod mollusks live in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms where they burrow and feed on organic particles in the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have elongated, screw-like shells with multiple whorls and prominent ridges or carinae that spiral around the shell, giving them their characteristic tower-like appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Turritellinella' literally means 'little tower,' perfectly describing these snails' architectural shell structure that can contain dozens of spiraling chambers.

children.description: Tower snails are marine gastropods known for their distinctive tall, spiral shells that resemble miniature towers or screws. These snails live on sandy and muddy ocean bottoms, where they use their elongated shells as anchors while filter-feeding on tiny particles in the water. They are primarily found in deeper waters along the continental shelf.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tower snails can be identified by their extremely elongated, tightly coiled shells with many whorls that create a distinctive tower-like appearance. Unlike most other marine snails, their shells are much taller than they are wide, giving them their characteristic screw-like shape.
children.funFact: Some tower snails can live for over 100 years, continuously adding new whorls to their shells throughout their lives, creating a spiral record of their growth history.

children.name: Cerithiopsidae
Seila
children.description: Seila is a genus of very small marine snails that live in shallow coastal waters. These tiny gastropods have elongated, cone-shaped shells with distinctive spiral ridges and are part of the cerith family of sea snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Seila snails are distinguished by their miniature size and slender, pointed shells with pronounced spiral sculpturing that creates a distinctive ribbed appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'miniature ceriths,' these tiny snails are active grazers that help keep marine surfaces clean by feeding on algae and organic debris.

children.name: Cerithiopsis
children.description: Cerithiopsis is a genus of very small marine snails that live in coastal waters. These tiny gastropods have elongated, spiral shells with many whorls and are typically found crawling on surfaces like rocks, seaweed, or other shells in shallow marine environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cerithiopsis snails are distinguished by their extremely small size (usually less than 10mm) and their tall, narrow shells with numerous fine spiral ridges and axial ribs that create a distinctive sculptured pattern.
children.funFact: These snails are so small that they're often overlooked by beachcombers, but their intricate shell sculptures are considered some of the most beautiful and detailed patterns found in tiny marine gastropods.

children.description: Cerithiopsidae is a family of tiny marine snails that live in ocean waters along the New England coast. These miniature gastropods have elongated, spiral shells with multiple whorls and are typically less than half an inch long. They are active predators that crawl along the seafloor and rocky surfaces hunting for small prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These snails can be distinguished from other marine gastropods by their distinctively tall, narrow shells with many tightly-coiled whorls and a pointed spire. Their shells often have fine spiral ridges or sculpturing that gives them a delicate, ornate appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these snails are fierce predators that use a specialized feeding structure called a radula to drill holes in their prey and consume the soft tissues inside.

children.name: Plakobranchidae
Elysia
children.description: Elysias are small, leaf-shaped sea slugs that belong to a fascinating group of marine creatures called sacoglossans. These delicate animals have evolved the remarkable ability to steal and use chloroplasts from the algae they eat, allowing them to photosynthesize like plants. They glide gracefully through shallow coastal waters and tidal pools, feeding on various types of marine algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs, Elysias have flattened, leaf-like body extensions called parapodia that can be folded over their backs. Their ability to retain functional chloroplasts from their algae food and use them for photosynthesis sets them apart from most other animal groups.
children.funFact: The Eastern Emerald Elysia can survive for months without eating by using stolen chloroplasts to make its own food through photosynthesis, earning it the nickname 'solar-powered sea slug.'

children.description: Plakobranchidae are a family of small, colorful sea slugs that have developed an amazing ability to steal and use chloroplasts from the algae they eat. These marine mollusks can actually photosynthesize like plants, using the captured chloroplasts to produce their own food from sunlight. They're often called 'solar-powered sea slugs' because of this remarkable adaptation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs, plakobranchids can maintain functional chloroplasts from their algae prey in specialized cells within their bodies, allowing them to supplement their diet through photosynthesis. Their flattened, leaf-like body shape helps maximize surface area for capturing sunlight.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can survive for months without eating by relying solely on photosynthesis from their stolen chloroplasts, essentially living like solar-powered animals.

children.name: Nacellida
Lottiidae
Testudinalia
children.description: Testudinalia is a genus of marine limpets that are characterized by their distinctive tortoiseshell-patterned shells. These small mollusks are cone-shaped gastropods that attach firmly to rocks in the intertidal zone, where they graze on algae and other organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their mottled brown and tan shell patterns that resemble a tortoise's shell, giving them their common name of tortoiseshell limpets.
children.funFact: The tortoiseshell limpet can live for over 20 years, making it one of the longest-lived small invertebrates in New England's rocky shores.

children.description: Lottiid limpets are small marine snails that have evolved a cone-shaped shell and live attached to hard surfaces like rocks in the intertidal zone. Unlike typical snails that can withdraw into spiral shells, these limpets have flattened, cap-like shells that they clamp down tightly against rocks to resist crashing waves. They scrape algae and other small organisms off rock surfaces using their rough, ribbon-like tongue called a radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lottiid limpets can be distinguished from other limpet families by their muscle scar pattern inside the shell and the position of their gills. They typically have a horseshoe-shaped muscle scar and gills located in a groove around the edge of their body.
children.funFact: Some lottiid limpets are so well-adapted to their specific rock that they create a perfectly fitted home scar on the surface, returning to the exact same spot after each feeding excursion like a living puzzle piece.

children.description: Nacellida is an order of marine gastropod mollusks that includes the true limpets, characterized by their cone-shaped shells and ability to clamp tightly to rocky surfaces. These small sea snails are perfectly adapted for life in the intertidal zone, where they graze on algae and other microorganisms growing on rocks. They can withstand the constant pounding of waves and exposure to air during low tide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other limpet-like mollusks, true limpets in Nacellida have a distinctive gill arrangement and internal anatomy that sets them apart from keyhole limpets and slipper shells. They also lack the holes or slots found in other limpet groups.
children.funFact: Limpets are incredibly strong for their size - some species can withstand pulling forces up to 4,000 times their own body weight when clamped to a rock!

children.name: Valvatidae
Valvata
children.description: Valvata is a genus of small freshwater snails that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These tiny aquatic gastropods have distinctive spiral shells and breathe through both gills and a primitive lung, allowing them to survive in various water conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Valvata snails are unique among freshwater gastropods because they have both gills and a lung-like structure, plus they possess a feathery gill that can extend outside their shell. Their shells typically have distinct ridges or keels that spiral around the shell.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 6mm in size, Valvata snails can live for several years and play an important role as both algae grazers and food for fish and waterfowl.

children.description: Valve snails are tiny freshwater snails that live in lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They get their name from a unique gill structure that acts like a valve, helping them breathe underwater. These small mollusks are typically less than 6mm across and have spiral shells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other freshwater snails, valve snails have a distinctive feathery gill that can extend outside their shell opening, along with a unique operculum (trap door) that seals their shell when they retract inside.
children.funFact: Valve snails can actually breathe both underwater through their gills and at the water surface using a simple lung, making them remarkably adaptable to changing water conditions.

children.name: Trochida
Margaritidae
Margarites
children.description: Globe snails are small marine snails that live in cold northern waters along rocky coastlines. They get their name from their rounded, globe-like shells that have a pearly, iridescent interior surface. These snails are herbivores that graze on algae and other tiny marine plants growing on rocks and seaweed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Globe snails can be identified by their small, rounded shells with a distinctive pearly or silvery interior that shimmers when light hits it. Unlike many other marine snails, they have a relatively low spire and wide opening.
children.funFact: The pearly interior of globe snail shells is made of nacre, the same material that creates the lustrous coating inside oyster shells and forms natural pearls.

children.description: Margaritidae is a family of small marine snails known as trochid gastropods that live in cold ocean waters. These snails have distinctive coiled shells and are typically found crawling on rocky surfaces in shallow coastal areas, where they graze on algae and microscopic organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their relatively small, turban-shaped shells with a pearlescent interior layer. Unlike many other marine snails, they have a distinctive umbilicus (a hollow depression) at the base of their shell.
children.funFact: The name 'Margaritidae' comes from the Latin word for pearl, referring to the beautiful iridescent, mother-of-pearl lining found inside their shells.

children.description: Trochida is an order of marine snails that includes some of the most ancient and primitive gastropods still living today. These sea snails are characterized by their typically cone-shaped or top-shaped shells and are found in oceans worldwide, from shallow tidepools to deep waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other marine snails, members of Trochida have a special gill structure and often possess a distinctive nacreous (pearl-like) shell interior that gives them an iridescent appearance.
children.funFact: The shells of many Trochida snails have been used by humans for thousands of years to make buttons, jewelry, and decorative items because of their beautiful mother-of-pearl lining.

children.name: Cerithiidae
Bittiolum
children.description: Bittiolum is a genus of small marine snails that live in shallow coastal waters along the Atlantic coast. These tiny gastropods are characterized by their elongated, spiral shells with distinctive ridged patterns that help distinguish them from other marine snails.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bittiolum snails have tall, slender shells with alternating spiral ridges and grooves that create a distinctive sculptured appearance. Their shells are typically brown or gray and much smaller than most other marine snails you'll encounter.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 6-12 millimeters long, Brown Bittium can be incredibly abundant on mudflats and in eelgrass beds, sometimes occurring in densities of thousands per square meter.

children.description: Cerith snails are marine gastropods with tall, spiral shells that often have a pointed, cone-like shape. These sea snails are typically found in shallow coastal waters where they graze on algae and organic matter on rocks, seaweed, and other surfaces. They move slowly along the seafloor or climb on underwater vegetation using their muscular foot.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cerith snails can be recognized by their elongated, tower-like shells with many whorls (spiral turns) and a distinctive pointed spire. Their shells often have spiral ridges or bumps, and they typically have a small opening at the bottom where the snail can extend its body.
children.funFact: Some cerith snails can actually leave the water and crawl around on wet rocks during low tide, using a special gill chamber that can function like a primitive lung to breathe air temporarily.

children.name: Pleuroceridae
Elimia
children.description: Elimia is a genus of freshwater snails that live in rivers and streams throughout eastern North America. These aquatic gastropods have elongated, spiral shells and are often found clinging to rocks or crawling along the bottom of flowing waters. They are herbivorous, feeding on algae and other plant matter that they scrape from surfaces using their rasping tongue called a radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Elimia snails are distinguished from other freshwater snails by their tall, conical shells with multiple whorls and their preference for fast-flowing, well-oxygenated streams and rivers rather than still waters like ponds or lakes.
children.funFact: Many Elimia species, including the Piedmont Elimia, are considered living fossils because they have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years and represent ancient lineages of freshwater snails.

children.description: Pleuroceridae is a family of freshwater snails that live in rivers and streams. These aquatic gastropods have elongated, cone-shaped shells and are commonly found crawling on rocks and other hard surfaces in flowing water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctively tall, pointed shells with multiple whorls that spiral upward, and they possess an operculum (a hard plate) that can seal their shell opening for protection.
children.funFact: These snails are excellent indicators of water quality - their presence usually signals clean, well-oxygenated streams and rivers.

children.name: Aplysiida
Aplysiidae
Aplysia
children.description: Aplysia is a genus of large sea slugs commonly known as sea hares. These soft-bodied marine animals are herbivorous mollusks that graze on seaweeds and algae in shallow coastal waters. They have reduced internal shells and can grow quite large compared to other sea slugs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sea hares are distinguished by their rabbit-like ear projections called rhinophores and their ability to release purple or white ink when threatened. Unlike many sea slugs, they retain a thin, flexible shell inside their body.
children.funFact: When disturbed, sea hares can release a cloud of purple ink that was once used by ancient civilizations to dye fabrics, earning them the nickname 'sea purple' producers.

children.description: Seahares are large, soft-bodied sea slugs that get their name from the rabbit-ear-like projections on their heads called rhinophores. These marine gastropods have lost most of their shell through evolution, retaining only a small, thin internal shell plate. They are herbivorous creatures that graze on seaweeds and algae in shallow coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs, seahares have a large, fleshy body with wing-like extensions called parapodia that they can flap for swimming. They also possess an internal shell remnant rather than an external shell or no shell at all.
children.funFact: When threatened, seahares can release a dramatic cloud of purple or reddish ink made from the pigments of the red and brown seaweeds they eat, creating a smokescreen to confuse predators.

children.description: Sea hares and akera snails are soft-bodied marine mollusks that have reduced or internal shells, unlike typical snails with prominent external shells. These sea slugs are herbivores that graze on seaweeds and algae in coastal waters. They get their name from their rabbit-like appearance, with tentacles that resemble ears.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sea slugs, sea hares have a thin, flexible internal shell remnant and can grow quite large. They also have four tentacles on their head, giving them their distinctive rabbit-like appearance.
children.funFact: When threatened, sea hares can release a cloud of purple or red ink to confuse predators and make their escape.

children.name: Lepetellida
Fissurellidae
Puncturella
children.description: Puncturellas are small marine snails known as keyhole limpets that live attached to rocks in cold ocean waters. They have cone-shaped shells with a distinctive keyhole-like opening at the top, which they use for breathing and waste removal. These tiny mollusks graze on algae and other organic matter growing on rocky surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true limpets, puncturellas have a characteristic oval or keyhole-shaped hole at the apex of their cone-shaped shell. This opening distinguishes them from other limpet-like mollusks that have solid, unperforated shells.
children.funFact: The keyhole opening in their shell acts like a natural chimney, creating water flow that helps them breathe efficiently while staying firmly attached to rocks in turbulent waters.

children.description: Keyhole limpets are marine snails with cone-shaped shells that have a distinctive hole or slit at the top. They use this opening to expel water after filtering it through their gills for breathing and feeding. Like other limpets, they cling tightly to rocks and hard surfaces in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The keyhole or slit at the apex of their shell sets them apart from true limpets, which have solid, unperforated shells. This opening serves as an exhaust port for their breathing current.
children.funFact: The hole in their shell acts like a natural snorkel, allowing them to breathe efficiently while staying clamped down tightly on rocks during rough surf.

children.description: Lepetellida is an order of small marine snails that includes the keyhole limpets and their relatives. These gastropods are characterized by their cone-shaped shells and their ability to cling tightly to rocky surfaces in coastal waters. Most members of this group are herbivores that graze on algae and other marine plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Lepetellida apart from other limpet groups is their distinctive shell opening - many have a keyhole-shaped hole or slit at the top of their cone-shaped shell that serves as an exhale opening for water circulation.
children.funFact: The keyhole-shaped opening in these limpets' shells acts like a natural chimney, allowing water to flow in around the bottom edge of the shell and exit through the top hole, creating a continuous flow that brings oxygen and food while removing waste.

children.name: Omalogyridae
Omalogyra
children.description: Omalogyra is a genus of tiny marine snails that are among the smallest gastropods in the world. These microscopic mollusks live in sandy and muddy ocean sediments, where they feed on organic matter and bacteria.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These snails are characterized by their extremely small size (usually less than 2mm) and their distinctive flat, spiral shells with a smooth, glossy surface.
children.funFact: Omalogyra snails are so small that dozens could fit on the head of a pin, making them easily overlooked despite being relatively common in marine sediments.

children.description: Omalogyrid snails are tiny marine gastropods that are among the smallest snails in the world, typically measuring less than 2 millimeters across. These microscopic creatures live in marine environments, often found among algae, in sand, or on other surfaces in coastal waters. They have delicate, translucent spiral shells that are almost glass-like in appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Omalogyrid snails are distinguished by their extremely small size and their uniquely thin, nearly transparent shells that often appear almost colorless or whitish. Unlike many other small marine snails, they lack an operculum (the door-like structure that closes the shell opening).
children.funFact: These snails are so tiny that they can easily pass through most standard sieves used by marine biologists, making them challenging to study and often overlooked in marine surveys despite being relatively common.

children.name: Newtoniellidae
Retilaskeya
children.description: Retilaskeya is a genus of tiny marine snails that belong to the cerith family. These miniature gastropods have elongated, spiral shells and are among the smallest marine snails found in New England waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size and delicate, finely-sculptured shells with numerous whorls relative to their tiny stature.
children.funFact: Despite being so small that they're easily overlooked, these tiny snails play an important role in marine ecosystems as both grazers of microscopic algae and food for larger invertebrates.

children.description: Newtoniellidae is a small family of marine gastropod mollusks, commonly known as sea snails. These tiny creatures live in ocean environments and are characterized by their spiral shells and soft bodies that can retract inside for protection.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their specific shell structure and anatomical features that separate them from other sea snail families, though they require microscopic examination to identify properly.
children.funFact: This family is so small and specialized that New England has only one known species, making any local specimen a relatively rare find for shell collectors.

children.name: Parhedylidae
Microhedyle
children.description: Microhedyle is a genus of tiny marine gastropods that are among the smallest sea slugs in the world. These microscopic creatures live in the spaces between sand grains in intertidal zones, where they feed on bacteria and other microorganisms. They are part of a specialized group of mollusks that have adapted to life in this unique sandy habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Microhedyle species are distinguished by their extremely small size (less than 2mm) and their simplified body structure adapted for living between sand grains. Unlike many other sea slugs, they have retained a small internal shell and have a cylindrical, worm-like body shape.
children.funFact: These tiny sea slugs are so small that dozens could fit on the head of a pin, yet they represent one of the most specialized adaptations to marine interstitial life found anywhere in the ocean.

children.description: Parhedylidae is a small family of tiny marine sea slugs that live in sandy and muddy seafloor environments. These microscopic mollusks are specialized for life in the spaces between sand grains, where they feed on organic matter and microorganisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most sea slugs, parhedylids have retained a small internal shell and have extremely simplified body structures adapted for their interstitial lifestyle between sand particles.
children.funFact: These sea slugs are so small that they can live their entire lives in the tiny water-filled spaces between grains of sand on the ocean floor.

children.name: Hermaeidae
Hermaea
children.description: Hermaea is a genus of tiny sea slugs that are specialized plant-eaters of the ocean. These small, colorful marine gastropods feed on algae and have the remarkable ability to incorporate the chloroplasts from their algal food into their own tissues, allowing them to photosynthesize like plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most sea slugs that are carnivorous, Hermaea species are herbivorous and have evolved finger-like projections called cerata that can store stolen chloroplasts from algae. They are typically very small, usually less than 10mm in length, with translucent bodies that often show green coloration from their incorporated plant cells.
children.funFact: Hermaea sea slugs are essentially solar-powered animals - they can survive for weeks without eating by using the stolen chloroplasts in their bodies to convert sunlight into energy, just like plants do.

children.description: Hermaeidae is a small family of tiny sea slugs that are specialized plant-eaters of the ocean. These delicate marine creatures feed exclusively on green algae, using their specialized feeding structures to pierce algal cells and suck out the contents.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other sea slugs, hermaeids have distinctive finger-like projections called cerata that contain extensions of their digestive system. They are among the smallest nudibranchs, typically measuring only a few millimeters in length.
children.funFact: Some hermaeids can actually steal chloroplasts from the algae they eat and use them to photosynthesize their own food, essentially becoming solar-powered animals for short periods.

children.name: Unionida
Unionidae
Lampsilis
children.description: Lampmussels are medium to large freshwater mussels found in rivers and lakes throughout New England. These filter-feeding mollusks have distinctive oval to elongated shells and play important roles in keeping waterways clean by filtering algae and particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lampmussels can be identified by their relatively large size, smooth shell surfaces, and often colorful patterns of green, yellow, or brown rays radiating from the shell's peak.
children.funFact: Female lampmussels use a clever trick to reproduce - they display a lure that looks like a small fish or worm to attract actual fish, then release their larvae which attach to the fish's gills for a free ride to new habitat.

children.name: Alasmidonta
children.description: Alasmidonta is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers and streams throughout New England. These filter-feeding mollusks have elongated, somewhat triangular shells and play important roles in keeping waterways clean by filtering particles from the water. Like other freshwater mussels, they have fascinating life cycles that depend on fish hosts to help their young develop and spread to new locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Alasmidonta can be identified by their relatively thin, elongated shells that are typically yellow-green to brown in color with distinctive growth rings. They tend to be smaller and more streamlined than many other freshwater mussel genera, with shells that are often somewhat compressed from side to side.
children.funFact: Brook Floaters are so sensitive to water quality that they're considered an indicator species - their presence tells scientists that a stream ecosystem is healthy and unpolluted.

children.name: Pyganodon
children.description: Floater mussels are large freshwater bivalves that live in the muddy or sandy bottoms of rivers, lakes, and ponds throughout New England. They get their name from their ability to 'float' or move slowly through sediment using their muscular foot, and they can live for decades while filtering water and algae for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Floater mussels are distinguished from other freshwater mussels by their thin, lightweight shells that lack the thick hinge teeth found in many related species. Their shells are typically elongated and can reach impressive sizes, especially in the Giant Floater.
children.funFact: A single floater mussel can filter up to 20 gallons of water per day, making them nature's water purifiers that help keep our freshwater ecosystems clean and healthy.

children.name: Potamilus
children.description: Potamilus is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers and streams. These filter-feeding mollusks have thin, relatively fragile shells compared to many other mussel species. They play an important role in keeping waterways clean by filtering particles and nutrients from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably thin, lightweight shells that can be quite delicate - hence names like 'papershell' and references to fragility. Their shells tend to be more compressed and have a distinctive elongated shape compared to bulkier freshwater mussel species.
children.funFact: These mussels have a fascinating reproductive strategy where their larvae, called glochidia, must attach to the gills or fins of specific fish species to complete their development before dropping off to live independently on the river bottom.

children.name: Lasmigona
children.description: Lasmigona is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the sandy and muddy bottoms of streams and rivers. These medium-sized bivalves filter water through their bodies to feed on tiny particles of algae and organic matter, playing an important role in keeping waterways clean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their elongated, somewhat compressed shells with distinctive ridges or furrows that give them their common names like 'heelsplitter' and 'flutedshell.'
children.funFact: Like many freshwater mussels, Lasmigona species have a fascinating life cycle where their larvae must attach to fish gills as parasites before developing into free-living adults.

children.name: Elliptio
children.description: Elliptio is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers and streams. These bivalve mollusks have elongated, oval-shaped shells and spend most of their lives filtering water through their bodies to feed on tiny particles like algae and bacteria.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Elliptio mussels are recognized by their distinctively flattened, elliptical shells that are typically brownish or greenish in color. Unlike many other freshwater mussel genera, they have relatively smooth shells without prominent ridges or sculpturing.
children.funFact: Elliptio mussels can live for decades and act as natural water filters, with a single adult capable of filtering several gallons of water per day to remove pollutants and excess nutrients.

children.name: Utterbackiana
children.description: Utterbackiana is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers and streams. These filter-feeding bivalves pump water through their shells to capture tiny particles of food like algae and bacteria. Like other freshwater mussels, they play an important role in keeping waterways clean by filtering large amounts of water each day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Utterbackiana mussels are distinguished by their relatively thin, elongated shells and their preference for flowing water habitats rather than still ponds or lakes. They have a distinctive shell shape that helps them burrow effectively into sandy river bottoms.
children.funFact: The genus Utterbackiana was named after William Utterback, an early 20th century malacologist who made significant contributions to our understanding of freshwater mussels in North America.

children.name: Atlanticoncha
children.description: Atlanticoncha is a genus of freshwater mussels found in Atlantic coastal rivers and streams. These bivalves are filter feeders that live buried in sandy or muddy river bottoms, playing important roles in aquatic ecosystems by cleaning water as they feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their yellowish-brown to olive shell coloration and their specific association with tidal freshwater habitats along the Atlantic coast.
children.funFact: The Tidewater Mucket can live for over 20 years and requires fish hosts to complete its larval development, with its larvae (called glochidia) attaching to fish gills before metamorphosing into juvenile mussels.

children.name: Strophitus
children.description: Strophitus is a genus of freshwater mussels found in rivers and streams across eastern North America. These bivalves are filter feeders that play an important role in keeping waterways clean by removing particles and nutrients from the water as they feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Strophitus mussels are distinguished by their elongated, kidney-shaped shells and their preference for flowing water habitats rather than still ponds or lakes.
children.funFact: Like many freshwater mussels, Strophitus species have a fascinating life cycle that requires fish hosts - their larvae attach to fish gills or fins to complete their development before dropping off to become free-living adults.

children.name: Sagittunio
children.description: Sagittunio is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the muddy or sandy bottoms of rivers and streams. These filter-feeding mollusks pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles like algae and bacteria. They play an important role in keeping waterways clean by filtering large amounts of water each day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sagittunio mussels are characterized by their elongated, arrow-like shell shape that gives the genus its name (sagittarius means 'archer' in Latin). They have a distinctive pointed posterior end that helps distinguish them from other freshwater mussel genera.
children.funFact: A single Eastern Pondmussel can filter up to 15 gallons of water per day, making them natural water purification systems in their aquatic ecosystems.

children.name: Utterbackia
children.description: Utterbackia is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the soft sediments of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These bivalves are filter feeders that play an important role in keeping water clean by straining tiny particles and algae from the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their thin, fragile shells and relatively small size compared to other freshwater mussels. They have a distinctive elongated, somewhat triangular shell shape that helps them burrow into soft substrates.
children.funFact: Paper Pondshells get their common name from their remarkably thin, almost papery shells that can be easily crushed by hand - a adaptation that allows them to thrive in soft sediments where thicker-shelled mussels might struggle.

children.name: Prolasmidonta
children.description: Prolasmidonta is a genus of small freshwater mussels found in clean, fast-flowing streams and rivers. These tiny bivalves are among the smallest freshwater mussels in North America, playing an important role in filtering water and maintaining stream ecosystem health.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their exceptionally small size compared to other freshwater mussels, and their preference for high-quality, well-oxygenated waters with rocky or sandy bottoms.
children.funFact: The Dwarf Wedgemussel is so small that a full-grown adult can fit on a quarter, yet it can live for over 30 years while filtering gallons of water daily through its tiny body.

children.description: River mussels are freshwater bivalves that live buried in the sandy or muddy bottoms of streams, rivers, and lakes throughout New England. These filter-feeding mollusks have two hinged shells that protect their soft bodies while they pump water through their gills to capture microscopic food particles. They play a crucial role in keeping our waterways clean by filtering enormous amounts of water each day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike marine mussels, river mussels have much thicker, heavier shells and lack the strong attachment threads (byssal threads) that ocean mussels use to cling to rocks. Their shells often display beautiful patterns of rays, bands, or colors that help distinguish different species.
children.funFact: River mussels have one of the most remarkable reproductive strategies in the animal kingdom - they trick fish into carrying their babies by disguising their larvae-filled gill flaps as worms, crayfish, or even small fish to lure host fish close enough to release clouds of tiny larvae that attach to the fish's gills.

children.name: Margaritiferidae
Margaritifera
children.description: Margaritifera is a genus of large, long-lived freshwater mussels that are famous for producing natural pearls. These ancient mollusks can live for over 100 years and play important roles as filter feeders in river ecosystems. They have thick, dark shells and require very clean, cold water to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other freshwater mussels, Margaritifera species have extremely long lifespans and can actually produce valuable pearls. Their shells are notably thick and heavy compared to other freshwater mussels.
children.funFact: The Freshwater Pearl Mussel can live for over 250 years, making it one of the longest-lived animals on Earth - some specimens alive today may have been filtering river water since before the American Revolution!

children.description: Margaritiferidae is a small family of freshwater mussels known for their exceptional longevity and ability to produce pearls. These ancient mollusks are filter feeders that bury themselves partially in river and stream bottoms, where they can live for over a century while cleaning the water around them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most freshwater mussels, margaritiferids have extremely thick, heavy shells and can produce high-quality freshwater pearls. They also have unusually long lifespans compared to their relatives, often living 80-200+ years.
children.funFact: Some margaritiferid mussels are among the longest-lived animals on Earth - the oldest recorded specimen lived to be 280 years old, meaning it was alive during the American Revolutionary War!

children.description: Freshwater mussels are bivalve mollusks that live their entire lives in rivers, streams, and lakes rather than in the ocean. These filter-feeding animals have two hinged shells that protect their soft bodies and use a muscular foot to burrow into sandy or muddy bottoms. They play a crucial role in keeping our waterways clean by filtering algae, bacteria, and particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their marine cousins, freshwater mussels have adapted to life in freshwater environments and have much thicker, less colorful shells. Most species have a unique reproductive strategy where their larvae must attach to fish gills to complete their development.
children.funFact: A single freshwater mussel can filter up to 15 gallons of water per day, making them nature's water purification systems that help keep our rivers and streams crystal clear.

children.name: Venerida
Veneridae
Mercenaria
children.description: Quahogs are large, thick-shelled clams that burrow in sandy and muddy bottoms of coastal waters. These hard-shell clams are prized for their sweet meat and have been an important food source for both Native Americans and European settlers for centuries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Quahogs have distinctively thick, heavy shells with prominent growth rings and a deep purple interior edge. Their shells are much more robust than other local clams like soft-shell clams or razor clams.
children.funFact: The purple portions of quahog shells were traditionally used by Native Americans to make wampum beads, which served as currency and ceremonial objects.

children.name: Petricolaria
children.description: Petricolaria is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks that are specialized for boring into hard substrates like rocks, shells, and pier pilings. These clams have evolved powerful digging abilities and modified shells that allow them to excavate permanent burrows in solid materials. They are filter feeders that extend their siphons from their burrows to capture plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other boring clams, Petricolaria species have thin, elongated shells with distinctive ridged surfaces that help them rasp through hard materials. Their shells are typically white to grayish and have a characteristic gaping posterior end where the siphons extend.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'False Angelwing,' Petricolaria pholadiformis can bore through materials as hard as concrete and limestone, creating perfectly fitted burrows that they rarely leave once established.

children.name: Ruditapes
children.description: Ruditapes is a genus of medium-sized saltwater clams that live buried in sandy and muddy bottoms of coastal waters. These clams are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny plants and organic particles for food. They have two hinged shells that can close tightly to protect the soft body inside.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ruditapes clams can be identified by their oval-shaped shells with distinct growth rings and a pattern of radiating lines from the hinge. Their shells are typically grayish-brown with darker markings and have a smooth, polished appearance.
children.funFact: The Japanese Littleneck clam was accidentally introduced to New England waters in the 1980s and has become so successful that it's now harvested commercially alongside native clams.

children.name: Gemma
children.description: Gemma is a genus of tiny marine clams that live buried in sandy and muddy sediments along coastlines. These small bivalve mollusks are characterized by their delicate, translucent shells and diminutive size, typically measuring less than 5 millimeters across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely small size and thin, fragile shells that are often nearly transparent or translucent, giving them a gem-like appearance that inspired their name.
children.funFact: The Amethyst Gem Clam can reproduce by hermaphroditic self-fertilization, meaning a single individual can produce offspring without needing to find a mate.

children.name: Agriopoma
children.description: Agriopoma is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks that includes clam-like creatures living in ocean waters. These shellfish have two hinged shells that protect their soft bodies and filter feed by drawing water through their shells to capture tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Agriopoma are distinguished from true quahogs and other clams by their specific shell characteristics and internal anatomy, though they share a similar overall appearance with other bivalves.
children.funFact: The False Quahog gets its common name because it resembles the familiar quahog clam that's popular in New England cuisine, but it's actually a different species entirely.

children.name: Chione
children.description: Chione is a genus of marine clams known as venus clams that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These bivalve mollusks have thick, sturdy shells with prominent ridges or cross-hatched patterns that help protect them from predators and wave action.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chione clams are distinguished by their heavy, sculptured shells with distinctive cross-barred or latticed surface patterns formed by intersecting ridges. Their shells are typically more robust and ornate compared to other venus clam genera.
children.funFact: The name Chione comes from the Greek goddess of snow, likely referring to the often whitish color of these clams' shells when found washed up on beaches.

children.name: Saxidomus
children.description: Saxidomus is a genus of large, thick-shelled clams that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These robust bivalves are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture plankton and other small particles for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their heavy, oval-shaped shells with prominent growth rings and a thick, sturdy construction that can withstand rough ocean conditions.
children.funFact: Purple Butterclams can live for over 20 years and their shells often develop a beautiful purple coloration on the interior, which is how they got their common name.

children.name: Turtonia
children.description: Turtonia is a genus of tiny marine bivalve mollusks that live attached to rocks, shells, and other hard surfaces in shallow coastal waters. These minute clams are among the smallest bivalves found in New England waters, typically measuring less than 3 millimeters across. They filter feed by drawing water through their shells to capture microscopic plankton and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Turtonia can be distinguished from other small bivalves by their extremely small size, rounded shell shape, and their habit of cementing themselves permanently to hard surfaces. Unlike many other bivalves that can move or burrow, these tiny mollusks remain fixed in place once they settle as juveniles.
children.funFact: Despite being one of the smallest bivalves in New England waters, Turtonia minuta was one of the last marine mollusks to be discovered in the region, not being formally recognized until the mid-20th century due to its tiny size and inconspicuous nature.

children.description: Venus clams are a diverse family of bivalve mollusks that live buried in sand, mud, or nestled in rocky crevices along our coastlines. These clams are characterized by their sturdy, often heart-shaped or oval shells with prominent growth rings that tell the story of their age. Most Venus clams are filter feeders, using their siphons to draw in water and extract tiny particles of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Venus clams can be identified by their thick, robust shells with well-defined hinge teeth that lock the two shell halves together securely. Unlike many other clam families, they typically have three cardinal teeth on each valve and distinct pallial sinuses (indentations) where their retractable siphons attach.
children.funFact: The famous quahog clam, a member of this family, can live for over 500 years - some specimens found off Iceland have been among the longest-lived animals ever discovered!

children.name: Mactridae
Spisula
children.description: Spisula is a genus of large, robust clams known as surf clams that live buried in sandy ocean bottoms. These bivalve mollusks are characterized by their thick, triangular to oval shells and their ability to thrive in the high-energy environment of the surf zone where waves constantly crash onto shore.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spisula clams are distinguished from other clam genera by their particularly thick, heavy shells and their large size, often growing much bigger than most other clam species in New England waters.
children.funFact: The West Atlantic Surfclam can live for over 30 years and grows so large that a single clam can weigh more than a pound, making it one of the largest clams found along New England's coast.

children.name: Mulinia
children.description: Mulinia is a genus of small, oval-shaped clams that live buried in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. These bivalves are filter feeders that pump water through their shells to capture tiny food particles like plankton and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mulinia clams have triangular, wedge-shaped shells that are typically white or pale yellow, with fine ridges running across their surface. Their shells are relatively thin compared to other clam species.
children.funFact: Dwarf surfclams can rapidly bury themselves up to 6 inches deep in sand when threatened, using their powerful muscular foot to disappear from view in just seconds.

children.name: Mactromeris
children.description: Mactromeris is a genus of large, cold-water clams that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean floors. These robust bivalves are well-adapted to harsh Arctic and subarctic marine environments, where they filter-feed on tiny particles in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mactromeris clams are distinguished by their exceptionally thick, heavy shells and large size compared to most other clams. Their shells have a distinctive triangular or wedge-like shape when viewed from the side.
children.funFact: Arctic Surfclams can live for over 40 years and grow shells up to 5 inches long, making them some of the largest clams found in northern New England waters.

children.description: Trough shells are medium to large clams that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. They have sturdy, oval-shaped shells that are typically white or cream-colored, and they use a muscular foot to dig themselves into the sediment where they filter feed on tiny particles in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These clams have a distinctive triangular depression or 'trough' on the inside of their shells behind the hinge, which gives them their common name. Their shells also have a characteristic gaping appearance where the siphons extend out.
children.funFact: Some trough shells, like the Atlantic surf clam, can live for over 200 years and grow to be the size of a dinner plate, making them among the longest-lived animals in New England waters.

children.name: Cyrenidae
Corbicula
children.description: Corbicula is a genus of small, freshwater clams that are native to Asia but have spread to waterways around the world. These clams are filter feeders that burrow into sandy or muddy bottoms of rivers, lakes, and ponds. They play important roles in aquatic ecosystems by filtering water and serving as food for fish and birds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Corbicula clams can be identified by their triangular to oval shells with distinct ridges running parallel to the shell edge, and they typically have a yellowish-brown to dark brown coloration. Unlike many other freshwater clams, they are hermaphroditic and can reproduce without a fish host.
