children.funFact: Asian clams can filter up to a liter of water per hour, making them incredibly efficient water cleaners that can significantly impact water clarity in the ecosystems they inhabit.

children.description: Basket clams are small to medium-sized freshwater bivalves with triangular to oval shells that live buried in sand, mud, or gravel at the bottom of rivers, lakes, and streams. They are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny particles of food like algae and organic matter. These clams are known for their ability to rapidly colonize new water bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Basket clams can be distinguished from other freshwater clams by their relatively thick, sculptured shells with prominent concentric ridges and their triangular shape when viewed from the side. Unlike many native freshwater mussels, they have short siphons and tend to live closer to the sediment surface.
children.funFact: The Asian clam, New England's only basket clam species, can reproduce without mating through a process called parthenogenesis, allowing a single individual to establish an entire population in a new location.

children.name: Arcticidae
Arctica
children.description: Arctica is a genus of large, thick-shelled clams that live buried in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. These robust bivalves are adapted for life in cold northern waters, where they burrow deep into sediment and filter-feed on tiny particles in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their extremely thick, heavy shells with prominent growth rings and their remarkably long lifespans compared to other clams.
children.funFact: Ocean quahogs hold the record as the longest-living non-colonial animals on Earth, with some individuals living over 500 years - meaning some clams alive today were already adults when Shakespeare was writing his plays!

children.description: Ocean Quahogs are a family of large, thick-shelled clams that live buried in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. These hardy bivalves are characterized by their robust, rounded shells and their ability to thrive in cold northern waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ocean Quahogs are distinguished from other clam families by their exceptionally thick, heavy shells and their preference for deeper, colder waters compared to most other clams.
children.funFact: Ocean Quahogs are among the longest-lived animals on Earth, with some individuals reaching over 500 years old - their age can be determined by counting growth rings in their shells, much like tree rings.

children.name: Mesodesmatidae
Mesodesma
children.description: Mesodesma is a genus of marine clams known as wedgeclams, named for their distinctive wedge-shaped shells. These bivalve mollusks are filter feeders that burrow into sandy beaches and coastal sediments, using their muscular foot to dig into the substrate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wedgeclams have thick, triangular shells that are distinctly wedge-shaped when viewed from the side, setting them apart from other clam genera with more oval or elongated shells.
children.funFact: The Arctic wedgeclam can live for over 100 years and is considered an indicator species for healthy sandy beach ecosystems in the North Atlantic.

children.description: Mesodesmatidae are medium-sized marine clams known as surf clams or bean clams that live buried in sandy beaches along ocean shores. These burrowing bivalves have thick, strong shells that help them withstand the constant pounding of waves in the surf zone. They are active filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture plankton and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clams, surf clams have a distinctive triangular shell shape and lack a pallial sinus (the indentation where the siphon retracts). Their shells are also notably thick and heavy compared to similar-sized clams, helping them stay anchored in shifting sand.
children.funFact: Surf clams are incredibly fast diggers and can burrow completely into wet sand in just seconds when a wave recedes, disappearing from view before the next wave crashes down.

children.description: Venerida is an order of marine clams that includes some of New England's most familiar and economically important bivalves. These clams are characterized by their two hinged shells and their ability to burrow into sandy or muddy seafloor sediments. They filter feed by drawing water through their shells to capture plankton and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Venerida have well-developed hinge teeth that lock their two shells together securely, and most have siphons that allow them to feed and breathe while buried in sediment. Unlike some other clam groups, they typically have relatively thick, sturdy shells.
children.funFact: This order includes the famous quahog clam, which can live for over 500 years and whose shells were traditionally used by Native Americans to make wampum beads for trade and ceremony.

children.name: Cardiida
Tellinidae
Ameritella
children.description: Ameritella is a genus of small, delicate clams commonly known as tellins that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These bivalve mollusks have thin, colorful shells and use their long siphons to filter food particles from the water while staying safely buried in the sediment. They are active burrowers that can quickly dig themselves back into the sand if disturbed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ameritella tellins are distinguished from other tellin genera by their relatively small size, thin shell construction, and their ability to move quickly through sandy substrates. Their shells often display vibrant colors and have a characteristic elongated oval shape with a slight twist.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'dwarf' tellins, these little clams are incredibly fast diggers and can completely bury themselves in sand in just a few seconds when threatened by predators or waves.

children.name: Macoma
children.description: Macoma is a genus of small to medium-sized saltwater clams that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These bivalve mollusks have thin, oval-shaped shells and are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to catch tiny particles of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Macoma clams can be identified by their laterally compressed (flattened from side to side) shells and their ability to twist their posterior end, which helps them burrow more effectively than many other clam species.
children.funFact: Macoma clams are incredibly efficient burrowers that can completely bury themselves in soft sediment in just seconds when they sense danger approaching.

children.name: Macoploma
children.description: Macoploma is a small genus of marine clams that belong to the tellin family. These bivalve mollusks are characterized by their thin, delicate shells and their ability to burrow in sandy or muddy ocean sediments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Macoploma clams are distinguished from other tellins by their particularly fragile, translucent shells and their distinctive oval shape with a slight posterior twist.
children.funFact: The Shining Macoma gets its name from its lustrous, pearl-like shell surface that can shimmer with an iridescent glow when wet.

children.description: Tellins and allies are bivalve mollusks (clams) that live buried in sandy or muddy sediments along coastlines and in shallow marine waters. They have thin, often colorful shells that are typically oval or elongated in shape, and they use a long siphon to filter feed on microscopic organisms and organic particles in the water above their burrows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clams, tellins have shells that are often compressed and slightly twisted, with the rear end typically more pointed than the front. Their long, separate siphons can extend well above the sediment surface, allowing them to feed and breathe while staying safely buried.
children.funFact: Many tellin clams can rapidly burrow deeper into the sand when threatened, using their muscular foot like a shovel to disappear from sight in just seconds.

children.name: Cardiidae
Laevicardium
children.description: Egg cockles are small, smooth-shelled clams that get their name from their distinctive egg-like shape and relatively smooth surface compared to other cockles. These marine bivalves burrow in sandy or muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters, using their muscular foot to dig into the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their bumpy relatives in the true cockle family, egg cockles have relatively smooth, glossy shells with fine radial lines rather than prominent ribs or ridges.
children.funFact: Morton's cockle can rapidly burrow into sand by extending its large, orange-colored foot and using it like an anchor to pull itself down into the sediment.

children.name: Parvicardium
children.description: Parvicardium is a genus of small, heart-shaped clams commonly known as cockles. These bivalve mollusks are characterized by their distinctive ribbed shells and compact, rounded shape that gives them their heart-like appearance when viewed from the side.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Parvicardium are distinguished from other cockles by their smaller size and finely detailed ribbing patterns on their shells. They typically have more delicate, closely-spaced ribs compared to their larger cockle relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'Parvicardium' literally means 'small heart' in Latin, perfectly describing these tiny heart-shaped shells that are often found washed up on beaches.

children.name: Dinocardium
children.description: Giant Heart Cockles are large, robust marine clams with distinctively heart-shaped shells when viewed from the side. These impressive bivalves are among the largest cockles found in Atlantic waters, with thick, sturdy shells that feature prominent radiating ribs running from the hinge to the outer edge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cockles, Giant Heart Cockles are notably larger and have exceptionally thick, heavy shells with deeply pronounced heart-shaped profiles. Their shells also feature more prominent and widely-spaced radiating ribs compared to smaller cockle species.
children.funFact: The Giant Atlantic Cockle can live for over 30 years and grow shells up to 5 inches long, making them one of the longest-lived and largest cockles in North American waters.

children.description: True cockles are heart-shaped bivalve mollusks that burrow in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These clams have distinctive rounded, ribbed shells with prominent ridges radiating from the hinge, giving them their characteristic cockle appearance. They use a muscular foot to dig into sediment and filter plankton from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True cockles can be identified by their nearly symmetrical, heart-shaped shells with strong radiating ribs or ridges. Unlike many other clams, their shells are typically quite rounded and inflated rather than flattened.
children.funFact: Cockles can leap several inches off the seafloor by rapidly extending their muscular foot, helping them escape from predators like crabs and fish.

children.name: Solecurtidae
Tagelus
children.description: Tagelus is a genus of elongated, razor-like clams that live buried deep in sandy and muddy sediments along the coast. These bivalves have thin, fragile shells that are much longer than they are wide, giving them a distinctive razor clam appearance. They are filter feeders that extend long siphons up to the surface to draw in water for food and oxygen.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tagelus clams are distinguished from other razor clams by their more rectangular shell shape and the presence of a distinct internal rib or ridge running along the inside of each shell valve.
children.funFact: When disturbed, Tagelus clams can rapidly withdraw their long siphons and burrow deeper into the sediment at speeds of up to several inches per minute.

children.description: Short razor clams are marine bivalves with elongated, razor-like shells that live buried in sandy or muddy sediments along coastlines. Unlike their close relatives the true razor clams, these clams have shorter, more robust shells and are excellent diggers that can quickly burrow deep into sand when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They differ from true razor clams by having shorter, thicker shells with more rounded ends, and their shells typically have a distinctive gape at both ends that allows their siphons and foot to extend.
children.funFact: These clams can burrow so quickly that they can disappear into sand in just seconds, earning them the nickname 'jackknife clams' for their rapid digging ability.

children.name: Semelidae
Cumingia
children.description: Cumingia is a genus of small, burrowing clams that live in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. These marine bivalves have thin, delicate shells and are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cumingia clams are distinguished by their fragile, translucent shells that are often somewhat triangular or wedge-shaped, and their ability to burrow quickly into soft sediments.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Cumingia clams are excellent burrowers that can disappear into sand in just seconds when disturbed by predators or waves.

children.description: Furrow-shells are small marine clams that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These bivalve mollusks have thin, delicate shells with distinctive radiating ridges or furrows that give them their common name. They are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Furrow-shells can be identified by their characteristic radial ridges or grooves that run from the hinge to the shell margin, creating a furrowed appearance. Their shells are typically more fragile and thinner than many other clam families.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, furrow-shells are surprisingly good diggers and can quickly burrow several inches deep into sand when disturbed by waves or predators.

children.description: Cockles, tellins, and allies are marine bivalves that live buried in sand, mud, or other soft sediments along our coastlines. These clams are characterized by their ability to burrow efficiently and their feeding strategy of filtering plankton and organic particles from the water through specialized siphons that extend up to the sediment surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike mussels or oysters that attach to hard surfaces, members of this group are active burrowers with streamlined shells and powerful muscular feet adapted for digging. Most species also have long, separate siphons for feeding and breathing while remaining safely buried.
children.funFact: Some tellins can actually change the direction they're facing while buried by doing a complete somersault in their burrow, allowing them to quickly escape predators or find better feeding positions.

children.name: Myida
Dreissenidae
Dreissena
children.description: Dreissena mussels are small freshwater bivalves known for their distinctive striped shells and ability to attach firmly to hard surfaces using strong protein threads called byssal threads. These invasive mussels originally come from Eastern Europe and have spread rapidly through North American waterways since the 1980s. They form dense colonies on rocks, boat hulls, pipes, and other underwater structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike native freshwater mussels, Dreissena mussels have a triangular shell shape and can attach themselves to hard surfaces rather than burrowing in sediment. They also have a distinctive flat underside where they attach, giving them a unique D-shaped cross-section.
children.funFact: A single zebra mussel can filter up to one liter of water per day, and their massive colonies can dramatically clear entire lakes of algae and microscopic organisms, fundamentally changing aquatic ecosystems.

children.name: Mytilopsis
children.description: Mytilopsis is a genus of small freshwater and brackish water mussels known as falsemussels. These bivalve mollusks have distinctively shaped shells and are filter feeders that attach themselves to hard surfaces in aquatic environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true mussels, falsemussels have a unique shell shape with a distinctive notch or gap near the hinge area, and they typically prefer lower salinity waters than their marine relatives.
children.funFact: The Dark Falsemussel is actually an invasive species in New England that was accidentally introduced from its native range in the southeastern United States and can rapidly colonize new waterways.

children.description: Dreissenidae is a family of small freshwater mussels that are notorious for their ability to rapidly colonize new waterways. These bivalve mollusks attach themselves to hard surfaces using strong protein threads called byssal threads, forming dense clusters on rocks, docks, boat hulls, and other underwater structures. Most species in this family are non-native to North America and are considered invasive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other freshwater mussels, dreissenid mussels have a distinctive triangular shell shape and can attach firmly to surfaces throughout their adult lives. They also have the ability to completely close their shells with a tight seal, allowing them to survive out of water for extended periods.
children.funFact: A single zebra mussel can filter up to one liter of water per day, and large colonies can actually make lake water clearer by removing so much plankton and particles from the water column.

children.name: Pholadidae
Zirfaea
children.description: Zirfaea is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks known as piddocks, which are specialized clams that bore into hard surfaces like rock, wood, and clay. These remarkable creatures use their ridged, file-like shells to drill cylindrical burrows where they spend their adult lives. They are filter feeders, extending siphons from their burrows to draw in water and capture plankton and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Zirfaea piddocks have uniquely sculptured shells with rough, rasp-like ridges that function as drilling tools, and they possess a distinctive gap at the front of their shells where the boring mechanism operates.
children.funFact: The Great Piddock can bore holes up to 6 inches deep into solid rock, creating perfectly round tunnels that become permanent homes they can never leave once they grow too large for the entrance!

children.name: Barnea
children.description: Barnea is a genus of marine clams known as piddocks that specialize in boring into soft substrates like mud, clay, and soft rock. These bivalve mollusks use their ridged, file-like shells to mechanically drill burrows where they spend their adult lives filter-feeding.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other boring clams, Barnea species have shells that are particularly well-adapted for excavating soft sediments rather than hard rock, with their anterior end modified into an effective drilling tool.
children.funFact: These industrious clams can bore tunnels up to a foot deep in muddy bottoms, and once they settle into their self-made homes as juveniles, they typically remain there for their entire adult lives.

children.name: Cyrtopleura
children.description: Cyrtopleura is a genus of large marine clams known as angelwings that are specialized for boring into soft substrates like mud, clay, and peat. These bivalves have distinctive thin, elongated white shells with prominent ridges that help them excavate burrows in the seafloor. They are filter feeders that extend siphons up to the surface to draw in water for feeding and breathing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cyrtopleura angelwings have uniquely fragile, translucent shells with sharp radiating ribs that distinguish them from other boring clams. Their shells often break easily when handled, and they possess an unusual spoon-shaped projection inside the shell called a chondrophore.
children.funFact: These clams can bore tunnels up to 3 feet deep into hard clay or peat using only the mechanical action of their ridged shells, rotating back and forth like a living drill bit.

children.description: Piddocks and angelwings are specialized marine clams that have evolved the remarkable ability to bore into hard substrates like wood, clay, soft rock, and even concrete. These bivalves use their ridged, file-like shells to mechanically drill circular burrows where they spend their adult lives. They are filter feeders that extend siphons from their burrows to draw in water containing plankton and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, piddocks have shells with rough, rasp-like ridges on the front end that function as drilling tools. Their shells often have distinctive wing-like extensions and may gape open at both ends, unable to close completely due to their specialized boring lifestyle.
children.funFact: Some piddock species are bioluminescent and can produce a blue-green glow when disturbed, earning them the nickname 'angel wings' for their ethereal appearance in the dark.

children.name: Myidae
Mya
children.description: Mya clams are large, soft-shelled bivalves that live buried deep in sandy or muddy sediments along the coast. These clams are characterized by their thin, chalky shells and long siphons that extend up to the surface to filter food and breathe. They're important both ecologically as filter feeders and economically as popular seafood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mya clams have distinctively thin, brittle shells with a characteristic spoon-shaped projection inside the left shell called a chondrophore. Their exceptionally long siphons can extend several times the length of their shell, much longer than most other clam species.
children.funFact: Soft-shelled clams can live for over 100 years and burrow as deep as 3 feet into the sediment, using their powerful foot to dig while their siphons remain connected to the surface like snorkels.

children.description: Softshell clams are a family of burrowing marine bivalves with thin, fragile shells that cannot close completely. These clams live buried in sand or mud in intertidal and shallow subtidal areas, extending long siphons up to the surface to filter water for food and oxygen.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clam families, softshell clams have shells with a characteristic gap at one end where their large siphons extend, and their shells are notably thin and brittle compared to hard clams.
children.funFact: The steamer clam (Mya arenaria) can live for over 100 years and is capable of burrowing up to 12 inches deep in the sediment while still reaching the surface with its siphons.

children.name: Corbulidae
Caryocorbula
children.description: Caryocorbula is a genus of small marine clams known as basket clams or corbulas. These bivalve mollusks have distinctively unequal shells, with one valve (shell half) being noticeably larger and more inflated than the other. They live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms, filter-feeding on tiny particles in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams that have two nearly identical shell halves, Caryocorbula species have markedly asymmetrical shells where the right valve is much larger and overlaps the smaller left valve, creating a distinctive basket-like appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Caryocorbula' literally means 'little nut basket,' referring to their characteristic asymmetrical shell shape that resembles a tiny woven basket.

children.description: Corbulid clams are small, marine bivalves that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These clams have distinctively unequal shells, with one valve (shell half) being noticeably larger than the other, giving them an asymmetrical appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams that have two equal-sized shells, corbulid clams are easily recognized by their markedly unequal valves, with the right shell typically being much larger and more inflated than the left.
children.funFact: Corbulid clams are sometimes called "basket clams" because their strongly ribbed shells reminded early naturalists of woven baskets.

children.description: Myida is an order of marine bivalves (two-shelled mollusks) that includes some of the most recognizable clams in New England waters. These clams are united by their specialized feeding and burrowing adaptations, with most species living buried in sand, mud, or even boring into wood and rock. They range from the familiar softshell clams you might dig for at the beach to the invasive zebra mussels that attach to hard surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clams, members of Myida have reduced or modified hinge teeth where their two shells connect, and many have developed elongated siphons for feeding while buried deep in sediment. Some species have evolved the remarkable ability to bore into hard substrates like wood, rock, or concrete.
children.funFact: Piddocks, members of this order, can actually bore into solid rock using only their shells, creating perfectly round holes by rotating their ridged shells like living drill bits.

children.name: Sphaeriida
Sphaeriidae
Sphaerium
children.description: Sphaerium fingernailclams are tiny freshwater bivalves that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These small clams get their common name from their size - most are only about the size of a fingernail, typically measuring less than half an inch across. They burrow into soft sediments on the bottom of waterways, where they filter feed on algae and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sphaerium clams can be distinguished from other fingernailclams by their more rounded, inflated shell shape and the position of their hinge teeth. Unlike some related genera, they have well-developed cardinal and lateral teeth that help identify individual species.
children.funFact: These tiny clams are hermaphroditic and brood their young internally, releasing fully-formed juvenile clams rather than free-swimming larvae like many other bivalves.

children.name: Musculium
children.description: Musculium is a genus of tiny freshwater clams known as fingernail clams, named for their small size and curved shape that resembles a fingernail. These diminutive bivalves typically measure less than half an inch across and live buried in the mud and sediment of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They filter feed by drawing water through their shells to capture microscopic algae and organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Musculium species are distinguished from other fingernail clams by their relatively elongated, curved shells and specific hinge tooth arrangements. They tend to be more streamlined than their rounder relatives in the genus Sphaerium.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, fingernail clams can live for several years and are hermaphroditic, meaning each individual can produce both eggs and sperm, though they typically cross-fertilize with other individuals.

children.name: Pisidium
children.description: Pill clams are tiny freshwater mollusks that get their name from their small, pill-like rounded shells. These miniature bivalves live in lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams where they filter feed on microscopic particles in the water. They are among the smallest clams in North America, typically measuring less than half an inch across.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pill clams can be distinguished from other small freshwater clams by their nearly spherical, inflated shells and their extremely small size. Unlike larger freshwater mussels, they have smooth, glossy shells without prominent ridges or growth lines.
children.funFact: Pill clams are hermaphrodites that brood their young inside their shells, releasing tiny fully-formed baby clams rather than larvae, allowing them to colonize isolated water bodies more easily than other freshwater mollusks.

children.name: Euglesa
children.description: Euglesa is a genus of tiny freshwater clams known as peaclams or fingernail clams. These small bivalves have delicate, translucent shells that are typically less than half an inch long and live buried in the mud and sediment of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euglesa peaclams are distinguished from other small clams by their extremely thin, fragile shells and their ability to reproduce without mating through a process called parthenogenesis.
children.funFact: Despite being only a few millimeters long, peaclams can live for several years and serve as important food sources for fish, ducks, and other aquatic wildlife.

children.description: Pea clams are tiny freshwater mollusks that get their name from their small, pea-sized shells. These miniature bivalves live in the sediment of ponds, lakes, streams, and rivers throughout New England, where they filter microscopic particles from the water for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger freshwater cousins, pea clams are hermaphroditic and brood their young inside their shells rather than releasing eggs and sperm into the water. Their shells are typically round to oval-shaped and rarely exceed half an inch in length.
children.funFact: Pea clams are among the few bivalves that can reproduce without a mate, carrying their developing young in special pouches inside their shells until they're ready to be released as tiny, fully-formed clams.

children.description: Sphaeriida is an order of small freshwater bivalves, commonly known as pea clams or fingernail clams. These tiny mollusks live in lakes, ponds, streams, and rivers throughout New England, where they burrow into muddy or sandy bottoms. They are filter feeders that help keep aquatic ecosystems clean by straining algae and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike marine clams, members of Sphaeriida are adapted specifically for freshwater environments and are much smaller in size, typically measuring less than half an inch across. They also have the unique ability among bivalves to brood their young internally rather than releasing eggs and sperm into the water.
children.funFact: Pea clams are hermaphrodites that can reproduce without a mate, and they give birth to live young that emerge as fully-formed miniature clams rather than going through a larval stage.

children.name: Pectinida
Pectinidae
Argopecten
children.description: Argopecten is a genus of scallops found in Atlantic coastal waters, known for their beautiful fan-shaped shells with distinctive ridges radiating from the hinge. These bivalve mollusks are active swimmers that can propel themselves through the water by rapidly clapping their shells together, unlike many other shellfish that remain stationary.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Argopecten scallops have relatively thin, lightweight shells with prominent radiating ribs and are excellent swimmers. They differ from other scallop genera by their smaller size, more delicate shell structure, and their ability to swim freely rather than attaching to surfaces.
children.funFact: When threatened, these scallops can jet through the water by rapidly opening and closing their shells, creating a propulsion system that allows them to escape predators in a zigzag pattern.

children.name: Placopecten
children.description: Placopecten is a genus of large, deep-water scallops found in cold northern Atlantic waters. These bivalve mollusks are characterized by their distinctive fan-shaped shells with prominent ridges radiating from the hinge area. They are commercially important shellfish that live on sandy and muddy ocean bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Placopecten scallops are much larger than most other scallop species, with shells that can reach over 8 inches across. Their shells have a flatter profile compared to many scallops and feature distinctive, well-defined radiating ribs.
children.funFact: Atlantic deep-sea scallops can live for over 20 years and are capable of swimming by rapidly clapping their shells together to jet-propel themselves through the water when escaping predators.

children.name: Chlamys
children.description: Dwarf Fan Shells are small to medium-sized scallops that live on the ocean floor in cold northern waters. These bivalve mollusks have the characteristic fan-shaped shells with radiating ribs that we associate with scallops, and they can swim by rapidly opening and closing their shells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike larger scallops, Dwarf Fan Shells are typically smaller and have more delicate, finely-ribbed shells. They often have colorful shells ranging from white to orange to purple, making them quite beautiful despite their small size.
children.funFact: The Icelandic Scallop can live for over 40 years and is an important food source for cod and other bottom-feeding fish in the North Atlantic.

children.name: Bractechlamys
children.description: Bractechlamys is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks commonly known as scallops. These creatures have two hinged shells and are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles from the ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive shell sculpture and specific hinge structure that sets them apart from other scallop genera.
children.funFact: The distant scallop gets its name because it was originally found far from where most related scallop species live, making it an unusual geographic outlier in its family tree.

children.description: Scallops are bivalve mollusks with distinctive fan-shaped shells featuring radiating ribs or ridges that spread out from the hinge like rays of the sun. They are unique among clams because many species can swim by rapidly clapping their shells together, propelling themselves through the water in a jet-like motion. Most scallops have colorful shells and dozens of tiny eyes along their shell edges that can detect light and movement.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bivalves, scallops have unequal shell valves (one is usually flatter than the other) and distinctive 'ears' or wing-like extensions on either side of the hinge. Their ability to swim actively sets them apart from most other clams and oysters that remain stationary.
children.funFact: Scallops can have up to 200 tiny blue eyes, each with its own lens and retina, arranged along the edge of their shells to watch for predators and prey.

children.name: Anomiidae
Anomia
children.description: Anomia is a genus of small, flattened marine bivalves commonly known as jingle shells. These mollusks are characterized by their thin, translucent shells that produce a distinctive jingling sound when shaken together. They attach themselves permanently to hard surfaces like rocks, other shells, or pier pilings using a strong byssal plug.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bivalves, jingle shells have a distinctive hole in their lower shell through which their attachment structure passes. Their shells are also notably thin and translucent, often with an iridescent, pearlescent interior.
children.funFact: Jingle shells get their name from the musical tinkling sound they make when waves wash them up on beaches and they knock against each other.

children.name: Heteranomia
children.description: Heteranomia is a genus of small marine bivalve mollusks commonly known as jingle shells. These flattened, irregularly-shaped clams attach themselves permanently to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or dock pilings using a strong muscular stalk called a byssus that passes through a hole in their lower shell.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams that can move around, Heteranomia species are permanently cemented to surfaces and have notably asymmetrical shells with a distinctive hole in the bottom valve where their attachment organ extends through.
children.funFact: When washed up on beaches, empty jingle shells make a characteristic tinkling sound when shaken, which is how they got their common name.

children.description: Jingle shells are small, thin-shelled marine bivalves that get their name from the soft jingling sound they make when washed up on beaches. These unusual mollusks have asymmetrical shells and attach themselves to rocks, other shells, or hard surfaces on the seafloor using a strong, calcified plug called a byssus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bivalves, jingle shells have very thin, translucent shells that are often irregularly shaped to conform to whatever surface they're attached to. The lower shell has a distinctive hole through which the attachment plug passes.
children.funFact: When jingle shells die and wash ashore, their empty shells are so thin and light that they create a distinctive musical tinkling sound when stirred by waves or footsteps, earning them the nickname 'mermaid's toenails.'

children.description: Scallops and allies are marine bivalve mollusks that have adapted for life on the seafloor, though some can swim by rapidly opening and closing their shells. This group includes the familiar fan-shaped scallops as well as jingle shells, which are known for their thin, translucent appearance. Most members of this group have shells with distinctive ridges or ribs that radiate outward from the hinge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bivalves that burrow into sand or mud, most scallops and their allies live on the surface of the seafloor or attach to hard surfaces. Many species in this group have unequal shell valves, with one being more curved or bowl-shaped than the other.
children.funFact: Scallops are among the few bivalves that can actually swim, propelling themselves through the water by clapping their shells together like underwater castanets!

children.name: Mytilida
Mytilidae
Mytilus
children.description: Black mussels are marine bivalves that attach themselves to rocks, docks, and other hard surfaces in coastal waters using strong protein threads called byssal threads. They have distinctive dark blue-black shells that are elongated and somewhat triangular in shape. These filter-feeding mollusks pump water through their bodies to capture plankton and other tiny particles for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Black mussels can be distinguished from other mussel genera by their smooth, relatively thin shells with a characteristic blue-black coloration and their preference for attaching to hard surfaces in intertidal and shallow subtidal zones.
children.funFact: A single blue mussel can filter up to 2 gallons of water per hour, making them important natural water purifiers in coastal ecosystems.

children.name: Geukensia
children.description: Geukensia is a genus of marine mussels that are specially adapted to live in salt marshes and estuarine environments. These mussels are characterized by their ribbed shells and their ability to tolerate changing salinity levels as tides bring in saltwater and freshwater runoff dilutes their habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most marine mussels, Geukensia species have prominent ribs running along their shells and are uniquely adapted to survive in the fluctuating salinity conditions of salt marshes and tidal creeks.
children.funFact: Atlantic Ribbed Mussels can filter up to 6 gallons of water per hour, making them incredibly important for keeping salt marsh waters clean and clear.

children.name: Crenella
children.description: Crenella is a genus of small marine bivalve mollusks, commonly known as bean mussels due to their distinctive bean-like shape. These tiny shellfish are filter feeders that attach themselves to rocks, shells, and other hard surfaces in marine environments using strong threads called byssal threads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crenella can be distinguished from other small mussels by their characteristic ribbed or striated shell surface and their compact, rounded bean-like shape rather than the elongated form of typical mussels.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'bean mussels,' Crenella are actually more closely related to ark clams than to true mussels, showing how common names can sometimes be misleading in the natural world.

children.name: Solamen
children.description: Solamen is a genus of freshwater mussels that live buried in the sandy and muddy bottoms of rivers and streams. These filter-feeding mollusks pump water through their bodies to capture tiny particles of food like algae and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their distinctive glandular structures, which give the Glandular Bean Mussel its common name.
children.funFact: Like other freshwater mussels, Solamen species have a fascinating life cycle where their larvae must attach to fish gills to develop, making them dependent on healthy fish populations for reproduction.

children.description: Mussels are marine bivalves that attach themselves to rocks, docks, and other hard surfaces using strong protein threads called byssal threads. These filter-feeding mollusks have elongated, dark-colored shells that are typically blue-black or brown, and they live in dense clusters along the intertidal zone where waves crash.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bivalves, mussels have a distinctive elongated, asymmetrical shell shape and produce tough, fibrous threads that allow them to anchor securely to surfaces in high-energy wave environments.
children.funFact: A single mussel can filter up to 25 gallons of seawater per day, removing plankton, bacteria, and pollutants from the water column.

children.name: Modiolidae
Modiolus
children.description: Modiolus is a genus of large marine mussels known for their distinctive horse-like shape, which gives them their common name of horse mussels. These bivalve mollusks are filter feeders that attach themselves to rocks and other hard surfaces in coastal waters using strong protein threads called byssal threads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Horse mussels are distinguished from other mussels by their larger size, more elongated shell shape, and the prominent rounded bulge (umbo) near the hinge area that gives them their horse-like appearance.
children.funFact: Northern Horse Mussels can live for over 100 years and grow to be nearly a foot long, making them some of the longest-lived and largest mussels in New England waters.

children.description: Horsemussels and their allies are marine bivalves that attach themselves to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or ship hulls using strong protein threads called byssal threads. These mussels have elongated, oval-shaped shells that are typically dark brown or black in color. They are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture plankton and other small particles for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike common blue mussels, horsemussels have a more elongated shell shape and their beak (the pointed tip of the shell) is positioned closer to the front edge rather than at the very tip.
children.funFact: The northern horsemussel can live for over 100 years and grow to be nearly a foot long, making it one of the longest-lived and largest bivalves in New England waters.

children.description: Mytilida is an order of marine bivalve mollusks that includes the familiar blue mussels and larger horsemussels found along New England's rocky shores and muddy bottoms. These filter-feeding shellfish have two hinged shells and use strong protein threads called byssal threads to anchor themselves to rocks, pilings, and other hard surfaces. They play important ecological roles by filtering water and providing food for many marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mytilida are distinguished by their elongated, triangular shells that are typically longer than they are wide, and their ability to produce strong byssal threads for attachment. Unlike many other bivalves, their shells often have a dark, smooth exterior and they lack prominent growth rings.
children.funFact: A single adult mussel can filter up to 15 gallons of seawater per day, helping to keep coastal waters clean by removing algae, bacteria, and other particles from the water column.

children.name: Ostreida
Ostreidae
Crassostrea
children.description: Crassostrea is a genus of large, commercially important oysters found in coastal waters around the world. These bivalve mollusks are characterized by their thick, irregularly shaped shells and their ability to form extensive reef systems in estuarine environments. They are filter feeders that play crucial ecological roles in maintaining water quality.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crassostrea oysters are distinguished from other oyster genera by their deeply cupped lower shells and relatively flat upper shells, along with their preference for brackish water environments where rivers meet the sea.
children.funFact: A single Eastern Oyster can filter up to 50 gallons of water per day, removing algae, sediments, and pollutants to help keep coastal waters clean.

children.name: Ostrea
children.description: Flat oysters are marine bivalves with distinctively flattened, circular to oval shells that lack the deep cupping of other oyster species. These filter-feeding mollusks attach permanently to hard surfaces on the seafloor and feed by pumping water through their bodies to capture tiny organisms and particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike the deeply cupped Eastern oysters common in New England, flat oysters have relatively flat, thin shells with both valves being similar in depth. Their shells also tend to be more circular and smoother than the irregular, ridged shells of cupped oysters.
children.funFact: European flat oysters are sequential hermaphrodites, starting life as males and then alternating between male and female throughout their lives, sometimes changing sex multiple times per year.

children.name: Dendostrea
children.description: Dendostrea is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks commonly known as frond oysters. These oysters are characterized by their distinctive leaf-like or frond-shaped shells that often grow in branching, tree-like formations attached to hard surfaces on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical oysters with rounded or elongated shells, frond oysters have flattened, leaf-shaped valves that create distinctive branching colonies resembling underwater plants or coral formations.
children.funFact: The name 'Dendostrea' literally means 'tree oyster,' reflecting their remarkable ability to grow in branching, tree-like colonies that can create small reef-like structures on the ocean floor.

children.description: True oysters are marine bivalve mollusks that cement themselves permanently to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or dock pilings. They have distinctively rough, irregularly-shaped shells with one flat upper shell and one deeply cupped lower shell that they filter seawater through to catch tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bivalves, true oysters permanently attach to surfaces and cannot move once they settle as juveniles. Their shells are also notably asymmetrical, with the right shell being flat and the left shell being deeply cupped.
children.funFact: Oysters can change their sex multiple times throughout their lives, often starting as males and switching to females when they grow larger and can produce more eggs.

children.name: Margaritidae
Pinctada
children.description: Pearl oysters are marine bivalve mollusks best known for their ability to produce lustrous pearls when irritants enter their shells. These filter-feeding shellfish live attached to hard surfaces on the ocean floor, where they pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles like plankton and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other oysters, pearl oysters have a smooth, iridescent mother-of-pearl lining inside their shells and can produce round, valuable pearls rather than irregular ones.
children.funFact: The Atlantic Pearl Oyster found in New England waters can live for over 40 years and was historically harvested for both its pearls and its beautiful mother-of-pearl shell, which was used to make buttons and decorative items.

children.description: Pearl oysters are marine bivalve mollusks known for their ability to produce lustrous pearls and mother-of-pearl. These filter-feeding shellfish have irregularly shaped shells and attach themselves to hard surfaces on the ocean floor using strong threads called byssal threads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true oysters, pearl oysters have a more symmetrical shell shape and possess a distinctive nacreous (mother-of-pearl) interior lining that gives them their characteristic iridescent shine.
children.funFact: The famous cultured pearl industry relies primarily on pearl oysters, which can take 2-6 years to produce a single cultured pearl through careful cultivation techniques.

children.description: Oysters and their allies are marine bivalve mollusks that have adapted to life attached to hard surfaces like rocks, shells, or dock pilings. These filter-feeding animals pump water through their bodies to capture tiny plankton and organic particles for food. Most members of this group cement themselves permanently to surfaces, though some can attach using strong threads called byssal fibers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bivalves that burrow in sand or mud, oysters typically have one shell that's deeply cupped and another that's relatively flat, allowing them to live attached to hard surfaces. Their irregular, often rough shell shapes help them fit snugly against rocks and other attachment sites.
children.funFact: Eastern oysters can filter up to 50 gallons of water per day, making them incredibly important for maintaining clean water in coastal ecosystems!

children.name: Adapedonta
Pharidae
Ensis
children.description: Ensis is a genus of razor clams known for their distinctive elongated, narrow shells that resemble old-fashioned straight razors. These marine bivalves are expert burrowers that live in sandy or muddy coastal areas, using their powerful foot to quickly dig deep vertical tunnels in the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ensis razor clams have exceptionally long, thin shells that are much more elongated than typical clams, with a distinctive rectangular shape when viewed from the side.
children.funFact: Atlantic Jackknife clams can burrow so quickly that they seem to disappear into the sand in seconds when disturbed, diving down as much as 3 feet deep to escape predators.

children.name: Siliqua
children.description: Siliqua is a genus of razor clams, marine bivalves known for their distinctively elongated, narrow shells that resemble old-fashioned straight razors. These clams are excellent burrowers that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms, using their powerful muscular foot to quickly dig vertically into the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Siliqua have exceptionally streamlined, rectangular shells that are much longer than they are wide, with a characteristic blunt front end and slightly tapered back end that sets them apart from other clam genera.
children.funFact: Razor clams can burrow so quickly that they can disappear completely into sand in just a few seconds when threatened, earning them a reputation as some of the fastest-digging clams in the ocean.

children.description: Pharidae, commonly known as razor clams, are a family of marine bivalve mollusks with distinctive long, narrow shells that resemble old-fashioned straight razors. These clams are excellent diggers, using their powerful muscular foot to burrow rapidly into sandy beaches and mudflats. They live buried in the sediment with their siphons extending to the surface to filter feed on plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Razor clams are easily recognized by their extremely elongated, rectangular shells that are much longer than they are wide, giving them their characteristic razor-like appearance. Unlike most other clams, their shells don't close completely, with gaps remaining at both ends even when the valves are pulled together.
children.funFact: Razor clams are incredibly fast diggers and can burrow into sand at speeds of up to one inch per second, often outpacing people trying to dig them up by hand.

children.name: Hiatellidae
Hiatella
children.description: Hiatella is a genus of marine clams known for their ability to bore into hard surfaces like rocks, wood, and even other shells. These bivalve mollusks create burrows where they live protected from predators and strong currents. They are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny particles of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clams, Hiatella species are active borers that use chemical secretions and mechanical rasping to excavate homes in hard substrates. Their shells are often irregularly shaped and gape open, reflecting their burrowing lifestyle.
children.funFact: Arctic Hiatella can live for over 100 years, making them some of the longest-lived clams in New England waters, with some individuals potentially witnessing more than a century of environmental changes.

children.name: Cyrtodaria
children.description: Cyrtodaria is a genus of large, elongated marine clams that live buried deep in mud and sand along cold northern coastlines. These bivalves have distinctive thin, fragile shells that cannot fully close around their soft body parts, giving them a gaping appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, Cyrtodaria shells are extremely thin and brittle, and they gape open at both ends because the large siphons cannot be fully retracted inside.
children.funFact: The propellerclam can live for over 100 years and grows continuously throughout its life, with some specimens reaching nearly a foot in length.

children.description: Rock-borers are marine clams that have developed the remarkable ability to drill into hard surfaces like rocks, wood, and shells. These bivalves use their shells like tiny jackhammers, rotating and scraping to create burrows where they live protected from predators and waves. They're found along rocky coastlines where they play an important role in slowly breaking down stone over time.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams that burrow in soft sand or mud, rock-borers have specially adapted shells with rough, file-like surfaces that allow them to mechanically bore into hard substrates. Their shells often don't close completely, with permanent gaps that accommodate their boring lifestyle.
children.funFact: Some rock-boring clams can live for over 100 years, slowly expanding their rocky homes throughout their incredibly long lives!

children.description: Rock-borers, jacknives, and razor clams are specialized burrowing bivalves that have adapted to life in sandy beaches and rocky substrates. These clams are known for their elongated, streamlined shells and powerful digging abilities that allow them to quickly burrow deep into sand or even bore into soft rock. They are filter feeders that extend siphons up to the surface to draw in water and plankton while remaining safely buried.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical round clams, members of this group have distinctly elongated, blade-like or cylindrical shells that are perfectly shaped for rapid burrowing. Their shells often gape open at both ends, and they lack the strong interlocking hinge teeth found in many other bivalve groups.
children.funFact: Atlantic razor clams can burrow so quickly into sand that they seem to vanish in seconds when disturbed, earning them the nickname 'jacknife clams' because they disappear as fast as a folding knife blade snaps shut.

children.name: Carditida
Astartidae
Astarte
children.description: Astarte is a genus of small, thick-shelled clams that live buried in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. These marine bivalves are cold-water specialists, thriving in the chilly waters of the North Atlantic where they filter tiny particles from the water for food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Astarte clams are recognized by their distinctive triangular or heart-shaped shells with prominent concentric ridges that create a sculptured appearance. Unlike many other clams, their shells are notably thick and heavy for their size.
children.funFact: Astarte clams are incredibly long-lived, with some individuals reaching over 100 years old, making them among the longest-living invertebrates in New England waters.

children.name: Isocrassina
children.description: Isocrassina is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks that includes thick-shelled clams living in coastal waters. These clams are filter feeders that burrow into sandy or muddy sediments on the ocean floor, where they pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their notably thick, heavy shells and robust build compared to other clam species. They have a distinctive rounded to oval shell shape with prominent growth rings.
children.funFact: The Chestnut Clam gets its name from its rich brown shell color, which resembles the deep reddish-brown hue of chestnuts.

children.description: Astarte clams are a family of small to medium-sized marine bivalves that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These sturdy clams have thick, heavy shells that are typically triangular or heart-shaped when viewed from the side. They are filter feeders that pump water through their shells to capture tiny food particles from the surrounding seawater.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Astarte clams can be distinguished from other clam families by their notably thick, heavy shells and their lack of a prominent gap (gape) when the shell is closed. Their shells also have a distinctive triangular outline and prominent growth lines that create a ribbed texture.
children.funFact: Some Astarte clam species can live for over 40 years, with their thick shells growing stronger and more ridged with age, making them remarkably durable survivors in harsh ocean floor environments.

children.name: Carditidae
Cyclocardia
children.description: Cyclocardia is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks commonly known as carditas. These clams have thick, heavy shells with prominent radiating ribs that give them a distinctive ridged appearance. They live buried in sandy or muddy sea floors in cold northern waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cyclocardia shells are characterized by their thick, triangular shape and strong radiating ribs that run from the hinge to the shell edge. Unlike many other clams, they have a very robust, almost rock-like shell structure.
children.funFact: The Northern Cardita can live for over 100 years, making it one of the longest-lived bivalves in New England waters.

children.description: False-cockles are marine bivalve mollusks with thick, sturdy shells that live buried in sand or mud on the ocean floor. They are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny particles of food like plankton and organic matter. These clams have strong, ridged shells that help protect them from predators and rough ocean conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: False-cockles can be distinguished from true cockles by their more elongated shell shape and different hinge structure where the two shell halves connect. Their shells also tend to be thicker and more robust than many other bivalves.
children.funFact: Despite their name, false-cockles are not closely related to true cockles at all - they got their common name simply because early naturalists thought their ridged shells looked similar to cockle shells.

children.description: Carditida is an order of marine bivalve mollusks that includes sturdy, thick-shelled clams found in cold northern waters. These clams are characterized by their robust shells with prominent ridges or ribs radiating from the hinge area. They are typically small to medium-sized and live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Carditida have distinctively thick, heavy shells with strong radial ribs or ridges that help distinguish them from other clam groups. Their shells often have a triangular or heart-shaped outline when viewed from the side.
children.funFact: Astarte clams, one of the main groups in Carditida, are so well-adapted to cold water that they're sometimes called 'Arctic clams' and can live for decades in the frigid waters of the North Atlantic.

children.name: Arcida
Arcidae
Lunarca
children.description: Lunarca is a genus of marine clams known as ark shells that live buried in sandy or muddy seafloors. These bivalves have thick, heavy shells with prominent ridges and are filter feeders that strain plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lunarca shells are distinctively thick and heavy with a boat-like or ark-like shape, and they have a long, straight hinge line with many small teeth along it.
children.funFact: The Blood Ark gets its name from its unusual red blood, which contains hemoglobin - making it one of the few clams with red blood like vertebrates.

children.name: Anadara
children.description: Anadara is a genus of ark clams, which are marine bivalve mollusks with thick, ribbed shells that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These clams are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles like plankton and organic matter. They're characterized by their distinctive boat-like or ark-shaped shells with prominent ridges running from the hinge to the outer edge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anadara clams can be distinguished from other ark clams by their relatively inflated, thick shells and their distinctive pattern of strong radial ribs. Unlike many other bivalves, they have a straight hinge line with many small teeth that interlock when the shell closes.
children.funFact: Ark clams like Anadara get their name because their boat-shaped shells reminded early naturalists of Noah's Ark, and some species can live for over 100 years while slowly growing layer upon layer of shell material.

children.description: Ark clams are marine bivalves with distinctive boat-shaped shells that often have a straight hinge line along the top. These clams are filter feeders that live buried in sand or mud, or attached to hard surfaces in coastal waters. They get their name from their resemblance to the biblical ark, with their elongated, rectangular shell shape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ark clams can be identified by their straight, long hinge line with many small teeth, and their shells are often covered with a thick, hairy outer layer called a periostracum. Unlike many other clams, they typically have unequal shell valves and may gape slightly at the ends.
children.funFact: Some ark clams can live for over 100 years and have been used by archaeologists to date ancient coastal settlements because their shells preserve well in shell middens.

children.description: Ark shells are marine bivalves with distinctively box-like or elongated shells that often have a straight hinge line. These clams are characterized by having numerous small teeth along their shell hinge, which helps them lock their two shell halves together securely. Most ark shells attach themselves to rocks or other hard surfaces using strong threads called byssal threads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clams, ark shells have a long, straight hinge with many small interlocking teeth arranged in a row. Their shells are typically more angular and less rounded than most other bivalves.
children.funFact: Some ark shells can live for over 500 years, making them among the longest-lived animals on Earth!

children.name: Solemyida
Solemyidae
Solemya
children.description: Solemya is a genus of small, elongated clams that live buried in muddy sediments in marine environments. These unusual bivalves have thin, fragile shells and are known for their symbiotic relationship with bacteria that help them obtain nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, Solemya species have a distinctive awning-like shell extension that partially covers their body, and they rely heavily on chemosynthetic bacteria rather than filter-feeding for nutrition.
children.funFact: Solemya clams can actually 'farm' sulfur-oxidizing bacteria in their gills, allowing them to thrive in low-oxygen environments where other clams cannot survive.

children.name: Petrasma
children.description: Petrasma is a genus of small marine clams that live in cold northern waters. These bivalve mollusks are filter feeders that burrow in sandy and muddy seafloors, using their shells to protect their soft bodies while they pump water through to capture tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Petrasma clams are characterized by their small, oval shells with a distinctive hinge structure and fine growth lines. They differ from other small clam genera by their specific shell proportions and the arrangement of teeth along the hinge line.
children.funFact: The Boreal Awningclam gets its common name from the tent-like appearance of its shell when viewed from the side, resembling a tiny camping shelter on the ocean floor.

children.description: Awning clams are a small family of primitive marine bivalves that live buried in muddy or sandy sediments on the ocean floor. These ancient clams have thin, fragile shells that are often covered by a dark, leathery covering called a periostracum that extends beyond the shell edges like an awning.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, awning clams lack siphons for feeding and instead pump water directly through gaps in their shells. Their shells are also notably thin and brittle compared to other bivalves.
children.funFact: Awning clams are considered living fossils, with a lineage dating back over 400 million years to the Devonian period, making them among the most ancient surviving bivalve groups.

children.description: Solemyida is an order of primitive marine clams that includes the awning clams, which are among the most ancient types of bivalve mollusks still alive today. These deep-sea dwelling clams have a distinctive elongated shell and live buried in muddy sediments on the ocean floor. They are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, awning clams have a unique shell structure with a glossy, brownish outer layer called a periostracum that extends beyond the shell edges like an awning. They also lack the complex hinge teeth found in more modern clam groups.
children.funFact: Awning clams are considered "living fossils" because their basic body plan has remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them older than the dinosaurs.

children.name: Lucinida
Lucinidae
Divalinga
children.description: Divalinga is a genus of small marine clams known as lucine clams that live buried in sandy and muddy seafloors. These bivalve mollusks have rounded, whitish shells and are filter feeders that pump water through their bodies to capture tiny food particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Divalinga clams are distinguished from other lucine clams by their distinctive cross-hatched or grid-like sculpture pattern on their shell surface, which gives them a unique textured appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Divalinga' comes from Sanskrit, reflecting the genus's distinctive two-valved shell structure that was thought to resemble certain symbolic forms in ancient cultures.

children.name: Lucinoma
children.description: Lucinoma is a genus of small, round clams that live buried in muddy or sandy ocean sediments. These bivalves have thick, white shells and are known for their ability to thrive in environments with low oxygen levels where many other clams cannot survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lucinoma clams can be identified by their distinctly thick, chalky white shells and their deeply sunken ligament area between the two shell halves.
children.funFact: These remarkable clams can survive in oxygen-poor sediments by hosting symbiotic bacteria in their gills that help them process sulfur compounds for energy.

children.description: Lucine clams are small to medium-sized bivalve mollusks that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. They have rounded, disc-like shells that are typically white or cream-colored, and they feed by filtering tiny particles from the water through specialized tubes called siphons.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clams, lucine clams have a unique circular muscle scar pattern inside their shells and often possess a distinctive fold or ridge along the shell's edge. Their shells are typically more compressed and disc-shaped compared to the oval shells of most other clam families.
children.funFact: Many lucine clams form symbiotic relationships with bacteria in their gills that help them obtain nutrients from sulfur compounds in the sediment, allowing them to thrive in low-oxygen environments where other clams cannot survive.

children.description: Lucinida is an order of marine bivalve mollusks that includes the lucine clams and their relatives. These clams are known for their distinctive circular to oval shells and their unique lifestyle of living in oxygen-poor sediments on the seafloor. They have developed special relationships with bacteria that help them survive in these challenging environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lucinida clams are distinguished by their ability to thrive in low-oxygen sediments where most other clams cannot survive. They typically have thick, white shells with a characteristic circular shape and often lack the colorful patterns found in many other bivalve groups.
children.funFact: Many lucinida clams harbor symbiotic bacteria in their gills that can convert chemicals from the sediment into food, allowing these clams to essentially 'farm' their own nutrition in nutrient-poor environments.

children.name: Nuculanida
Yoldiidae
Yoldia
children.description: Yoldia is a genus of small, elongated clams that live buried in marine sediments. These bivalve mollusks have thin, delicate shells and are typically found in deeper, colder waters where they feed by filtering nutrients from the water and sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Yoldia clams can be distinguished from other bivalves by their distinctive elongated, boat-shaped shells with a prominent pointed end called a rostrum. They also have a unique hinge structure with numerous small teeth arranged in rows.
children.funFact: File yoldia clams are sometimes called 'nut clams' and can extend long, thread-like feeding tubes called siphons that help them capture food particles while remaining safely buried in the seafloor sediment.

children.name: Megayoldia
children.description: Megayoldia is a genus of marine clams that live buried in soft sediments on the ocean floor. These bivalves have elongated, thin shells and are filter feeders that strain tiny particles of food from the water around them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Megayoldia clams are distinguished by their notably large size compared to other yoldia clams, with thin, fragile shells that have a characteristic elongated oval shape.
children.funFact: The broad yoldia can live for over 100 years, making it one of the longest-lived clam species in New England waters.

children.description: Yoldiidae are small, elongated clams that live buried in soft sediments on the ocean floor. These bivalves have thin, delicate shells and are equipped with long, thread-like feeding tentacles that they extend into the sediment to capture tiny organic particles and microorganisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams that filter food from water, yoldiids are deposit feeders that use specialized palp proboscides (feeding tentacles) to selectively pick up food particles from the seafloor sediment.
children.funFact: These ancient clams are sometimes called 'nut clams' and are considered living fossils, with their basic body plan remaining virtually unchanged for over 400 million years.

children.description: Nuculanida are a group of marine bivalve mollusks (clams) that live buried in soft sediments on the ocean floor. These small, elongated clams are filter feeders that use specialized gills to capture tiny particles of food from the water. They are commonly found in deeper waters along the Atlantic coast.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clams, nuculanids have a distinctive pointed, elongated shell shape rather than a rounded one. They also have a unique hinge structure with many small teeth arranged in rows.
children.funFact: These ancient clams have remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them true living fossils that survived multiple mass extinction events.

children.name: Pandoridae
Pandora
children.description: Pandora is a genus of small, thin-shelled marine clams that live buried in sandy or muddy seafloors. These bivalves have distinctively flattened, elongated shells that are often translucent white or pearly in appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pandora clams are easily recognized by their extremely compressed, almost paper-thin shells and their distinctive asymmetrical shape, with one shell valve being flatter than the other.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Pandora clams are efficient filter feeders that can live for many years buried several inches deep in the sediment, extending their siphons up to the surface to feed and breathe.

children.description: Pandora clams are small, flattened marine bivalves with distinctly unequal shells - one valve is notably smaller and flatter than the other. These burrowing clams live in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms, where they filter-feed on tiny particles in the water. They're part of a unique group of clams known for their asymmetrical shell design.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams that have two similarly-sized shell halves, Pandora clams have dramatically unequal valves, with the right valve being much flatter and smaller than the left. This gives them a distinctly lopsided, almost triangular appearance when viewed from the side.
children.funFact: Pandora clams are sometimes called 'spoon clams' because their flattened right valve resembles the bowl of a spoon, while the curved left valve looks like the handle.

children.name: Periplomatidae
Cochlodesma
children.description: Cochlodesma is a genus of marine bivalve mollusks commonly known as spoon clams. These clams are characterized by their elongated, somewhat cylindrical shells and their ability to burrow deep into sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. They are filter feeders that extend siphons up to the surface to draw in water containing food particles and oxygen.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spoon clams are distinguished from other burrowing clams by their distinctive spoon-shaped internal shell structures called chondrophores, which support the ligament that opens and closes the shell. Their shells are also notably more cylindrical and elongated compared to the more oval or round shells of most other clam species.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they look like spoons, spoon clams are actually named for the spoon-shaped internal structures in their shells, not their overall appearance.

children.description: Spoon clams are unusual bivalves that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. They have thin, fragile shells that don't close completely, leaving gaps that allow their long siphons to extend out for feeding and breathing.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, spoon clams have shells with a distinctive spoon-shaped projection called a chondrophore that holds part of the hinge ligament. Their shells are also notably thin and brittle compared to typical clam shells.
children.funFact: Spoon clams are sometimes called 'lantern clams' because their thin, translucent shells can glow softly when light passes through them.

children.name: Lyonsiidae
Lyonsia
children.description: Lyonsia is a genus of small, delicate marine clams known for their thin, translucent shells that give them a glass-like appearance. These bivalves are typically found burrowing in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms along the Atlantic coast. They are filter feeders that pump water through their shells to capture tiny particles of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lyonsia clams are distinguished by their extremely thin, fragile shells that are so translucent you can see through them like frosted glass. Their shells are also notably unequal in size, with one valve being slightly larger than the other.
children.funFact: The Glassy Lyonsia's shell is so thin and delicate that it's often damaged during collection, making intact specimens prized finds for shell collectors.

children.description: Lyonsia clams are small, delicate marine bivalves that live buried in soft sediments like mud and sand on the ocean floor. They have thin, fragile shells that are often translucent or pearly white in appearance. These clams are filter feeders, using their siphons to draw in water and capture tiny particles of food.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other clam families, Lyonsia clams have extremely thin, brittle shells that can be nearly transparent. Their shells are also notably asymmetrical and often have a distinctive pearly or iridescent interior surface.
children.funFact: Lyonsia clams are sometimes called 'paper clams' because their shells are so thin and delicate that they can break with just gentle handling, making them challenging specimens for shell collectors to preserve intact.

children.name: Thraciidae
Thracia
children.description: Thracia is a genus of marine clams known as spoon clams or dipper clams, characterized by their distinctive fragile, translucent shells. These burrowing bivalves live buried in sandy or muddy seafloor sediments, where they filter feed on plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Thracia clams are easily recognized by their thin, brittle shells that are often somewhat transparent or translucent, and their shells typically gape slightly at both ends even when closed.
children.funFact: The shells of Thracia clams are so delicate that they often break when the living clam is disturbed, which is why beachcombers more commonly find fragments rather than intact shells.

children.description: Lantern shells are soft-bodied marine clams that live buried in sand and mud on the ocean floor. They have thin, fragile shells that don't close completely, leaving gaps where their soft tissues extend out. These burrowing bivalves use a muscular foot to dig into sediment and feed by filtering tiny particles from the water.
