children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, lantern shells have shells that can't close tightly together, creating permanent openings. Their shells are also notably thin and translucent, giving them a delicate, almost papery appearance.
children.funFact: Lantern shells get their name from their translucent shells that can glow softly when light passes through them, resembling old-fashioned paper lanterns.

children.name: Nuculida
Nuculidae
Nucula
children.description: Nucula is a genus of small, primitive clams known as nut clams due to their rounded, nut-like shells. These marine bivalves are ancient creatures that have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years, living buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms where they feed on organic particles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nut clams have distinctive rows of small, comb-like teeth along both sides of their shell hinges, and their shells are typically smooth and shiny with a nacreous (pearl-like) interior.
children.funFact: Nucula clams are considered "living fossils" - their basic body plan has remained so successful that it's barely changed since the Ordovician Period, over 400 million years ago!

children.description: Nut clams are small marine bivalves that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean floors. They have distinctive triangular or oval shells that are often shiny and smooth, resembling tiny nuts when closed, which gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other clams, nut clams have a row of small, comb-like teeth along both edges of their shell hinge, and their shells typically have a mother-of-pearl interior lining.
children.funFact: Nut clams are considered living fossils, with some species virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them among the most ancient surviving clam lineages on Earth.

children.description: Nuculida is an order of small marine clams known as nut clams that live buried in muddy or sandy seafloor sediments. These ancient bivalves are deposit feeders, meaning they consume organic matter and bacteria from the sediment around them rather than filter-feeding from the water column like most other clams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most clams, nut clams have a row of small, comb-like teeth along the hinge of their shell and lack siphons for pumping water. They use their muscular foot to burrow and move through sediment while feeding directly on organic particles in the mud.
children.funFact: Nut clams are considered living fossils, with their basic body plan remaining virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them one of the oldest surviving groups of bivalves on Earth.

children.name: Myopsida
Loliginidae
Doryteuthis
children.description: Doryteuthis is a genus of medium-sized squid that live in coastal waters and are excellent swimmers. These squid have torpedo-shaped bodies with prominent fins running along their sides, and like all squid, they have ten arms including two longer tentacles used for catching prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their relatively long fins that extend along most of their body length, which is where the common name 'longfin' comes from. They can be distinguished from other squid by their fin shape and the specific arrangement of their tentacle hooks and suckers.
children.funFact: Longfin squid can rapidly change color and create complex patterns on their skin using specialized cells called chromatophores, allowing them to communicate with other squid and camouflage from predators.

children.name: Lolliguncula
children.description: Brief squids are small, coastal squid that live in shallow waters along the Atlantic coast. They are among the smallest squid species in New England waters, typically growing only 2-4 inches long. These active predators use their tentacles to catch small fish, shrimp, and other marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Brief squids are much smaller than other local squid species and have proportionally shorter bodies and arms. They also prefer very shallow coastal waters, unlike their larger relatives that live in deeper ocean waters.
children.funFact: Atlantic brief squid can change color rapidly using special cells called chromatophores, flashing different patterns to communicate with other squid or blend in with their surroundings.

children.description: Pencil squids are small to medium-sized squid that live in shallow coastal waters and are excellent swimmers. They have streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies with triangular fins and ten arms - eight shorter ones and two longer tentacles used for catching prey. These active predators hunt fish, crabs, and other small marine animals in nearshore environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pencil squids can be distinguished from other squid families by their relatively slender bodies, diamond-shaped fins that don't extend along the full length of their body, and their preference for shallow coastal waters rather than the open ocean.
children.funFact: Pencil squids are masters of camouflage, able to rapidly change both their color and skin texture to blend perfectly with their surroundings or communicate with other squids.

children.description: Inshore squids are a group of squid species that live in shallow coastal waters rather than the deep ocean. These cephalopods have eyes covered by a clear membrane (like a contact lens) and relatively short tentacles compared to their oceanic cousins. They're active swimmers that hunt fish and crustaceans in nearshore environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike deep-sea squids, inshore squids have corneas that completely cover their eyes, giving them better vision in brighter, shallower waters. Their bodies are also typically more elongated and streamlined for life in coastal currents.
children.funFact: Many inshore squids can rapidly change color and pattern using specialized skin cells called chromatophores, creating dazzling displays for communication and camouflage.

children.name: Octopoda
Octopodidae
Octopus
children.description: Octopus is a genus of soft-bodied marine animals known for their eight muscular arms lined with suction cups. These intelligent cephalopods have large heads, prominent eyes, and no internal skeleton, allowing them to squeeze through surprisingly small spaces. They are master camouflage artists, able to change both their color and skin texture to blend with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the genus Octopus are distinguished from other cephalopods by having exactly eight arms (rather than ten like squids) and lacking the internal shell structures found in cuttlefish. They also have a more rounded body shape compared to the elongated forms of their squid relatives.
children.funFact: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood, with two hearts pumping blood to their gills and one pumping blood to the rest of their body.

children.description: Typical octopuses are soft-bodied marine animals with eight muscular arms lined with suction cups. They have large, well-developed eyes and highly flexible bodies that lack any internal or external shell. These intelligent creatures are found in oceans worldwide, from shallow tide pools to deep sea environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other octopus families, typical octopuses have relatively short arms compared to their body size and lack specialized fins or webs between their arms. They are distinguished from squid and cuttlefish by having eight arms instead of ten appendages and no internal shell.
children.funFact: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood, with two hearts pumping blood to their gills and a third pumping blood to the rest of their body.

children.name: Argonautidae
Argonauta
children.description: Argonauts are fascinating marine cephalopods closely related to octopuses, but with one remarkable difference - the females produce delicate, paper-thin shells that they use as floating nurseries for their eggs. These graceful creatures drift through the open ocean, using their specialized arms to hold onto their beautiful spiral shells. Unlike true nautiluses, argonaut shells aren't permanently attached to their bodies and serve primarily for reproduction rather than protection.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Argonauts are distinguished from other cephalopods by the females' ability to secrete thin, white, spiral shells that they can enter and exit at will. The males are tiny and shell-less, living a completely different lifestyle than the larger, shell-bearing females.
children.funFact: Female argonauts can actually repair their delicate shells if they become damaged, secreting new shell material to patch holes or cracks.

children.description: Argonauts are a fascinating family of pelagic octopuses that live in the open ocean rather than on the seafloor like most of their relatives. The females are famous for secreting delicate, paper-thin shells that they use as portable homes and nurseries for their eggs. These beautiful spiral shells wash up on beaches around the world, often mistaken for those of ancient nautiluses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other octopuses, female argonauts produce external shells made of calcite that they can leave and re-enter at will. The males are dramatically smaller than females and lack shells entirely, living as tiny free-swimming creatures.
children.funFact: Female argonauts can actually use their shell like a submarine, trapping air inside to control their buoyancy as they rise and sink through the water column.

children.description: Octopuses are soft-bodied marine animals with eight muscular arms lined with suction cups. They are highly intelligent cephalopods known for their ability to change color and texture to blend with their surroundings. These solitary hunters use their arms to capture prey and navigate through rocky crevices on the ocean floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their cephalopod relatives, octopuses have eight arms instead of ten appendages and lack an internal shell or bone structure. They have a soft, flexible body that can squeeze through incredibly small spaces.
children.funFact: Octopuses have three hearts - two pump blood to their gills while the third pumps blood to the rest of their body, and the main heart actually stops beating when they swim, which is why they prefer crawling!

children.name: Oegopsida
Ommastrephidae
Illex
children.description: Shortfin squids are fast-swimming oceanic cephalopods with relatively short fins compared to their body length. They are active predators that hunt fish, crustaceans, and other squids in open ocean waters, using their ten arms and tentacles to capture prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike longfin squids, shortfin squids have fins that are less than half the length of their mantle (body), giving them a more torpedo-like appearance for rapid swimming.
children.funFact: Northern shortfin squids can change color almost instantly using specialized skin cells called chromatophores, flashing different patterns to communicate with each other or camouflage from predators.

children.description: Flying squids are fast-swimming oceanic squids that get their name from their ability to propel themselves out of the water and glide through the air for short distances. These sleek predators are built for speed, with streamlined bodies and powerful fins that help them chase down fish and other prey in the open ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other squid families, flying squids have particularly muscular mantles and well-developed fins that enable their unique aerial abilities. They also tend to be more elongated and torpedo-shaped than their coastal relatives.
children.funFact: Flying squids can launch themselves up to 30 feet above the water surface and glide for distances of over 150 feet, making them some of the most accomplished aerial cephalopods in the ocean.

children.description: Pelagic squids are open-ocean dwellers that spend their lives swimming freely in the water column rather than living near the seafloor. These squids have evolved specialized features for life in the vast, three-dimensional environment of the open sea. They are active hunters that can rapidly change color and often form large schools.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their bottom-dwelling relatives, pelagic squids have corneas that are not fused to their eyes, allowing their eyes to be more exposed and better adapted for spotting prey and predators in open water.
children.funFact: Some pelagic squids can actually glide above the water's surface for short distances, earning them the nickname 'flying squids' as they leap from the ocean to escape predators.

children.name: Sepiolida
Sepiolidae
Semirossia
children.description: Shining Bobtails are small, deep-water cephalopods that belong to the bobtail squid family. These tiny marine creatures have compact, rounded bodies and large eyes relative to their size, living on or near the seafloor in deeper waters off the New England coast.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their shallow-water relatives, Shining Bobtails lack the light-producing bacterial symbionts that many bobtail squids use for camouflage, instead relying on their translucent bodies and deep-water habitat for protection.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'squids,' bobtail squids like the Shining Bobtail are actually more closely related to cuttlefish and have a small internal shell remnant called a gladius.

children.description: Bobtails are small, stocky cephalopods that look like a cross between a squid and a cuttlefish. They have rounded bodies with short tentacles and typically live on or near the ocean floor, where they bury themselves in sand or mud during the day. These fascinating creatures are masters of camouflage, able to change their color and texture to blend perfectly with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their squid relatives, bobtails have much shorter, rounder bodies and lack the long fins that extend along a squid's sides. They also have a unique internal shell called a gladius that's much shorter than those found in squid.
children.funFact: Many bobtail species have a special relationship with bioluminescent bacteria that live in a light organ on their underside, helping them create a soft glow that matches moonlight filtering down through the water to avoid casting shadows that predators might spot.

children.description: Sepiolida is an order of small, rounded cephalopods commonly known as bobtail squids. These tiny marine creatures have compact, globular bodies and are among the smallest members of the squid family, typically measuring just a few centimeters in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their elongated squid relatives, bobtail squids have distinctively short, rounded bodies and lack the long tentacles typical of other cephalopods. They also have a unique internal shell called a cuttlebone that helps control their buoyancy.
children.funFact: Many bobtail squids have a symbiotic relationship with bioluminescent bacteria that live in a special light organ, allowing them to glow and blend in with moonlight filtering down from above to avoid predators.

children.name: Chitonida
Tonicellidae
Boreochiton
children.description: Boreochiton is a genus of chitons, which are marine mollusks with eight overlapping shell plates arranged along their back like armor. These flattened, oval-shaped creatures cling tightly to rocky surfaces in cold northern waters using their strong muscular foot. They feed by scraping algae and other organic matter from rocks with their rasping tongue-like radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boreochiton chitons are distinguished from other chiton genera by their relatively large size, thick shell plates, and preference for deeper, colder waters. Their girdle (the fleshy border around the shell plates) is typically covered with small scales rather than spines or hairs.
children.funFact: Despite looking like they barely move, chitons can actually 'home' back to the exact same spot on a rock after wandering around to feed, much like a limpet returning to its favorite resting place.

children.name: Tonicella
children.description: Tonicella is a genus of chitons, which are oval-shaped marine mollusks that look like armored ovals clinging to rocks. These creatures have eight overlapping shell plates on their backs that allow them to flex and curl up when disturbed. They are herbivorous grazers that scrape algae and other small organisms off rocky surfaces using a specialized feeding structure called a radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tonicella chitons are distinguished from other chiton genera by their relatively smooth, colorful shell plates and their preference for deeper, cooler waters. Their shells often display intricate patterns and vibrant colors that help them blend in with encrusted rocks.
children.funFact: When threatened, Tonicella chitons can roll up into a tight ball like a pillbug, earning them the nickname 'sea cradles' from early naturalists.

children.description: Tonicellidae are a family of chitons, which are marine mollusks with eight overlapping shell plates that look like they're wearing armor. These creatures live attached to rocks in cold ocean waters, where they slowly graze on algae and other tiny organisms using their rasping tongue-like structure called a radula.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have relatively smooth, oval-shaped shells with plates that fit tightly together, and they typically show beautiful patterns and colors on their shells that help them blend in with rocky surfaces.
children.funFact: Chitons have been called 'living fossils' because their basic body plan has remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them one of the most ancient groups of mollusks still alive today.

children.name: Chaetopleuridae
Chaetopleura
children.description: Hairy Chitons are a genus of marine mollusks that get their name from the distinctive hair-like bristles that cover their shells and surrounding girdle. These oval-shaped creatures have eight overlapping shell plates and use their muscular foot to cling tightly to rocks in the intertidal zone. They are grazers that scrape algae and other organic matter from rock surfaces using their radula, a specialized feeding organ.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike smooth chitons, members of Chaetopleura are covered in dense, hair-like bristles called chaetae that give them a fuzzy appearance. Their shell plates also tend to have more pronounced beading or sculptural patterns compared to other chiton genera.
children.funFact: When threatened or exposed at low tide, hairy chitons can curl up into a tight ball like a pill bug, protecting their soft underside while their bristly exterior helps them blend in with algae-covered rocks.

children.description: Chaetopleuridae is a family of marine mollusks commonly known as chitons or coat-of-mail shells. These fascinating creatures have eight overlapping shell plates arranged along their backs, giving them a segmented appearance like ancient armor. They live attached to rocks and other hard surfaces in coastal waters, where they graze on algae and other small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by having distinctive bristles or hairs (called chaetae) around the edges of their girdle - the fleshy band that surrounds their eight shell plates. This gives them their common name of 'hairy chitons' and helps distinguish them from other chiton families.
children.funFact: When disturbed or removed from their rock, hairy chitons can roll up into a ball like a pill bug, using their flexible shell plates to protect their soft undersides.

children.name: Ischnochitonidae
Stenosemus
children.description: Stenosemus is a genus of marine mollusks known as chitons, which are oval-shaped creatures that live attached to rocks in coastal waters. These animals have eight overlapping shell plates arranged along their backs, giving them a segmented appearance similar to a pill bug or armadillo.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Stenosemus are distinguished by their relatively narrow, elongated body shape compared to other chitons, and their distinctive white or pale coloration.
children.funFact: Chitons have been called 'living fossils' because their basic body plan has remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them one of the most ancient groups of mollusks still alive today.

children.description: Ischnochitonidae is a family of chitons, which are marine mollusks that look like flattened ovals with eight overlapping shell plates arranged along their backs. These creatures cling tightly to rocks in the intertidal zone, where they scrape algae and other small organisms from surfaces using their specialized rasping tongue called a radula. They're often called "coat-of-mail shells" because their segmented plates resemble medieval armor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished from other chitons by having relatively narrow, elongated shell plates and specific arrangements of their girdle scales (the tough, flexible border around their shells). They typically have smooth or only slightly sculptured shell surfaces compared to some of their more ornate chiton relatives.
children.funFact: When disturbed, these chitons can roll up into a tight ball like a marine armadillo, protecting their soft undersides with their hard shell plates!

children.description: Chitonida represents the most diverse order of chitons, those distinctive oval-shaped marine mollusks that look like they're wearing a suit of armor made of eight overlapping plates. These creatures are the most commonly encountered chitons along rocky shores, where they use their powerful muscular foot to clamp tightly onto rocks while grazing on algae and other small organisms with their rasping tongue.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Chitonida are distinguished from other chiton orders by having insertion plates (the parts of their shell plates that extend under the girdle) that are either solid or have just simple slits, rather than the complex pectinations found in other groups.
children.funFact: Some chitons in this order can live for over 20 years and return to the exact same spot on a rock after each nighttime foraging expedition, creating a perfectly fitted depression in the rock surface called a 'home scar.'

children.name: Dentaliida
Dentaliidae
Antalis
children.description: Antalis is a genus of tusk shells, marine mollusks that live buried in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms. These creatures have distinctive curved, tube-shaped shells that are open at both ends and resemble tiny elephant tusks. They use a muscular foot to burrow into sediment and extend feeding tentacles to capture microscopic organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mollusks, tusk shells in the genus Antalis have perfectly straight or slightly curved tubular shells with no coiling. Their shells are typically smooth and pale colored, distinguishing them from other tusk shell genera that may have ridges or different shell textures.
children.funFact: Tusk shells were once so highly valued by Pacific Northwest Indigenous peoples that they were used as currency, with longer shells being worth more than shorter ones.

children.description: Dentaliidae is a family of marine mollusks commonly known as tusk shells or tooth shells. These creatures live in elongated, curved, tube-like shells that are open at both ends and burrow in sandy or muddy ocean bottoms with their pointed end sticking up into the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mollusks, tusk shells have a distinctive curved, hollow shell that resembles an elephant's tusk or a tiny horn. They lack eyes and gills, instead using specialized thread-like structures called captacula to capture food particles.
children.funFact: Tusk shells have been used as currency and jewelry by indigenous peoples for thousands of years, with some Native American tribes considering them more valuable than gold.

children.description: Dentaliida is an order of marine mollusks commonly known as tusk shells or tooth shells. These creatures live buried in sandy or muddy ocean floors with only the tip of their curved, tube-like shell protruding above the sediment. They use thread-like tentacles called captacula to capture tiny organisms and particles of food from the surrounding water and sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mollusks, tusk shells have a distinctive curved, tubular shell that is open at both ends and resembles an elephant's tusk or a hollow tooth. They lack eyes, gills, and a heart, making them quite different from their snail and clam relatives.
children.funFact: Native American tribes along the Pacific Coast once used tusk shells as a form of currency, with longer shells being more valuable than shorter ones.
